## **Sanctuary Setting**

## <span id="page-38-1"></span><span id="page-38-0"></span>*Overview*

American Samoa is an unincorporated territory of the United States consisting of the eastern part of the Samoan archipelago, located in the south-central Pacific Ocean.

--- SENTENCE 448 ---
It is located approximately 2,600 km northeast of New Zealand and 3,500 km southwest of Hawai'i.

--- SENTENCE 449 ---
American Samoa includes the inhabited islands of Tutuila and Aunu'u, as well as the Manu'a islands (Ta'u, Olosega, and Ofu).

--- SENTENCE 450 ---
Additional islands in the territory include Rose Atoll, an uninhabited coral atoll, and Swains Island, a formerly inhabited coral atoll.

--- SENTENCE 451 ---
The capital of American Samoa is Pago Pago, located on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 452 ---
In 2020, the population of American Samoa was 49,710 (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021), with the majority of residents living on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 453 ---
The total land area is 199 km<sup>2</sup> , slightly larger than the size of Washington, D.C.

--- SENTENCE 454 ---
American Samoa is the southernmost territory in the U.S. and one of two U.S. territories south of the Equator (the other is the uninhabited Jarvis Island; ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 455 ---
National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa (NMSAS) is composed of six protected areas covering 13,581 mi<sup>2</sup> of marine habitat that includes nearshore coral reef, deep-sea, and pelagic areas across the Samoan archipelago (Figure SS.1).

--- SENTENCE 456 ---
It was formerly known as Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary, established in 1986 to protect 0.25 mi<sup>2</sup> of coral reef habitat in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 457 ---
In 2012, the sanctuary expanded to include Fagalua/Fogama'a on Tutuila Island, as well as areas surrounding Aunu'u, Ta'u, and Swains Island, and Muliāva, a unit that overlays Rose Atoll Marine National Monument and includes nearby Vailulu'u Seamount.

--- SENTENCE 458 ---
NMSAS is located in the cradle of Polynesia's oldest culture.

--- SENTENCE 459 ---
It is home to a great diversity of marine life, including corals and other invertebrates, fish, turtles, marine plants, and marine mammals.

--- SENTENCE 460 ---
It also includes some of the oldest and largest *Porites* coral colonies in the world, along with deep-sea coral and sponge habitats, an undersea volcano, and important fishing grounds.

!

--- SENTENCE 461 ---
** NMSAS is comprised of six protected areas (Fagatele Bay, Fagalua/Fogama'a, Aunu'u, Ta'u, Swains Island, and Muliāva), covering 13,581 mi<sup>2</sup> of marine habitats, including nearshore coral reef, deep-sea, and pelagic areas across the Samoan archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 462 ---
Image: NOAA

## <span id="page-39-0"></span>*Designation of the Sanctuary*

In 1982

--- SENTENCE 463 ---
, the governor of American Samoa proposed Fagatele Bay to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) as a candidate for national marine sanctuary designation.

--- SENTENCE 464 ---
After a lengthy public process, Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary was designated on April 29, 1986 by an act of Congress.

--- SENTENCE 465 ---
Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary became part of American Samoa's conservation strategy, which includes the National Park of American Samoa and a community-based marine protected area program coordinated by the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR; Raynal et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 466 ---
On January 6, 2009, President George W. Bush established Rose Atoll Marine National Monument under the Antiquities Act (Proc. 8337, 74 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 467 ---
The proclamation ordered the Department of Commerce to initiate a process to add the marine areas of the monument to Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 468 ---
In 2008, NOAA initiated a process to expand Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 469 ---
The Office of National Marine Sanctuaries (ONMS) worked closely with the American Samoan government and local communities, who wanted to protect these special places for future generations, to evaluate areas for proposed inclusion in the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 470 ---
Through a series of public meetings, public input on the proposed areas was solicited and reviewed based on the metrics of ecological, cultural,

and scientific importance.

--- SENTENCE 471 ---
Eventually, from an initial list of 11 proposed sites, five areas were selected for final evaluation: Swains Island, Ta'u, Aunu'u, Fagalua/Fogama'a, and Muliāva.

--- SENTENCE 472 ---
On July 26, 2012, a draft management plan and draft environmental impact statement were published, adding five new areas to the existing Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary, for a total of six discrete management units; the name of the sanctuary was changed to National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa (77 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 473 ---
NOAA also amended existing sanctuary regulations and applied these regulations to activities in the expanded sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 474 ---
These final regulations took effect on October 15, 2012 (77 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 475 ---
NOAA co-manages the sanctuary with the American Samoa government and works closely with local communities to support Samoan cultural traditions and practices.

## <span id="page-40-0"></span>*Fa'a Samoa: The Samoan Way*

American Samoans hold on to ancient traditions tightly (U.S. Department of Labor, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 476 ---
Despite decades of foreign influence, most Samoans are still fluent in their native language and practice Fa'a Samoa, the traditional communal Samoan lifestyle, or way of life.

--- SENTENCE 477 ---
Fa'a Samoa is the foundation of Polynesia's oldest culture—dating back 3,000 years.

--- SENTENCE 478 ---
It emphasizes reciprocity rather than individual accumulation, and similarly, prestige is gained through generous distribution (not accumulation) of wealth.

--- SENTENCE 479 ---
While it holds on to these traditions, Samoan culture has inherent flexibility, allowing ceremonial and traditional customs to be modified to suit modern situations (U.S. Department of Commerce, 1984).

--- SENTENCE 480 ---
One key factor in the integrity of Samoan culture is the endurance of the Samoan language.

--- SENTENCE 481 ---
Samoan is spoken in the workplace, including in the NMSAS offices and the American Samoa government.

--- SENTENCE 482 ---
Samoans take pride in the tenets of respect, humility, and service as guiding principles of their culture.

--- SENTENCE 483 ---
In this regard, as a courtesy and sign of respect, permission from families is required to cross or enter family lands.

--- SENTENCE 484 ---
This includes beach areas that may be access points to NMSAS (Figure SS.2).

!

--- SENTENCE 485 ---
Reaching Fagatele Bay from Futiga requires permission, and sometimes a fee, from the local family.

--- SENTENCE 486 ---
The site warden is responsible for unlocking the gate at the entrance to the Fagatele Bay Trail, which traverses private family land.

--- SENTENCE 487 ---
Photo: Nerelle Que Moffitt/NOAA

NMSAS staff place a high value on partnerships with sanctuary communities and maintain great respect for Fa'a Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 488 ---
The relationship between sanctuary staff and the matai (chiefs) is critical to successful resource management.

--- SENTENCE 489 ---
The American Samoa Office of Samoan Affairs helps facilitate the sanctuary's community consultations in a culturally appropriate manner that is respectful of Fa'a Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 490 ---
This includes consultations at saofa'iga a le nu'u (village council meeting) and individual matai (ONMS, 2012).

## <span id="page-41-0"></span>*Human Settlement and Political History*

Human history in American Samoa dates back about 3,000 years (Craig, 2009;

--- SENTENCE 491 ---
Linnekin et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 492 ---
Polynesian culture developed following the voyaging discovery and settlement of the Fiji/Tonga/Samoa region.

--- SENTENCE 493 ---
The settlement of the Pacific Islands millennia ago was guided by ancient seafarer navigation using the stars and other natural cues and observations—a vehicle for cultural renewal and pride to this day.

--- SENTENCE 494 ---
This voyaging and settlement of the Pacific has been called the greatest ocean-borne human migration in history.

--- SENTENCE 495 ---
The first European contact with American Samoa occurred in 1722 (Davidson, 1969;

--- SENTENCE 496 ---
Linnekin et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 497 ---
The subsequent wave of outside visitors included European missionaries and explorers.

--- SENTENCE 498 ---
The Wilkes Expedition from the U.S. in 1839 conducted the first systematic natural history and cultural surveys of Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 499 ---
This expedition, along with the arrival of Christian missionaries, established Western influence over Samoan society that continues today (Figure SS.3).

!

--- SENTENCE 500 ---
** Fagatogo (Tutuila) during the time of European settlement.

--- SENTENCE 501 ---
Note the pile of coal stored on the beach.

--- SENTENCE 502 ---
Image: De Olivares, 1899

During the 1800s, three colonial powers, Germany, England, and the U.S., laid claim to the Samoan Islands, nearly coming to war before signing a tripartite agreement in 1899 that granted control of Upolu and Savai'i to Germany and control of Tutuila, Aunu'u, and Manu'a to the U.S.

--- SENTENCE 503 ---
That year, the U.S. Department of the Navy assumed administration of "Tutuila Station" (Enright et al., 1997; Figure SS.4).

--- SENTENCE 504 ---
The family chiefs, or matais, of Tutuila and Aunu'u ceded these islands to the U.S. on April 17, 1900.

--- SENTENCE 505 ---
Tui Manu'a and other Manu'a chiefs ceded the Manu'a islands to the U.S. four years later on July 16, 1904.

--- SENTENCE 506 ---
Several years later, the Navy began to refer to the region as "American Samoa" (Linnekin et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 507 ---
On March 4, 1925, Olohega, or Swains Island, was annexed by the U.S. and became part of American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 508 ---
In 1951, per Executive Order 10264, administration of American Samoa transferred from the Department of the Navy to the Department of the Interior (DOI).

Today, American Samoa is an unincorporated, unorganized, and self-governing territory of the U.S. and remains administered by the DOI Office of Insular Affairs.

--- SENTENCE 509 ---
Congress gave plenary authority over the territory to the President of the U.S., who then delegated that authority to the DOI.

--- SENTENCE 510 ---
The Secretary of the Interior enabled American Samoans to draft a constitution, under which the American Samoa government functions (Office of Insular Affairs, 2010; U.S. Department of Labor, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 511 ---
Individuals born in American Samoa are classified as U.S. nationals rather than full citizens.

--- SENTENCE 512 ---
Consequently, they cannot vote in national elections, but have freedom of entry into the U.S. American Samoa has had an elected, non-voting member of Congress in the U.S. House of Representatives since 1981 (U.S. Department of Labor, 2007).

!

--- SENTENCE 513 ---
Tutuila Naval Station in 1900 (left) and Fagatele Bay (right).

--- SENTENCE 514 ---
Images: American Samoa Office of Archives and Records Management

## <span id="page-42-0"></span>*Commerce*

Today, the territorial government and tuna processing plants are the territory's largest employers and the mainstay of the economy.

--- SENTENCE 515 ---
The government employs 36.9% of the local workforce (American Samoa Department of Commerce

--- SENTENCE 516 ---
Two large U.S. tuna canneries once formed the basis of an industry that employed more than 3,000 Samoan and foreign workers.

--- SENTENCE 517 ---
In 2016, one of the canneries closed due to economic difficulties.

--- SENTENCE 518 ---
The industry has also struggled due to staffing and supply chain issues associated with the COVID-19 pandemic.

--- SENTENCE 519 ---
International fishing fleets supply catches to the canneries for export, while smallscale artisanal fisheries supply fish to local markets.

--- SENTENCE 520 ---
Retail trade and services dominate the rest of the territory's economy.

--- SENTENCE 521 ---
Small-scale agriculture on the islands of American Samoa mainly supply local markets.

--- SENTENCE 522 ---
The most important crops include taro, coconuts, bananas, citrus fruits, pineapples, papayas, breadfruit, and yams.

--- SENTENCE 523 ---
Tourism is not well developed in American Samoa, with only a handful of small hotels on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 524 ---
However, short visits by cruise ships periodically supplement the economy.

--- SENTENCE 525 ---
Cruise traffic ceased during the 2019 measles outbreak and COVID-19 pandemic.

## <span id="page-43-0"></span>*Geology*

The Samoan archipelago's geologic features are the result of plate tectonics, volcanism, and reef accretion.

--- SENTENCE 526 ---
The archipelago is 124 mi north of the convergence of the Australian and Pacific plates.

--- SENTENCE 527 ---
A geologic hotspot (a stationary source of molten rock) located 31 mi east of Ta'u created the main islands in the archipelago as the Pacific Plate moved over the hotspot in a westwardly direction at about three in yr-1 (Craig, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 528 ---
Consequently, the age of the islands increases to the west (Thornberry-Ehrlich, 2008).

--- SENTENCE 529 ---
Tutuila is about 1.5 million years old, Ofu and Olosega are about 300,000 years old, and Ta'u is about 100,000 years old (Brainard et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 530 ---
Vailulu'u seamount, which sits on top of the Samoan hotspot, has recently grown due to volcanic activity (Staudigel et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 531 ---
Swains Island and Rose Atoll arose from much older volcanoes and are geologically separate from the Samoan volcanic chain (Hart et al., 2004).

## <span id="page-43-1"></span>*Climate*

The climate of American Samoa is characterized by warm, relatively stable air temperatures, variable precipitation, high humidity, predominant southeast tradewinds, and periodic tropical cyclone activity (ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 532 ---
Rainfall and tradewinds in American Samoa are influenced by the South Pacific Convergence Zone, a low-pressure area that seasonally moves over and around the archipelago, resulting in a long rainy season from October–May and a slightly cooler and drier period with higher southeasterly trade wind activity from June–September (Finucane et al., 2012; ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 533 ---
Average air temperature is 80.6°

--- SENTENCE 534 ---
F (1967–2020) and has been increasing (Keener et al., 2021).

--- SENTENCE 535 ---
Average monthly mean sea surface temperatures range from 82–84°F (Coral Reef Watch, 2021).

--- SENTENCE 536 ---
The Pacific Islands region experiences high inter-annual and inter-decadal climate variability as a result of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), and the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO; Finucane et al., 2012; ONMS, 2012; Cheng & Gaskin, 2011).

--- SENTENCE 537 ---
ENSO events, including La Niña (cold phase) and El Niño (warm phase), influence a variety of regional climate factors, such as tradewind activity, rainfall, storm tracks, ocean temperature, and sea level (Finucane et al., 2012; ONMS, 2012).

## <span id="page-43-2"></span>*Currents, Tides, and Waves*

Ocean currents transport, among other things, nutrients, marine life, heat, oxygen, and carbon dioxide.

--- SENTENCE 538 ---
At the broadest scale, the Samoan archipelago lies along the northern edge of the South Pacific Gyre, a series of connected ocean currents with a counterclockwise flow that spans the Pacific basin (Alory & Delcroix, 1999; Tomczak & Godfrey, 2003; Craig, 2009; Figure SS.5).

--- SENTENCE 539 ---
At a regional scale centered on the Samoan archipelago, the major surface currents and eddies that affect the archipelago are the westward flowing South Equatorial Current, which occurs all year

between 5 and 15 °S; the South Equatorial Counter Current, which interrupts the South Equatorial Current between 9 and 12 °S during the summer; and the Tonga Trench Eddy, which regularly occurs between September and December south of the archipelago (Kendall & Poti, 2011).

--- SENTENCE 540 ---
Of these, the South Equatorial Counter Current is the most prominent current feature in the region, occurring at approximately 200 m depth, and is strongest in January and February (Kessler & Taft, 1987; Chen & Qiu, 2004).

--- SENTENCE 541 ---
In addition to surface currents, deep-sea currents play an important role in regulating conditions in the deep sea.

--- SENTENCE 542 ---
American Samoa lies along the Pacific Meridional Overturning Circulation (Voet et al., 2015), commonly referred to as the global ocean conveyor belt.

--- SENTENCE 543 ---
The Circumpolar Deep Water flow is a deep thermohaline current that originates in Antarctica and flows past American Samoa along the Kermadec and Tonga Trenches before entering a region known as the Samoan Passage, just north of the exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

--- SENTENCE 544 ---
This current carries oxygen and nutrients to deep-sea areas and is believed to be an important dispersal mechanism for deep-sea species across the tropical central Pacific.

!

--- SENTENCE 545 ---
** Major surface currents of the Southern Pacific Ocean.

--- SENTENCE 546 ---
EEZs of Samoa and American Samoa are outlined in the center of the map.

--- SENTENCE 547 ---
Image: Kendall & Poti, 2011

#### Sanctuary Setting

Tides in the archipelago consist of two daily highs and lows with a mean range of 0.78 m (as measured at Pago Pago) and extremes of 0.9 m and -0.84 m (NOAA, 2022) during king tides and ENSO events.

--- SENTENCE 548 ---
Tides may influence nearshore currents.

--- SENTENCE 549 ---
Extreme high tides may flood lowlying areas and extreme low tides can expose reef flat areas to the air.

--- SENTENCE 550 ---
NOAA maintains one tidal station in American Samoa, located within Pago Pago harbor.

--- SENTENCE 551 ---
Wave height and power are highest on average on the eastern- and southern-facing coasts of the Samoan islands, but can vary seasonally and among years (Barstow & Haug, 1994).

--- SENTENCE 552 ---
Seasonally, ocean swells from the south are highest during May–September (2–3 m wave height is common) due to the increased intensity and frequency of the trade winds at higher latitudes (Barstow & Haug, 1994; Brainard et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 553 ---
November–March is a period often characterized by shorter-period waves, lower wave heights (about 2 m), and more variable directionality (Brainard et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 554 ---
Large anomalous wave events occur when cyclones pass (e.g., wave heights greater than 8 m were recorded during Cyclone Ofa in 1990 and Cyclone Heta in 2004).

--- SENTENCE 555 ---
Storms in the north Pacific can even cause unusually large swells on the typically calmer northern coasts of the islands (Barstow & Haug 1994;

--- SENTENCE 556 ---
Brainard et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 557 ---
## <span id="page-45-0"></span>*Habitat and Living Resources*

American Samoa is an oceanic archipelago with a small insular shelf.

--- SENTENCE 558 ---
Therefore, shallow-water habitats, such as rocky shore, reef flat, and coral reef, generally only occur within 0.5 to 2 mi from shore because of the steep slope of the seafloor (Craig, 2009; Figure SS.6).

--- SENTENCE 559 ---
Pelagic (openocean) waters constitute the primary habitat within the archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 560 ---
NMSAS also includes banks, deep ocean floor habitats, hydrothermal vents, and seamounts.

--- SENTENCE 561 ---
Nearshore benthic (bottom) habitats include coral reefs (reef flats and reef slopes); seagrass beds; mangrove forests; and sandy, hard bottom, and rubble substrates in the subtidal and intertidal zones (see Fenner et al., 2008a; Brainard et al., 2008; Kendall & Poti, 2011 for habitat characterizations and benthic habitat maps for the entire archipelago).

--- SENTENCE 562 ---
Each sanctuary unit contains shallow coral reefs (<30 m) and mesophotic reefs (30–150 m), with Aunu'u containing the largest area of known bottomfish habitat, and Fagatele Bay and Fagalua/Fogama'a containing submarine canyons.

--- SENTENCE 563 ---
The Muliāva unit contains the greatest area of pelagic and deepsea habitat, including Vailulu'u and Malulu seamounts (ONMS, 2012).

!

### **Intertidal**

Intertidal habitats in NMSAS include rocky cliffs and terraces, caves, beaches, and reef flats.

--- SENTENCE 569 ---
These habitats experience frequent changes from tidal and wave action.

--- SENTENCE 570 ---
Rocky intertidal fauna include limpets, chitons, blennies, and crabs that have specialized features to help them survive in these dynamic environments.

--- SENTENCE 571 ---
Seabirds and shorebirds may also use these areas for resting and foraging.

--- SENTENCE 572 ---
Intertidal reef flat areas and tide pools have more diversity and may support corals, macroalgae, fish, and a wide variety of invertebrates, but community development is limited by low tide exposure and is at elevated risk from disturbance events like cyclones and large waves.

### **Coral Reefs**

Coral reef ecosystems extend from sea level to a depth of approximately 150 m and include both shallow coral reefs (SCRs; <30 m) and mesophotic coral ecosystems (MCEs; 30–150 m; Figure SS.7).

--- SENTENCE 573 ---
Shallow coral reefs are some of the most diverse habitats on the planet.

--- SENTENCE 574 ---
Within NMSAS,

#### Sanctuary Setting

fringing coral reefs extend from shore, often including reef flat terraces and shallow reef crests where waves break, and create extensive fore reef slope habitats (Table SS.1).

--- SENTENCE 575 ---
These reefs house a high diversity of framework-building species, such as scleractinian corals and coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 576 ---
Below 30 m, light is diminished and the species composition shifts to corals, sponges, and algae that can tolerate low light conditions.

--- SENTENCE 577 ---
Recent work suggests that MCEs in American Samoa have distinct coral community assemblages compared to shallow reefs (Montgomery et al., 2019).

--- SENTENCE 578 ---
Both SCRs and MCEs serve as essential fish habitat for some economically and ecologically important fish species, which use these areas for spawning, breeding, feeding, and growth to maturity.

--- SENTENCE 579 ---
Approximately 2,700 species have been documented on the reefs of American Samoa (Fenner et al., 2008a), but the actual number is likely much higher as sampling has been limited, particularly for invertebrates.

A diver surveys the mesophotic habitat in NMSAS at a depth of approximately 90 m. Photo: Daniel Wagner/NOAA

A total of 342 stony coral species are currently considered present or possibly present in American Samoa (Montgomery et al., 2019; Figure SS.8).

--- SENTENCE 588 ---
Corals are part of the phylum Cnidaria, and are related to jellyfish.

--- SENTENCE 589 ---
Coral colonies are made up of a collection of individual modules known as polyps.

--- SENTENCE 590 ---
Living coral tissue secretes calcium carbonate to build the colony's skeleton.

--- SENTENCE 591 ---
The slowest growing corals grow at a rate of 0.5–2.5 cm yr-1 and the fastest can grow up to 20 cm yr-1 (Gladfelter et al., 1978).

--- SENTENCE 592 ---
Growth rates vary with light, temperature, nutrients, and aragonite saturation state (the measure of available calcium carbonate ions in seawater).

--- SENTENCE 593 ---
Corals may extend their tentacles to actively feed on plankton in the water column, however in most shallow reef habitats, suspension feeding does not supply enough energy to sustain coral growth.

--- SENTENCE 594 ---
Instead, corals rely on a highly productive symbiotic relationship with a type of singlecelled algae called zooxanthellae.

--- SENTENCE 595 ---
These algae live inside the coral polyps, converting sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into food for the coral.

--- SENTENCE 596 ---
Most stony corals above a depth of 100–200 m have zooxanthellae.

--- SENTENCE 597 ---
This relationship is sensitive to temperature, and most reef building corals prefer temperatures between 73–84°F.

--- SENTENCE 598 ---
If temperatures exceed a coral's preferred range for too long, the coral may expel the algae in a process known as coral bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 599 ---
The combined loss of the algae and heat stress may result in death if temperatures exceed a coral's temperature threshold for too long or if the temperature exceeds the coral's thermal tolerance.

!

--- SENTENCE 600 ---
A coral reef at Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 601 ---
Photo: Wendy Cover/NOAA

Algae found on the coral reefs in American Samoa include zooxanthellae, microalgae, macroalgae, filamentous algae (turf), and coralline algae (both crustose and branching forms).

--- SENTENCE 602 ---
Algae play different roles in ecosystem function and are important to the coral reef environment.

--- SENTENCE 603 ---
Macroalgae and filamentous algae provide food for herbivorous fish and shelter for juvenile fish and invertebrates, but also compete for space with corals.

--- SENTENCE 604 ---
Skelton and South (2007) described 243 species of benthic macroalgae in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 605 ---
Since their extensive survey, further species have been identified (e.g., Kraft & Saunders, 2014).

--- SENTENCE 606 ---
While corals are the primary reef builders on coral reefs, other calcifiers, such as crustose coralline algae (CCA), are also very important to the ecosystem because they bind the reef together (Skelton, 2003; Craig, 2009) and provide substrate for settlement of coral larvae (Craig, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 607 ---
Rose Atoll is known for its high CCA cover, which gives its slopes an incredible purple coloration.

--- SENTENCE 608 ---
The distinctive CCA formations on the reef slopes at Rose Atoll are not common elsewhere in American Samoa (Figure SS.9).

!

--- SENTENCE 609 ---
** Purple CCA formations at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 610 ---
Photo: Mareike Sudek/NOAA

Coral reefs in American Samoa provide habitat for over 900 species of reef fish (Wass, 1984; Montgomery et al., 2019) and over 1,000 known invertebrate species (ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 611 ---
This includes a variety of species harvested for food, such as surgeonfish, jacks, snappers, parrotfish, groupers, lobsters, octopus, sea cucumbers, and giant clams.

--- SENTENCE 612 ---
Fish and invertebrate biomass is generally higher in the more remote islands, presumably due to less human fishing pressure.

--- SENTENCE 613 ---
Large fish like reef sharks, humphead wrasse, and groupers are rare throughout the territory (Fenner et al., 2008a).

--- SENTENCE 614 ---
The lagoon at Rose Atoll was known for an exceptionally high density of giant clams (Green & Craig, 1999), but those numbers have declined precipitously in recent years (B. Peck/FWS, personal communication, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 615 ---
Endangered green and hawksbill sea turtles are found on reefs throughout the territory.

--- SENTENCE 616 ---
Coral reefs also serve as resting areas for resident spinner dolphin pods, and humpback whales with newborn calves are frequently observed near reefs from June to November.

--- SENTENCE 617 ---
## **Pelagic Zone**

Most of American Samoa's marine habitat is pelagic.

--- SENTENCE 618 ---
Even though the pelagic habitat consists entirely of water hundreds of kilometers wide and thousands of meters deep, it should not be considered to lack structure and associated ecosystem zones.

--- SENTENCE 619 ---
There are four distinct zones: epipelagic (<200 m), mesopelagic (200–1,000 m), bathypelagic (1000–4,000 m), and abyssopelagic (<4,000 m).

--- SENTENCE 620 ---
Pelagic species are closely associated with their physical and chemical environments, and thus, their habitat range and distribution may be significantly altered by oceanographic variability, like ENSO events.

--- SENTENCE 621 ---
Some organisms migrate through pelagic zones, or between pelagic and benthic habitats, during life cycle phases.

--- SENTENCE 622 ---
Others are found in different zones during different activities such as migration, foraging, and reproduction (Garrison, 1999).

--- SENTENCE 623 ---
The epipelagic zone is highly dynamic, affected by the South Equatorial Current and the South Equatorial Countercurrent, which display seasonal and interannual variability.

--- SENTENCE 624 ---
These currents, and their resultant eddies, are affected by ENSO events (Domokos et al., 2007; Domokos, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 625 ---
Only 45 pelagic fish species have been identified in this zone (Wass, 1984), including important pelagic fishery targets such as albacore (*Thunnus alalunga*) and yellowfin tuna (*T. obesus),* blue marlin (*Makaira nigricans*), wahoo (*Acanthocybium solandri*), masimasi (*Coryphaena hippurus*), and skipjack tuna (*Katsuwonus pelamis*).

--- SENTENCE 626 ---
Seabirds forage in these upper layers and some marine mammals spend most of their time in this zone.

--- SENTENCE 627 ---
Thirteen species of marine mammals have been observed in American Samoan waters (Craig, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 628 ---
This includes two mysticetes (baleen whales): humpback and minke whale (Utzurrum et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 629 ---
In addition, 11 odontocetes (toothed cetaceans) are found in American Samoa: sperm whale, killer whale, short finned pilot whale, common bottlenose dolphin, spinner dolphin, pantropical spotted dolphin, striped dolphin, rough toothed dolphin, Cuvier's beaked whale, dwarf sperm whale, and false killer whale (Utzurrum et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 630 ---
Each year, from July–October, humpback whales use the waters around American Samoa for breeding and calving (Lindsey et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 631 ---
The darker mesopelagic zone is a haven during the daylight hours for micronekton that comprise the deep scattering layer (small fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods), but these animals migrate to the epipelagic zone each night to feed on phytoplankton and smaller zooplankton found there (Domokos et al., 2007).

--- SENTENCE 632 ---
Little is known about the bathypelagic and abyssopelagic zones in American Samoa.

### **Seamounts and Deep Sea**

Deep ocean benthic habitats include hard, soft, and biogenic habitats at water depths below 150 m; these are by far the largest benthic habitat by area in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 633 ---
Soft sediments are mostly mud and sand, and are generally low in biological productivity.

--- SENTENCE 634 ---
Deep-sea corals are found on hard bottom substrate in dark waters, where temperatures range from 4–12°C.

--- SENTENCE 635 ---
For this reason, these corals are known as cold-water or deep-sea corals.

--- SENTENCE 636 ---
Cold-water corals are also part of the taxonomic group Cnidaria, and are related to shallow corals.

--- SENTENCE 637 ---
However, these corals lack the symbiotic algae that live in the tissues of shallow corals.

--- SENTENCE 638 ---
Instead, cold-water corals feed by waiting for small food particles to flow past, then use their stinging cells to capture them.

--- SENTENCE 639 ---
They also provide habitat for other species.

--- SENTENCE 640 ---
Radiocarbon dating of deep-sea corals suggests that they may live for thousands of years (Roark et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 641 ---
Deep-sea habitats have been poorly studied in American Samoa, but recent exploratory work indicates that deep-sea coral and sponge communities serve as fish habitat and are hotspots of biodiversity.

--- SENTENCE 642 ---
The deep NMSAS units support a diverse biological community that includes deep-sea corals, crinoids, octocorals, and sponges (Kennedy et al., 2019; Deep Sea Coral Research and Technology Program [DSCRTP], 2020).

--- SENTENCE 643 ---
Biological hotspots may be found on ridgelines, near hydrothermal vents, and around seamounts.

--- SENTENCE 644 ---
Seamounts are underwater volcanic mountains that rise from the seafloor and occur throughout all ocean basins (Wessel et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 645 ---
Generally, seamounts are highly productive and support a rich biodiversity of organisms.

--- SENTENCE 646 ---
Some species of bottomfish found on seamounts are important to commercial fisheries, such as snappers (Lutjanidae), groupers (Serranidae), jacks (Carangidae), and emperors (Lethrinidae).

--- SENTENCE 647 ---
Most bottomfish are associated with hard substrates, holes, ledges, or caves, and are not believed to migrate between isolated seamounts.

--- SENTENCE 648 ---
In comparison, highly migratory species, including bigeye and yellowfin tuna, traverse across the entire south Pacific basin, and are also attracted to geological features such as seamounts and islands (Morato et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 649 ---
There are 48 documented seamounts within the American Samoa EEZ (Kendall & Poti, 2011) rising from as deep as 4,000 m (Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council

--- SENTENCE 650 ---
Vailulu'u Seamount (Figure SS.10) is located between Manu'a and Rose Atoll and is the only hydrothermally active seamount within the EEZ (Koppers et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 651 ---
Discovered in 1975 and first mapped in 1999, Vailulu'u sits atop the active volcanic hotspot that created the Samoan archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 652 ---
The caldera of Vailulu'u has risen and collapsed repeatedly over time and currently sits at about 708 m below the water's surface.

--- SENTENCE 653 ---
Between 2001 and 2005, a new cone formed in the middle of the crater and was named Nafanua (after the Samoan goddess of war).

--- SENTENCE 654 ---
Researchers have estimated that if activity continues at the observed rate, the seamount could eventually breach the surface within decades, forming a new island in the Samoan island chain (Staudigel et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 655 ---
Vailulu'u supports a diverse biological community including polychaetes, crinoids, octocorals, sponges, and cutthroat eels (Staudigel et al., 2006).

--- SENTENCE 656 ---
Malulu Seamount is located near Vailulu'u, but much less is known about this seamount.

--- SENTENCE 657 ---
It is very deep, extending from 2,400 m to 4,800 m in depth (Seamount Biogeosciences Network, 2022).

!

--- SENTENCE 658 ---

## <span id="page-53-0"></span>*Maritime Heritage Resources*

Maritime heritage resources can provide insight on specific portions of American Samoan history and serve as windows to the past, though few specific surveys for heritage sites have been conducted.

--- SENTENCE 663 ---
In general, known and potential maritime heritage resources in American Samoa fall into five categories:

- 1.

--- SENTENCE 664 ---
Historical shipwrecks—35 reported lost; two located/assessed
- 2.

--- SENTENCE 665 ---
World War II naval aircraft—43 lost between 1942–1944; none located
- 3.

--- SENTENCE 666 ---
World War II fortifications, gun emplacements, and coastal pillboxes—multiple sites assessed, but none reported in NMSAS
- 4. Archaeological sites—more than fifty coastal/nearshore archaeological sites or features were identified following the 2009 tsunami, including coastal settlements, stone tool manufacturing sites, and isolated artifact scatters (Addison et al., 2010)
- 5.

--- SENTENCE 667 ---
Marine/coastal natural resources associated with the legends and folklore of American Samoa—described by the American Samoa Historic Preservation Office as sites "of extraordinary significance to Samoan culture" (Volk et al., 1992, p. 32)

## <span id="page-53-1"></span>*Sanctuary Units*

The sanctuary includes six discrete units that have unique habitats and varying regulations (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 668 ---
These units are Fagatele Bay, Fagalua/Fogama'a, Aunu'u, Ta'u, Swains Island, and Muliāva.

## **Fagatele Bay**

The Fagatele Bay unit is a 0.65 km<sup>2</sup> coastal embayment that extends from Fagatele Point to Steps Point along the southwestern coast of Tutuila Island (Figure SS.11, Figure SS.12).

--- SENTENCE 669 ---
This naturally protected bay was formed by a collapsed volcanic crater and is surrounded by steep, forested cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 670 ---
It was designated as a national marine sanctuary in 1986 to protect its extensive coral reef ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 671 ---
In 2012, Fagatele Bay was declared a no-take marine protected area (ONMS, 2012), and as such, fishing and other extractive uses are not allowed.

--- SENTENCE 672 ---
Activities that are allowed include non-extractive research, education, and recreation (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 673 ---
The shore of Fagatele Bay was the site of a historical coastal village from prehistoric times to the 1950s, but at present, no human settlement exists near the shoreline.

!

--- SENTENCE 674 ---
The Fagatele Bay and Fagalua/Fogama'a units are located on the island of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 675 ---
Aunu'u is approximately 1.9 km southeast of Tutuila and includes two zones—a Multiple Use Zone (A) and a Research Zone (B).

--- SENTENCE 676 ---
Image: Tony Reyer/NOAA

!

--- SENTENCE 677 ---
In 1986, NOAA established Fagatele Bay as a national marine sanctuary in order to protect and preserve the 0.65 km<sup>2</sup> of coral reef ecosystem within the bay.

--- SENTENCE 678 ---
Photo: Matt McIntosh/NOAA

### **Fagalua/Fogama'a**

Fagalua/Fogama'a unit is a 1.2 km<sup>2</sup> bay on the southwest shore of Tutuila, just east of Fagatele Bay (Figure SS.13).

--- SENTENCE 679 ---
Fagalua and Fogama'a coves make up the inner western portion of the entire bay area, which extends from Steps Point to Sail Point Rock.

--- SENTENCE 680 ---
Like Fagatele Bay,

Fagalua/Fogama'a was formed by a flooded volcanic crater and is surrounded by steep, forested cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 681 ---
The importance of the relationship between this bay and the surrounding environment is comparable to Fagatele Bay, with both bays having high coral cover, as well as many different types of coral and fish species.

--- SENTENCE 682 ---
Thus, this area provides additional protection for and increases resilience of these important coral reef ecosystems, and also creates additional opportunities for scientific research (ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 683 ---
A variety of activities are allowed in the Fagalua/Fogama'a unit, including research, education, recreation, hook-and-line fishing, cast nets, spearfishing (non-scuba-assisted), and traditional methods used for sustenance and cultural purposes such as gleaning, enu, and ola (traditional basket fishing; see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 684 ---
The Turtle and Shark Lodge is found on the cliffs of Fogama'a alongside a few scattered houses and plantations, but otherwise no settlements are found on the shore of Fagalua/Fogama'a bay.

!

--- SENTENCE 685 ---
** Fagalua/Fogama'a was formed by a flooded volcanic crater and is surrounded by steep, forested cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 686 ---
Photo: Michelle A. Johnston/NOAA

### **Aunu'u**

Aunu'u is a small, volcanic island approximately 2 km southeast of Tutuila with a land area of 1.5 km<sup>2</sup> .

--- SENTENCE 687 ---
The Aunu'u unit encompasses 15 km<sup>2</sup> and borders the island on three sides.

--- SENTENCE 688 ---
The unit consists of coral reef, pelagic, and deep-sea habitat, including extensive mesophotic habitat.

--- SENTENCE 689 ---
Based on limited survey data, the coral cover and number of species present in the Aunu'u sanctuary unit is generally moderate compared to other areas around Aunu'u.

--- SENTENCE 690 ---
The Aunu'u unit includes two zones—a Multiple Use Zone (4.9 km2) and a Research Zone (10.1 km<sup>2</sup> ; Figure SS.14).

--- SENTENCE 691 ---
The Multiple Use Zone is located on the southern side of the island, near the village.

--- SENTENCE 692 ---
Allowed activities in the Multiple Use Zone include research, education, and recreation.

--- SENTENCE 693 ---
Hook-and-line fishing, casting nets, spearfishing (non-scuba-assisted), and other nondestructive fishing methods, including those traditionally used for sustenance and cultural purposes, such as gleaning, enu, and ola (traditional basket fishing), are also permitted (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 694 ---
The Research Zone is located on the eastern side of the island.

--- SENTENCE 695 ---
Allowed activities in the research zone include research, education, recreation, and surface fishing for pelagic species, including fishing by trolling.

--- SENTENCE 696 ---
Bottom fishing, trawling, and fishing for bottom-dwelling species are prohibited in the Research Zone (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 697 ---
The island of Aunu'u is home to one small village with a population of 402 (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021).

--- SENTENCE 698 ---
The sanctuary unit is of high ecological and cultural significance for local residents, who commonly use the area for subsistence fishing.

!

--- SENTENCE 699 ---
** Dolphins are frequently observed within NMSAS, including this pod in the Aunu'u Research Zone.

--- SENTENCE 700 ---

### **Ta'u**

Ta'u, part of the Manu'a island group, is a volcanic island located approximately 112 km east of Tutuila Island (Figure SS.15).

--- SENTENCE 701 ---
Ta'u is ringed by extremely steep sea cliffs and a steeply sloped seafloor.

--- SENTENCE 702 ---
The island has a south-facing embayment, the result of collapse of and landslides from the remnants of a southern caldera similar to the Fagatele Bay formation.

--- SENTENCE 703 ---
The Ta'u unit encompasses 37.8 km<sup>2</sup> and includes waters from Vaita Point to Si'ufa'alele Point along the western coast, and from Si'ufa'alele Point to Si'u Point along the southern coast (Figure SS.16).

--- SENTENCE 704 ---
The inner sanctuary boundary along the southern coast is adjacent to, but does not include, the nearshore waters of the National Park of American Samoa, which extend 0.46 km from shore.

--- SENTENCE 705 ---
The Ta'u unit includes the "Valley of the Giants," home to many large *Porites* corals.

--- SENTENCE 706 ---
Among these is Big Momma, which is more than 500 years old, with a height greater than six m and a circumference of 41 m (Figure SS.17; Brown et al., 2009; Tangri et al., 2018).

--- SENTENCE 707 ---
It is one of the largest recorded coral colonies in the world.

--- SENTENCE 708 ---
Activities allowed in the Ta'u unit include research, education, recreation, hook-and-line fishing, cast nets, spearfishing (non-scuba-assisted), and other non-destructive fishing methods, including those traditionally used for sustenance and cultural purposes (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 709 ---
The island of Ta'u is home to 553 people (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021).

!

### **Swains Island**

Swains Island is a privately owned, low-lying emergent seamount and coral atoll located about 350 km northwest of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 716 ---
It is geologically part of the Tokelau volcanic island group and not the Samoan volcanic chain.

--- SENTENCE 717 ---
The Swains Island unit encompasses 135.5 km<sup>2</sup> of territorial waters (Figure SS.18, Figure SS.20).

--- SENTENCE 718 ---
Swains Island is approximately 2.4 km in diameter, with approximately 2.6 km<sup>2</sup> of highly vegetated land that has a maximum elevation of 1.8 m above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 719 ---
The coral reef area is small and has a steep slope.

--- SENTENCE 720 ---
The reef is dominated by *Pocillopora*  and plating *Montipora* corals and large schools of predators, mostly barracudas, jacks, and snappers, can be encountered.

--- SENTENCE 721 ---
Activities allowed in the Swains Island unit include research, education, recreation, hook-andline fishing, cast nets, spearfishing (non-scuba-assisted), and other non-destructive fishing methods including those traditionally used for sustenance and cultural purposes such as gleaning, enu, and ola (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

--- SENTENCE 722 ---
Swains Island, initially known as Olosega, has a unique history of human occupation, but the island has been uninhabited since 2008 (Van Tilburg et al., 2013).

--- SENTENCE 723 ---
In 2013, ONMS, along with partner agencies and institutions, conducted an eight-day on-island multidisciplinary survey of Swains Island.

--- SENTENCE 724 ---
The field work focused on the unique environmental setting (including a survey of the geomorphology of the atoll) and past cultural heritage resources of the island (including a maritime archaeology survey to identify historic and prehistoric maritime heritage resources; Van Tilburg et al., 2013).

!

### **Muliāva**

The Muliāva unit is the largest NMSAS unit, encompassing 34,985 km<sup>2</sup> .

--- SENTENCE 729 ---
It includes the marine waters of Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, as well as the waters surrounding Vailulu'u Seamount, a submerged volcanic cone and the only hydrothermally active seamount within the American Samoa EEZ.

--- SENTENCE 730 ---
Rose Atoll National Wildlife Refuge lies within the center of Muliāva unit and includes the lagoon and islands within Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 731 ---
The refuge is managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and is not part of NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 732 ---
The sanctuary begins at the mean low water mark on the outside of the lagoon and includes the outer reef slopes and deep-sea habitat around the atoll (Figure SS.20–Figure SS.22).

--- SENTENCE 733 ---
Rose Atoll is approximately 240 km eastsoutheast of Tutuila Island's Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 734 ---
It is the easternmost Samoan island and the southernmost point of the United States.

--- SENTENCE 735 ---
One of the smallest atolls in the world, Rose Atoll consists of about 0.08 km<sup>2</sup> of land and 6.5 km<sup>2</sup> of lagoon surrounded by a narrow reef flat (ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 736 ---
Rose Atoll, also known as Motu o Manu (island of the birds) or Nu'u o Manu (village of the birds) is a distinct environment within the archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 737 ---
The lagoon at Rose Atoll supports the highest densities of giant clams in the Samoan archipelago, and Rose Island is an important site for green turtle and seabird nesting in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 738 ---
The outer reefs of the atoll are characterized by very high CCA cover and large numbers of fish.

--- SENTENCE 739 ---
The atoll is positioned upstream in the South Equatorial Current relative to the rest of the Samoan archipelago and

therefore may be an important larval source for the territory (Kendall & Poti, 2011).

--- SENTENCE 740 ---
The name Muliāva means "the end of the current" and refers to the marine waters around Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 741 ---
In addition to Rose Atoll, the Muliāva unit also includes vast deep-sea areas, as well as the submerged volcanic Vailulu'u Seamount, which is outside of Rose Atoll Marine National Monument boundaries but within NMSAS boundaries (Figure SS.22).

--- SENTENCE 742 ---
Fishing in Rose Atoll Marine National Monument is regulated by NOAA Fisheries, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and the American Samoa government.

--- SENTENCE 743 ---
Commercial fishing is prohibited within the monument, and in 2013, NOAA Fisheries enacted additional regulations that prohibited all fishing within 22 km of Rose Atoll unless authorized by a permit for sustenance or recreational fishing (78 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 744 ---
Activities allowed in the area include research, education, recreation, and limited fishing with a permit (see Table R.1 and Table R.2 in the Response section for further information).

!

--- SENTENCE 745 ---
The Muliāva unit includes the marine waters of Rose Atoll Marine National Monument and the Vailulu'u Seamount.

--- SENTENCE 746 ---
Image: Tony Reyer/NOAA

## **Drivers on the Sanctuary**

<span id="page-64-0"></span>

--- SENTENCE 751 ---
For the purposes of condition reports, drivers are defined as societal values, policies, and socioeconomic factors that influence different human uses of the ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 752 ---
Drivers can influence the condition, or state, of the environment, creating both negative results, considered pressures, and positive results that benefit the environment.

--- SENTENCE 753 ---
Drivers can result in pressures that affect the condition, or state, of the environment.

--- SENTENCE 754 ---
They help us understand the forces behind pressures and are the ultimate cause of anthropogenic changes in ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 755 ---
Further, drivers may be local, regional, national, or global in scale.

--- SENTENCE 756 ---
Because the most influential drivers originate and operate at large geographic scales, this section begins with a broad focus on drivers, followed by a more locally focused discussion of pressures that directly affect water, habitat, living resources, and maritime heritage resources in National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa (NMSAS).

--- SENTENCE 757 ---
Trends in drivers and pressures support the assessment of these resources and can aid in forecasting the direction and influence of future pressures.

--- SENTENCE 758 ---
Pressures may be affected by one or more driving forces, which often affect multiple pressures.

--- SENTENCE 759 ---
The most influential drivers of pressures at NMSAS are shown in Table DP.1 and are integrated into discussions of each pressure.

--- SENTENCE 760 ---
Table DP.1 shows the relationships between drivers and pressures.
