Drivers operate at different, and sometimes multiple, scales, including global, national, regional, and local.

--- SENTENCE 776 ---
Most affect demand for resources (e.g., government relationships, per capita income, fuel prices, etc.) and, thus, levels of activities (e.g., coastal development, fishing, visitation) that alter resource conditions.

--- SENTENCE 777 ---
Some drivers, like the gross domestic product (GDP) of foreign countries, have global influence.

--- SENTENCE 778 ---
Among other things, GDP affects global demand for seafood and commercial fishing pressure.

--- SENTENCE 779 ---
Local drivers, on the other hand, are those that originate from and influence the NMSAS "local economy" (sometimes called the "study area" or "sanctuary economy").

--- SENTENCE 780 ---
This area is identified by first including villages adjacent to NMSAS boundaries, then working with NMSAS leadership to determine the spatial footprint of localized socioeconomic contributions stemming from the use of sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 781 ---
These contributions include income, jobs, and economic output, all of which respond to changes in resource conditions that are influenced by changing pressures.

--- SENTENCE 782 ---
Some drivers influence the supply of or access to resources.

--- SENTENCE 783 ---
These stem mostly from management and policy actions, whether local, state, tribal, national, or international, and may increase or decrease the pressures on resources.

--- SENTENCE 784 ---
Some, such as relationships established and dictated through treaties, create cooperative management approaches that can preempt pressures (e.g., cooperative fisheries management, preparation of oil spill response plans).

--- SENTENCE 785 ---
Importantly, these drivers also exemplify a concept frequently expressed by Indigenous peoples, namely the reciprocal relationship between people and the environment.

--- SENTENCE 786 ---
This originates from Indigenous peoples' sense of oneness with nature and emphasizes the mutual roles of both in supporting each other.

--- SENTENCE 787 ---
Advocates of the modern conservation movement will recognize this as a foundational aspect of their efforts as well.

--- SENTENCE 788 ---
In this way, both can be considered "positive" drivers.

--- SENTENCE 789 ---
It is important to consider NOAA and ONMS mandates as institutional drivers.

--- SENTENCE 790 ---
Starting with federal agencies' basic obligation of public service, each employee has an oath-bound responsibility to the United States government and its citizens to display loyalty to the Constitution, laws, and ethical principles (5 C.F.R. § 2635.101).

--- SENTENCE 791 ---
This includes fulfilling the responsibilities outlined in the National Marine Sanctuaries Act (16 U.S.C. § 1431), which:

"establishes areas of the marine environment [that] have special conservation, recreational, ecological, historical, cultural, archeological, scientific, educational, or esthetic qualities as national marine sanctuaries managed as the National Marine Sanctuary System will—(A) improve the conservation, understanding, management, and wise and sustainable use of marine resources; (B) enhance public awareness, understanding, and appreciation of the marine environment; and (C) maintain for future generations the habitat, and ecological services, of the natural assemblage of living resources that inhabit these areas.

--- SENTENCE 792 ---
"

This guiding language ensures that the National Marine Sanctuary System acts in a manner to improve conservation and management for generations to come.

--- SENTENCE 793 ---
NMSAS was expanded in response to the American Samoa governors Tauese Sunia and Togiola Tulafono committing to the goal of setting aside 20% of coral reef habitat within the territory for long-term protection.

--- SENTENCE 794 ---
Additionally, Presidential Proclamation 8337 stated that "[t]he Secretary of Commerce shall initiate the process to add the marine areas of…[Rose Atoll Marine National

Monument] to…Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary in accordance with the National Marine Sanctuaries Act" (74 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 795 ---
This section provides an overview of several key drivers; the discussion below is not an exhaustive list of all drivers affecting NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 796 ---
## <span id="page-67-0"></span>*Government Relationships*

Samoans are known as people who share a common language and a 3,000-year-old cultural code.

--- SENTENCE 797 ---
A significant difference between Samoa and American Samoa is how the people are governed.

--- SENTENCE 798 ---
Samoa is an independent nation with its head of state, while American Samoa is a self-governing territory of the U.S. American Samoans are classified as U.S. nationals rather than U.S. citizens.

--- SENTENCE 799 ---
American Samoa has an intergovernmental relationship with Samoa to collaborate effectively on shared environmental concerns.

--- SENTENCE 800 ---
As part of a shared environmental agenda, the leaders of these two jurisdictions hold an annual forum to discuss areas of common interest (e.g., trade, health, education, communication and technology, fisheries, agriculture, food security, enforcement).

--- SENTENCE 801 ---
This partnership allows both governments to collaborate and share information.

--- SENTENCE 802 ---
This cooperation among peoples to ensure continued conservation, stewardship, and adaptation to environmental challenges may be considered a positive driver.

# <span id="page-67-1"></span>*Traditional Management and Governance Structure of American Samoa*

The government of American Samoa is based on the United States party system, while honoring the Fa'a Samoa traditional village protocol, also known as the matai system (council of chiefs).

--- SENTENCE 803 ---
This system is relevant at all levels of Samoan life—from the family, to the village, to the government.

--- SENTENCE 804 ---
The matai (chiefs) are chosen by consensus of the fono (a group composed of matai) of the extended family and village(s) concerned.

--- SENTENCE 805 ---
The matai and the fono decide on the distribution of family exchanges and the tenancy of communal lands; the majority of lands in American Samoa are communal.

--- SENTENCE 806 ---
A matai can represent a small family group or a great extended family that reaches across islands and to both American Samoa and Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 807 ---
Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way of life, emphasizes loyalty to family, respect for one's elders, and a commitment to serving the community, which is considered vitally important.

--- SENTENCE 808 ---
For example, a seasonal village marine protected area may be guided and overseen by the council of chiefs.

--- SENTENCE 809 ---
The village protected area is allowed to open for a short period to support village events or special occasions.

--- SENTENCE 810 ---
The government is also informed of these arrangements and provides scientific and technical support, including data analysis.

--- SENTENCE 811 ---
Since the local people control communal lands and waters, conservation and stewardship are entrusted with those who have an extended relationship with these areas across generations and space.

--- SENTENCE 812 ---
This approach promotes more responsive and localized monitoring of the resources, promoting community well-being, continued cultural engagement, and environmental health of the sanctuary and surrounding waters.

## <span id="page-68-0"></span>*Population and Per Capita Income*

International and domestic demand for goods and services at all scales, ranging from local to global, is directly tied to changes in population and real per capita income.

--- SENTENCE 813 ---
It is and will remain a ubiquitous, primary driver of pressures on sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 814 ---
For example, as income or population increases, demand for goods like clothes, technology, and other consumer goods also increases.

--- SENTENCE 815 ---
Because the majority of these goods are imported to American Samoa, higher demand for goods can increase vessel traffic.

--- SENTENCE 816 ---
On the other hand, declines in income or population may have the opposite effect.

--- SENTENCE 817 ---
From 2010–2020, the population of American Samoa decreased by 10.5% from 55,519 to 49,710 people (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021).

--- SENTENCE 818 ---
In 2010,<sup>2</sup> annual per capita income in American Samoa was \$6,311 and the poverty rate was 57.8% (ASDOC, 2018).

--- SENTENCE 819 ---
A relatively high poverty rate in a place with strong cultural linkages to ancestral practices may result in higher reliance on subsistence harvest to meet nutritional needs.

--- SENTENCE 820 ---
If not managed sustainably, subsistence harvest could become a significant pressure on resources.

--- SENTENCE 821 ---
## <span id="page-68-1"></span>*Fuel Prices*

Fuel prices are an important, and often immediate, driver of many ocean activities.

--- SENTENCE 822 ---
Ocean users consider fuel prices in their decisions about whether to conduct activities like commercial fishing, buy and register boats for ocean recreation, or explore for offshore oil and gas (and in the longer term, install offshore renewable energy facilities).

--- SENTENCE 823 ---
Figure DP.1 shows the average retail price for unleaded gasoline from 2007–2019 (ASDOC, 2018; ASDOC, 2019).

--- SENTENCE 824 ---
Gasoline prices declined from 2014–2017, indicating that the cost of recreational and commercial activities within the sanctuary that utilize fuel were also likely declining.

--- SENTENCE 825 ---
Lower activity cost may result in increased activities and thus pressure on sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 826 ---
<sup>2</sup> 2020 per capita income and poverty rate data for American Samoa were not available at the time of publication.

!

--- SENTENCE 827 ---
** Average retail price for unleaded gasoline in American Samoa from 2007 to 2019.

--- SENTENCE 828 ---
Source: ASDOC, 2018, 2019

## <span id="page-69-0"></span>*Demand for Seafood*

As global and domestic demand for seafood grows, effective management of wild-caught fish and continued expansion of aquaculture will be required (NOAA Fisheries, 2020a).

--- SENTENCE 829 ---
Yet, while these approaches are needed to meet demand, they may also lead to increased pressures on resources and ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 830 ---
While this section considers global and national demand, local and regional markets are likely to be affected and face increased pressures to meet global and national demands.

--- SENTENCE 831 ---
Further, as prices fluctuate locally, this may change the willingness of commercial fishers to expend time and resources targeting specific species.

--- SENTENCE 832 ---
For example, if the price of tuna increases while the price of surgeonfish stays the same, more effort may shift to harvesting tuna.

--- SENTENCE 833 ---
For more information on harvest revenue and landings of species within NMSAS, see the Commercial Harvest section of this report.

--- SENTENCE 834 ---
The tuna canning industry plays a significant role in American Samoa's economy and trade.

--- SENTENCE 835 ---
Processed tuna accounted for over 88% of exports to the United States from 1995 to 2018.

--- SENTENCE 836 ---
The industry also provides direct and indirect benefits to transportation, warehousing, retail, wholesale, and construction industries and may offset the costs of shipping, transportation, and energy for the territory (U.S. Government Accountability Office, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 837 ---
American Samoa's tuna canning industry faces multiple challenges, including increased competition and minimum wage increases, which led to cannery closures in 2018.

--- SENTENCE 838 ---
The impact of the canneries completely closing would be significant, as canneries employ 14% of American Samoa's workforce (as of 2018; U.S. Government Accountability Office, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 839 ---
Additionally, transportation, energy, and utility costs would rise because the canneries would no longer be available to share those costs.

## <span id="page-70-0"></span>*Technological Advancement*

Technological advancement may be viewed as either a positive and negative driver depending on the technology and what it promotes.

--- SENTENCE 840 ---
For example, requirements for seafloor mapping may act as a positive driver by increasing knowledge and awareness of sensitive habitats and refining our understanding of species distributions.

--- SENTENCE 841 ---
Significant efforts to increase seafloor mapping in NMSAS by vessels, such as the NOAA Ship *Okeanos Explorer* and the E/V *Nautilus*, have taken place in the past decade.

--- SENTENCE 842 ---
Seafloor mapping may identify previously unknown deposits of resources, which could increase pressures to extract those resources.

--- SENTENCE 843 ---
Advancements in fishing technology in the past have increased harvests while decreasing the effort needed to catch fish.

--- SENTENCE 844 ---
Improvements in fishing gear technology can also reduce bycatch of sensitive species.

--- SENTENCE 845 ---
Advancements in autonomous vehicles have helped to estimate fish abundance to promote sustainable fishing while reducing risks to human health and fish (NOAA Fisheries, 2020b).

--- SENTENCE 846 ---
## <span id="page-70-1"></span>*Societal Values and Practices*

Public access to beaches in American Samoa, and consequently the marine ecosystem, is under the purview of the village or individual families that reside adjacent to the water and public places.

--- SENTENCE 847 ---
One must obtain permission or approval for access out of respect and courtesy.

--- SENTENCE 848 ---
These families are the caretakers of these special places and help to maintain and safeguard them for current and future generations.

--- SENTENCE 849 ---
This community-based approach to resource management helps to reduce pressures and identify changing conditions more rapidly.

--- SENTENCE 850 ---
The relationship between the peoples of Samoa and American Samoa may also provide a mix of positive and negative influences on drivers.

--- SENTENCE 851 ---
This relationship exemplifies the longstanding connections between Samoa and American Samoa through trade of fish and the exportation of other foods based upon need (e.g., in response to tsunamis or other disasters).

--- SENTENCE 852 ---
As a societal value, the desire to ensure food security across the region is a driver, as is the sharing of knowledge.

--- SENTENCE 853 ---
Another example of societal values that reduce fishing pressure is the belief that one does not play with their food.

--- SENTENCE 854 ---
As such, participation in recreational activities on reefs is not common among native Samoans (Levine et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 855 ---
In addition, NMSAS promotes awareness of allowable and responsible fishing practices within the sanctuary by bringing together and educating local fishing groups.

--- SENTENCE 856 ---
For places like American Samoa that have long-standing and vibrant Indigenous cultures, the associated cultural practices of communities are, collectively, a driver that may exert positive and/or negative impacts on resources.

--- SENTENCE 857 ---
Religion significantly influences the Samoan way of life and society.

--- SENTENCE 858 ---
Ceremonial events such as a church dedication or a death in the family may result in temporary pressures caused by more people fishing within the community.

--- SENTENCE 859 ---
Most cultural practices in Indigenous cultures tend to reflect deep connections between people and the resources they depend on, and care is generally taken to moderate impacts while still respecting long-held traditions.

--- SENTENCE 860 ---
## <span id="page-71-0"></span>*Ocean Policy*

The U.S. is party to numerous agreements that have established international entities composed of member governments that focus on various topics, ranging from managing shipping (International Maritime Organization), global whale stocks (International Whaling Commission), fisheries (Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission, Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, etc.), and oil spill response (Pacific Ocean Pollution Prevention Programme).

--- SENTENCE 861 ---
Since 2010, the United States has had an ocean policy, first through Executive Order 13547 (2010) and later replaced with Executive Order 13840 (2018).

--- SENTENCE 862 ---
While the primary focus differs between these policies, both emphasize improving cross-agency coordination on management of the ocean and its resources, as well as access to data.

--- SENTENCE 863 ---
Mapping the seafloor is a priority, as it will enhance navigation and development of the blue economy.

--- SENTENCE 864 ---
Furthermore, a 2019 presidential memorandum set forth a strategy for mapping, exploring, and characterizing the U.S. EEZ through enhanced collaboration (86 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 865 ---
The *American Samoa Ocean Plan* (Department of Port Administration, 2018) was an outcome of this executive order and includes the first spatial plan to be completed by the U.S. for its jurisdictions in the Pacific Ocean.

--- SENTENCE 866 ---
In 2009, President George W. Bush established Rose Atoll Marine National Monument through Presidential Proclamation 8337 (74 Fed.

--- SENTENCE 867 ---
The proclamation banned commercial fishing within the monument, but does allow for limited subsistence and recreational fishing with a permit from NOAA Fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 868 ---
This proclamation also directed the Secretary of Commerce to initiate the process to add the marine areas of the monument to Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 869 ---
These areas became part of NMSAS 2012 and provide an example of ocean policy contributing to conservation and stewardship.

## **Pressures on Sanctuary Resources**

<span id="page-72-0"></span>Human activities and natural processes affect the condition of natural, cultural, and maritime heritage resources in national marine sanctuaries.

--- SENTENCE 870 ---
The following section discusses the nature and extent of the most prominent human influences upon NMSAS, including impacts from accelerated climate change, fishing, pollution, marine debris, vessel groundings, visitor use, scientific and management activities, and nuisance species outbreaks.

--- SENTENCE 871 ---
## <span id="page-72-1"></span>*Accelerated Climate Change and Ocean Acidification*

Rising ocean temperatures associated with climate change were recognized as a pressure on coral reef ecosystems in Fagatele Bay in the 2007 condition report (National Marine Sanctuary Program, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 872 ---
Ocean temperatures have continued to increase, and ocean acidification and stratification, increasing storm intensity, and rising sea levels are now known to affect marine ecosystems across the entire sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 873 ---
Pacific Islands are among the most vulnerable areas in the world to the predicted effects of climate change (Mimura et al., 2007;

--- SENTENCE 874 ---
Howes et al., 2018).

### **Sea Surface Temperature**

Since the 1970s, sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Islands region have been increasing and are projected to continue increasing over the next century (Howes et al., 2018; Coral Reef Watch, 2021; Keener et al., 2021).

--- SENTENCE 875 ---
Elevated water temperature is a well-known trigger for coral bleaching, a phenomenon where corals lose their colorful zooxanthellae, revealing their white skeleton in a process known as coral bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 876 ---
Bleaching can be caused by short-term exposure (1–2 days) to temperature elevations of 3–4°C above ambient conditions, or by long-term exposure (weeks) to elevations of only 1–2°C.

--- SENTENCE 877 ---
Depending on the severity of bleaching, zooxanthellae may repopulate and corals can survive.

--- SENTENCE 878 ---
However, when high temperature stress occurs over extended periods, corals suffer high mortality, as observed during several mass bleaching events throughout the tropics (Glynn, 1984;

--- SENTENCE 879 ---
Eakin et al., 2010; Eakin et al., 2019; Skirving et al., 2019).

--- SENTENCE 880 ---
In American Samoa, mortality due to coral bleaching was documented in 1994 (Goreau & Hayes, 1994) and observed in 2002 and 2003 (Craig et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 881 ---
Mass mortality of staghorn corals was documented at Airport Pools reef on Tutuila during a 2015 bleaching event (Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, 2015; XL Catlin Seaview Survey, 2015; Figure DP.2).

--- SENTENCE 882 ---
Since 2005, bleaching around Tutuila has been documented in shallow back reef pools nearly every summer, but until 2015 it had only caused minimal mortality (Fenner & Heron, 2009; Fenner, 2019).

--- SENTENCE 883 ---
Widespread bleaching events were documented in 2015, 2017, and 2020 (Coward, et al., 2021; McCoy, et al., 2016; Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019; NMSAS, 2020b).

!

--- SENTENCE 884 ---
** Time series of staghorn corals at Airport Pools reef on Tutuila during the 2015 coral bleaching event.

--- SENTENCE 885 ---
Photos: Underwater Earth/XL Catlin Seaview Survey

### **Disease**

Epizootics are predicted to increase with climate warming (Harvell et al., 2002), and many coral diseases have been linked to increasing ocean temperatures (Randall & Van Woesik, 2015; Howells et al., 2020; Aeby et al., 2020).

--- SENTENCE 886 ---
Even on a small scale, disease can alter community structure, reduce reproductive output, and decrease coral cover (Hughes, 1994; Kim & Harvell, 2004).

--- SENTENCE 887 ---
Several diseases of corals and crustose coralline algae (CCA) have been documented in NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 888 ---
Coralline lethal orange disease, a bacterial infection that affects CCA (Littler & Littler, 1995), was found to be more prevalent in Fagatele Bay than in other sites examined around Tutuila (Aeby et al., 2008; Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019).

--- SENTENCE 889 ---
A black fungal infection affecting CCA has also been reported in American Samoa (Littler & Littler, 1998).

--- SENTENCE 890 ---
White syndrome, a general term used to describe coral disease lesions, is characterized by rapid tissue loss and a distinct lesion boundary between apparently healthy tissue and exposed white skeleton (Sussman et al., 2008) and is one of the most common coral diseases around Tutuila (Aeby et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 891 ---
This disease can be very virulent and can result in acute tissue loss (Roff et al., 2011).

--- SENTENCE 892 ---
*Acropora* table corals in American Samoa can display growth anomalies (hyperplasia) with distorted, tumor-like growths on the surface of the coral (Work et al., 2008a).

--- SENTENCE 893 ---
This disease affects numerous table corals in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 894 ---
Over 35 coral diseases may be present in American Samoa, but many have not been fully investigated (Fenner, 2013a).

--- SENTENCE 895 ---
A possible cyanobacterial disease has recently been reported in Ofu Pools (Manu'a islands), but appears to progress slowly and be influenced by temperature (D. Fenner/NOAA, personal communication, 2019; K. Nalasere, personal communication, February 24, 2021).

### **Ocean Acidification**

Corals and other calcifying organisms, including certain types of phytoplankton, coralline algae, crustaceans, mollusks, echinoderms, and other taxa, are threatened by ocean acidification,

which results in a reduction of the pH of ocean water due to uptake of increased atmospheric carbon dioxide (Caldeira & Wickett, 2003).

--- SENTENCE 896 ---
Acidified waters compromise calcium carbonate accretion and therefore directly affect the ability of these organisms to secrete their calcareous skeletal structures (Orr et al., 2005; Fabry et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 897 ---
Aragonite saturation state is directly linked to this process and is an important metric for assessing ocean acidification on coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 898 ---
Calcium carbonate accretion (i.e., coral calcification) declines at aragonite saturation values below 3.3 (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007).

--- SENTENCE 899 ---
In 2018, NOAA's Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center (PIFSC) Ecosystem Services Division (ESD) reported near-optimum aragonite saturation states across the American Samoa archipelago (Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019).

--- SENTENCE 900 ---
However, ocean acidification scenarios predict detrimental conditions for calcifying organisms that could lead to widespread changes in marine ecosystems (Orr et al., 2005; Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007; Fabry et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 901 ---
Ocean acidification does not just affect calcifying organisms.

--- SENTENCE 902 ---
Lowered pH may alter the behavior of larval fish and invertebrates, influence settlement success due to changes in suitable settlement substrate, and alter larval development and/or energy budgets (Espinel-Velasco et al., 2018).

### **Shifting Processes**

Rising temperatures are also shifting oceanographic processes that control ocean currents and mixing at both local and global scales.

--- SENTENCE 903 ---
One potential impact is water column stratification.

--- SENTENCE 904 ---
As surface temperatures increase and the ocean absorbs more heat energy, the upper layers warm more quickly and create sheets of warm water that reduce mixing between layers and block cycling of oxygen, carbon, nutrients, and heat within the water column.

--- SENTENCE 905 ---
Stratification has increased globally by 5.3% since 1960 (Li et al., 2020).

--- SENTENCE 906 ---
Most of the increase (~71%) occurred in the upper 200 m of the ocean and was largely influenced by temperature changes (>90%).

## **Salinity**

Salinity changes may play an important role at local scales.

--- SENTENCE 907 ---
Ocean regions are connected by large thermohaline currents that transfer oxygen and nutrients from the poles toward the equator.

--- SENTENCE 908 ---
American Samoa lies within the Pacific meridional overturning circulation (PMOC).

--- SENTENCE 909 ---
North of American Samoa, the geological feature known as the Samoan Passage is an important conduit and mixing zone for these currents that move from Antarctica to the North Pacific (Roemmich et al., 1996; Voet et al., 2015).

--- SENTENCE 910 ---
Recent studies have indicated that the PMOC is changing both in strength and temperature as surplus heat associated with climate change is reaching the deep ocean.

--- SENTENCE 911 ---
Voet et al. (2016) assessed the abyssal flow through the Samoan Passage in 2012–2013.

--- SENTENCE 912 ---
Over the past two decades, volume transport decreased by about 0.6 Sv (10%), and water temperature increased by 0.001°C/yr.

--- SENTENCE 913 ---
This is consistent with numerical simulations that demonstrate the possibility of a slowing meridional overturning circulation due to climate change (Schmittner et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 914 ---
It is unknown if this shift is already affecting deep-sea communities, but it could have significant implications for deep-sea habitats throughout NMSAS and the broader region in the coming years.

--- SENTENCE 915 ---
## **Cyclones**

American Samoa is susceptible to tropical cyclones during the austral (southern) summer from November to April.

--- SENTENCE 916 ---
In 1990, 1991, 2004, 2005, and 2018, cyclones caused damage to coral reefs in American Samoa (Figure DP.3).

--- SENTENCE 917 ---
Impacts included large amounts of coral rubble and redistributed sediments in shallow water in affected areas.

--- SENTENCE 918 ---
As a result of climate change, storms are predicted to decrease in frequency, but increase in intensity (Howes et al., 2018; Knutson et al., 2020; Keener et al., 2021), providing an additional challenge to maintaining high coral cover in the future.

--- SENTENCE 919 ---
In addition, rainfall is expected to increase by up to 10%, particularly during episodic heavy rain events such as cyclones and monsoons (ONMS, 2020a).

--- SENTENCE 920 ---
These processes are infrequent and influenced by a number of factors including the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and other complex ocean-atmospheric interactions, so it is difficult to determine if these have been affected by climate change.

--- SENTENCE 921 ---
Fifty-three tropical cyclones have passed within 370 km of Tutuila since 1959 (Office for Coastal Management [OCM], 2020).

### *Impacts to Heritage Resources*

While only a few tangible heritage properties have been located within NMSAS boundaries, intangible heritage resources, including practices, traditions, belief systems, and Samoan knowledge related to the marine environment, exist within the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 922 ---
These practices are threatened by climate change impacts, including ocean acidification, sea level rise, increased water temperatures, and increased storm intensity.

--- SENTENCE 923 ---
Threats to culturally valued species (e.g., corals, fish, and invertebrates) from changing environmental conditions may negatively impact community valuation of offshore areas and the local environment, while more intense storm activity has the potential to affect human on-water activities such as boating, fishing, or gathering.

--- SENTENCE 924 ---
Cultural heritage and sense of place are intertwined; social roles and customs rely on strong attachments to specific locations.

--- SENTENCE 925 ---
Climate change threatens these attachments in many ways, including direct destruction of coastal sites, weakening of social bonds as people relocate to avoid climate impacts, and loss of traditions as coastal access and resources change (Peau et al., 2022).

--- SENTENCE 926 ---
The fautasi (Samoan long boat) race held on flag day in April, for example, may be threatened by more intense storms, as boats are vulnerable to cyclone impacts.

--- SENTENCE 927 ---
Novel weather patterns and altered seasonality as a whole present similar concerns, as they may alter or limit pre-existing practices such as the timing of cultural events, such as akule (bigeye scad, *Selar crumenophthalmus*) fishing or the palolo (epitokes of the worm *Palola viridis)* harvest, or the ability to apply traditional knowledge and skill sets to localized resource management (McMillen et al., 2014).

--- SENTENCE 928 ---
Further identification and documentation of intangible heritage resources will provide a better understanding of the impact of climate change to these resources.

!

## <span id="page-76-0"></span>*Fishing*

Worldwide, there is heavy pressure on fish assemblages from fishery activities, and assessments have demonstrated declines in reef fish abundance across the Pacific Islands (McCoy et al., 2018).

--- SENTENCE 931 ---
These results suggest that the current level of harvest of reef fish and invertebrates is unsustainable in many locations (Secretariat of the Pacific Community [SPC], 2013).

--- SENTENCE 932 ---
Assessment of the U.S. Pacific Islands indicated that reefs in American Samoa had only a quarter of the fish biomass observed in remote areas (Williams et al., 2011) and that reef fish populations in all islands, except for Swains, are well below the biological potential for these systems (Williams et al., 2015).

--- SENTENCE 933 ---
Destructive fishing methods, including explosives and chemicals, that affect corals and non-target species are also a concern.

--- SENTENCE 934 ---
Possible fishing with explosives has occurred in Fagatele Bay as recently as 2004 (National Marine Sanctuary Program, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 935 ---
Although there has been no recent evidence of this practice, damage to the reef structure is still visible.

--- SENTENCE 936 ---
Anchoring boats within fishing areas can also cause mechanical damage to reefs.

--- SENTENCE 937 ---
Evidence of anchor damage, in the form of numerous flipped tabletop corals, was found on towboard surveys along southwest Aunu'u bank and Nafanua bank in 2014 (J. Paulin/NOAA, personal communication, 2022).

--- SENTENCE 938 ---
Anchor damage and two illegal moorings have also been found in Fagatele Bay (J. Paulin/NOAA, personal communication, 2022).

--- SENTENCE 939 ---
A 2019 assessment of the Bottomfish Management Unit Species complex in American Samoa determined that the area is in an overfished state (Langseth et al., 2019).

--- SENTENCE 940 ---
This includes shallow coral reef fish species such as bluestripe snapper (*Lutjanus kasmira),* green jobfish *

--- SENTENCE 941 ---
(Aprion virescens),* yellow-edged lyretail *(Variola louti),* black jack *(Caranx lugubris),* and spotcheek

emperor *(Lethrinus rubrioperculatus),* as well as deeper species, including deep-water snappers (*Etelis coruscans* and *E. carbunculus)*.

--- SENTENCE 942 ---
Pelagic resources appear to be more resilient to fishing pressure, but it is unclear how climate change may affect pelagic species distributions across the region (SPC, 2013).

--- SENTENCE 943 ---
Fishing is prohibited in Fagatele Bay and limited in Aunu'u Zone B and Muliāva; however, direct observation and enforcement of fishing activity in these areas is difficult.

--- SENTENCE 944 ---
Fishing may quickly reduce the population of target reef fish species in constrained bays like Fagatele Bay and remote sites like Rose Atoll with limited fish recruitment.

--- SENTENCE 945 ---
Several large species of reef fishes, characteristic of unfished reefs in the Indo-Pacific region, are conspicuously absent or small in size in Fagatele Bay and found in lower abundance at Rose Atoll than what oceanographic and habitat conditions would predict (Williams et al., 2015).

--- SENTENCE 946 ---
These include species such as humphead wrasse (*Cheilinus undulatus*), sharks, and large species of grouper and parrotfish, all of which are known to be particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure.

## <span id="page-77-0"></span>*Coastal Development and Nearshore Construction*

Due to the islands' small size, all terrestrial areas within American Samoa are considered "coastal."

--- SENTENCE 947 ---
Development can significantly affect coastal habitats because of the small watershed size and short distances from ridge to reef.

--- SENTENCE 948 ---
On Tutuila, developed areas increased by 5.8% from 2004–2010, despite a decline in population during this period (OCM, 2021).

--- SENTENCE 949 ---
Additional development has taken place since 2010, but has not been quantified.

--- SENTENCE 950 ---
Due to rising sea levels, many coastal areas have been armored with seawalls to protect valuable infrastructure and homes.

--- SENTENCE 951 ---
In some areas, coastal protection structures have resulted in the loss of coastal and marine habitat, including benthic organisms, and ecological function associated with these habitats.

--- SENTENCE 952 ---
This may, in turn, reduce larval connectivity through habitat fragmentation and the loss of brood stock (Hughes et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 953 ---
Coastal armoring also disrupts the movement of sand and beach development which may affect both terrestrial and marine resources.

--- SENTENCE 954 ---
Ongoing development and coastal armoring have reduced nesting habitat for sea turtles in Tutuila and Manu'a and may impair the recovery of sea turtles in the region (Tuato'o-Bartley et al., 1993; Saili, 2005).

--- SENTENCE 955 ---
Based on data collected from 2007–2013, Seminoff et al. (2015) estimated that 105 green sea turtles nest at Rose Atoll, 23 nest at Swains Island, but only three nest in Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 956 ---
As of 2020, the only new development directly adjacent to NMSAS waters was a small seawall built on the south side of Aunu'u.

--- SENTENCE 957 ---
It was built by the village from available debris following storm waves that inundated the Aunu'u power plant in 2019.

--- SENTENCE 958 ---
Agriculture in American Samoa is still largely at subsistence scale with mostly traditional staple food crops, chickens, and pigs.

--- SENTENCE 959 ---
With shifting land use patterns, American Samoa is likely to experience increased agricultural development, including the land surrounding NMSAS units.

--- SENTENCE 960 ---
Such development may threaten water quality, habitat integrity, and the biological health of the reefs, particularly if fertilizer and pesticide use and erosion are not controlled.

--- SENTENCE 961 ---
Heavy sedimentation is currently not a problem in sanctuary units, but this could change with increasing coastal development and agricultural demand.

## <span id="page-78-0"></span>*Nonpoint Source Pollution*

Land-based sources of pollution, including nutrients, sedimentation, and chemical contaminants, are major threats to coral reefs worldwide and can promote algae growth, cause stress to corals, and increase the likelihood of disease and bleaching (Vega-Thurber et al., 2014).

--- SENTENCE 962 ---
Pollutants can be an issue in American Samoa, primarily in areas adjacent to populated coastal areas and industries (Houk et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 963 ---
All NMSAS units are remote and not near highly populated coastal areas.

--- SENTENCE 964 ---
However, pollutants could drift into the sanctuary and affect the condition of resources.

--- SENTENCE 965 ---
Human sewage/cesspool outflows, runoff of agricultural fertilizers, and animal waste (e.g., from piggeries) can increase loading of nutrients, primarily nitrogen and phosphorus, in nearshore waters.

--- SENTENCE 966 ---
Nutrient inputs from surface runoff and submarine groundwater discharge contribute to eutrophication and algal blooms, which can hinder coral growth or recovery following disturbance (D'Angelo & Wiedenmann, 2014).

--- SENTENCE 967 ---
Nutrients are also implicated in promoting crown-of-thorns sea star (CoTS; *Acanthaster planci* or alamea in Samoan) outbreaks (Brodie et al., 2005;

--- SENTENCE 968 ---
Fabricius et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 969 ---
Available data indicate that nutrient levels in sanctuary units are below recommended thresholds, but in Fagatele Bay, there is evidence nutrient input may be increasing, likely due to the presence of a landfill and increased agriculture in the surrounding watershed.

--- SENTENCE 970 ---
The Fagatele Bay and Fagalua/Fogama'a sanctuary units lie within one mile of the main landfill for the island of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 971 ---
Although separated from Fagatele Bay by the high ridge that surrounds the bay, the Futiga landfill is unlined and contaminants such as heavy metals, petrochemicals, and pharmaceuticals may leach into groundwater that flows into the bay through ocean seeps.

--- SENTENCE 972 ---
Heavy metals, hydrocarbons, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals were detected in low levels in water and sediment in Fagatele Bay in 2019 (Whitall et al., 2022).

--- SENTENCE 973 ---
Aunu'u and Ta'u have their own landfills, but these are smaller.

## <span id="page-78-1"></span>*Point Source Pollution*

Point source pollution originates from single, identifiable sources from which pollutants are discharged, such as a stream mouth.

--- SENTENCE 974 ---
NMSAS units are far from major pollution sources, including the large sewage and cannery outfalls on Tutuila, but there are small pollution sources in the Aunu'u and Muliāva units.

--- SENTENCE 975 ---
For instance, the sewage outfall in Aunu'u discharges in shallow waters just outside the reef margin and may be a source of contamination, but the chemical composition of the effluent is unknown and no testing has been conducted.

--- SENTENCE 976 ---
The discharge zone is highly mixed and accumulation is unlikely.

--- SENTENCE 977 ---
In Muliāva, there may be waste, ballast, and bilge discharges from ships transiting in or near the area.

--- SENTENCE 978 ---
## <span id="page-78-2"></span>*Marine Debris*

Trash in its many forms has long been a problem on the shorelines and coastal waters of American Samoa, especially plastic trash, which persists and accumulates in the environment.

--- SENTENCE 979 ---
Another problem is derelict fishing gear, which snags on reefs and can entangle marine mammals and turtles.

--- SENTENCE 980 ---
Marine debris has a comparatively lower presence underwater in NMSAS, but it does accumulate on adjacent shorelines in some locations.

--- SENTENCE 981 ---
The Fagalua/Fogama'a unit has persistent accumulation of both ocean- and shore-based debris, including abandoned fishing gear and discarded trash left by visitors.

--- SENTENCE 982 ---
Recent deep-sea exploration cruises noted significant accumulations of marine debris in the deep sea near Tutuila, but presence was low in sanctuary units (Amon et al., 2020).

--- SENTENCE 983 ---
The potential environmental impact of microplastics—plastic debris that breaks down in the marine environment—has become a growing concern worldwide (Cole et al., 2011;

--- SENTENCE 984 ---
Wright et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2021).

--- SENTENCE 985 ---
The extent to which microplastics are a concern in American Samoa and whether food fish are negatively impacted through trophic accumulation is currently known.

## <span id="page-79-0"></span>*Vessel Groundings*

Ship groundings on coral reefs can cause extensive physical damage to the reef structure and can release toxic petrochemicals and harmful cargo, killing reef organisms.

--- SENTENCE 986 ---
Any wreckage left on the reef can continue to cause physical damage and may release iron into nearby waters.

--- SENTENCE 987 ---
Iron inputs are thought to be especially damaging on atolls, because unlike high volcanic islands, these systems do not have natural inputs of iron.

--- SENTENCE 988 ---
Iron can contribute to blooms of cyanobacteria on the already damaged reef, preventing recovery of corals and other reef organisms, turning them into "black reefs" (Kelly et al., 2012).

--- SENTENCE 989 ---
Other unanticipated consequences can occur, such as the corallimorph outbreak on Palmyra Atoll following a ship grounding in 1991 (Work et al., 2008b).

--- SENTENCE 990 ---
On Rose Atoll, the grounding of a 135-ft Taiwanese long-line tuna-fishing vessel in October 1993 released diesel lube oil into refuge waters.

--- SENTENCE 991 ---
Prevailing currents carried these contaminants across the reef flat and into the lagoon, killing invertebrates and algae.

--- SENTENCE 992 ---
The grounding itself physically damaged the reef when the ship hit the upper portion of the outer reef slope and moved across the reef before coming to rest (Green et al., 1997).

--- SENTENCE 993 ---
Extensive removal efforts were undertaken over many years by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, but some iron debris remains.

--- SENTENCE 994 ---
Subsequent monitoring and assessment studies indicate that the reef has suffered ongoing injury due to the release of iron from the decaying ship debris (Schroeder et al., 2008).

--- SENTENCE 995 ---
In April 2016, the 62-ft F/V *No.1 JiHyun* lost its main engines and grounded off the west side of Aunu'u Island in the Multiple Use Zone.

--- SENTENCE 996 ---
This area is of ecological and cultural significance for the local residents and is considered an important location for fishing and gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 997 ---
After a number of unsuccessful attempts, the vessel was removed in August 2016.

--- SENTENCE 998 ---
The grounding impaired 4,250 km<sup>2</sup> of reef habitat, leaving a large rubble field with low complexity and rugosity that has not recovered (Symons et al., 2017).

--- SENTENCE 999 ---
## <span id="page-79-1"></span>*Visitation*

There is relatively little tourism in American Samoa and it is likely to be some years before the territory enters the mainstream of South Pacific tourism.

--- SENTENCE 1000 ---
Due to the remote location of NMSAS units, even on the main island of Tutuila, visitation numbers are low compared to other South Pacific island destinations.

--- SENTENCE 1001 ---
For example, in 2017, 5,579 tourists arrived in American Samoa (ASDOC, 2018); in contrast, 869,000 and 199,000 total visitors arrived in Fiji and Papua New Guinea, respectively, in the same year (Cheer et al., 2018).

--- SENTENCE 1002 ---
Access to Fagatele Bay is limited, as the adjacent land is privately owned and requires a small fee for access.

--- SENTENCE 1003 ---
However, Fagatele Bay is visited by eco tours associated with cruise ship visits.

--- SENTENCE 1004 ---
The beach at Fogama'a is becoming

more popular with local residents and visitors and is used for both day access and overnight camping.

--- SENTENCE 1005 ---
However, visitor numbers remain fairly low (<20 people on busy days).

--- SENTENCE 1006 ---
The Aunu'u and Ta'u units are used by local residents, but are not currently significant tourist destinations.

--- SENTENCE 1007 ---
There are no maintained trails to reach the Ta'u unit, so access by land is limited.

--- SENTENCE 1008 ---
Swains Island and Rose Atoll are occasionally visited by researchers but are not readily accessible to tourists.

--- SENTENCE 1009 ---
There are few locally owned pleasure or charter boats.

--- SENTENCE 1010 ---
Local alia (fishing vessels based on traditional design) and sportfishing boats visit the Fagalua/Fogama'a, Aunu'u Multiple Use Zone, and Ta'u units to engage in fishing activities, including bottom fishing and spearfishing.

--- SENTENCE 1011 ---
Sportfishing for pelagic tuna, masimasi, and marlin is popular, and occasional fishing tournaments are held.

--- SENTENCE 1012 ---
The Aunu'u and Ta'u units are visited for pelagic fishing, but most pelagic fishing activity takes place in offshore waters outside sanctuary units.

--- SENTENCE 1013 ---
There are currently two commercial scuba diving operations in American Samoa, but recreational diving is infrequent due to lack of demand.

--- SENTENCE 1014 ---
Yachts occasionally enter Pago Pago Harbor to buy provisions and find shelter during the cyclone season and may visit the sanctuary units, but the sanctuary's anchoring prohibitions and lack of mooring buoys make this difficult for yacht operators.

--- SENTENCE 1015 ---
Potential impacts to NMSAS units due to visitation include unregulated fishing, illegal collection of invertebrates, and damage to the reef from boat anchors and walking on the reef flat.

## <span id="page-80-0"></span>*Nuisance Species Outbreaks*

American Samoa has not identified any significant marine invasive species threats, but there are a number of species that experience outbreaks that are detrimental to ecosystem health.

--- SENTENCE 1016 ---
These include CoTS, a tunicate (*Diplosoma similis*), and a green bubble algae (*Valonia fasciculata*).

--- SENTENCE 1017 ---
The most serious of these is CoTS, which are coral-eating echinoderms whose populations periodically increase to outbreak levels and cause widespread coral mortality.

--- SENTENCE 1018 ---
CoTS are a natural component of Indo-Pacific coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 1019 ---
Under normal conditions, CoTS prefer fast growing coral species (e.g., *Acropora* and *Montipora*; Pratchett, 2007) and may open up space for slower growing coral species (e.g., *Porites*) to recruit.

--- SENTENCE 1020 ---
As long as disturbances are infrequent, new coral recruitment and growth will replace the damage caused by the sea star.

--- SENTENCE 1021 ---
At outbreak levels, however, CoTS can have severe impacts on reef ecosystems (Pratchett et al., 2014).

--- SENTENCE 1022 ---
CoTS eat the soft tissues of corals, often killing the coral colony, and each sea star consumes 13 to 134 km<sup>2</sup> of coral each year (Dixon, 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1023 ---
In the late 1970s, a major outbreak of CoTS around Tutuila destroyed 80–90% of corals in Fagatele Bay (Birkeland et al., 1987).

--- SENTENCE 1024 ---
This severe and destructive event in one of the most pristine and coral-rich bays in American Samoa propelled the designation of Fagatele Bay as a national marine sanctuary, which would promote the future designation of NMSAS and its protection as a special place.

--- SENTENCE 1025 ---
More recently, another CoTS outbreak in 2014–2017 threatened corals around the island of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 1026 ---
There is increasing evidence that overfishing of CoTS natural predators and eutrophication associated with land based sources of pollution contributes to the increased frequency of outbreaks throughout the Pacific (Brodie et al., 2005; Fabricius et al., 2010; Cowan et al., 2017, 2020; Pratchett et al., 2021).

--- SENTENCE 1027 ---
Management agencies across the Pacific, including NMSAS and the

#### Pressures on Sanctuary Resources

National Park of American Samoa, are increasingly taking direct action, such as physical removal or injections, to reduce problematic populations of CoTS.

--- SENTENCE 1028 ---
In 2008, the tunicate *Diplosoma similis* was observed overgrowing live coral and benthic substrate along the north-northwest side of Swains Island (Vargas-Ángel et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 1029 ---
This raised concern about a potential shift in the reef habitat, but the outbreak subsided by 2010.

--- SENTENCE 1030 ---
More recently, the American Samoa Coral Reef Advisory Group and the National Park of American Samoa have been following an outbreak of the green bubble algae *Valonia fastigiata* in the Ofu pools.

--- SENTENCE 1031 ---
This algae has spread from a small patch to an extensive area and is now overgrowing corals in the area.

--- SENTENCE 1032 ---
No outbreaks have been reported in NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 1033 ---
Corallivorous snails (*Drupella* and *Coralliophila* spp.) can also form smaller outbreaks and impact corals (Cumming, 2009; Hamman, 2018).

--- SENTENCE 1034 ---
Managers are concerned that shifts in land-based sources of pollution and changes in ocean conditions related to climate change may increase outbreaks or introduce invasive species.

--- SENTENCE 1035 ---
## <span id="page-81-0"></span>*Research Activities*

The NMSAS science program is growing and research is encouraged within sanctuary units.

--- SENTENCE 1036 ---
Projects often require the installation of scientific instruments, markers, or buoys.

--- SENTENCE 1037 ---
This has included the placement of two oceanographic buoys (a Moored Autonomous Partial Pressure of Carbon Dioxide [MAPCO2] buoy in Fagatele Bay and a wave buoy in the Aunu'u Research Zone), a climate station in Fagatele Bay with oceanographic instruments and settlement structures, an ecological acoustic recorder in Fagatele Bay, monitoring markers, and contaminant and sediment monitoring devices.

--- SENTENCE 1038 ---
NMSAS evaluated the value of each project and worked with the researchers to minimize impacts to sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 1039 ---
Although there is a potential for impacts, no significant damage due to research activities has been observed.

--- SENTENCE 1040 ---
This section provides summaries of resource status and trends within four areas: water quality, habitat, living resources, and maritime heritage resources.

--- SENTENCE 1041 ---
Virtual workshops were convened with subject matter experts from August to November 2020 to discuss and evaluate a series of questions about each resource area.

--- SENTENCE 1042 ---
It is important to note that, in general, the assessments of status and trends in National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa (NMSAS) are for the period from 2007–2020.

--- SENTENCE 1043 ---
However, in some cases, data series extend into 2021.

--- SENTENCE 1044 ---
Answers for each question are supported by data and the rationale is provided at the end of each section for each resource area.

--- SENTENCE 1045 ---
Where published or additional information exists, the reader is provided with appropriate references.

--- SENTENCE 1046 ---
Workshop discussions and ratings were based on data available at the time (e.g., through 2020).

--- SENTENCE 1047 ---
However, in some instances, sanctuary staff later incorporated newly available data in order to more accurately describe the current status and trends of resources.

--- SENTENCE 1048 ---
Situations where data were used by sanctuary staff to support a rating, but were not presented or discussed during the workshop, are noted in the text.

--- SENTENCE 1049 ---
More information about each question can be found in Appendix A and additional information about the methods used to complete the assessments can be found in Appendix D.

## <span id="page-83-0"></span>*Water Quality (Questions 1–5)*

The following is an assessment of the status and trends of water quality indicators in NMSAS from 2007–2020.

--- SENTENCE 1050 ---
Question 1 focuses on eutrophication and its impacts on sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 1051 ---
Eutrophication is usually caused by an excess amount of nutrients (primarily nitrogen and phosphorus) entering the ocean and leading to an increase in the growth of algae, including microalgae (phytoplankton), macroalgae (seaweed), and filamentous algae (turf).

--- SENTENCE 1052 ---
Question 2 focuses on parameters affecting public health.

--- SENTENCE 1053 ---
Human health concerns can arise from water, beach, and/or seafood contamination (bacteria or chemical).

--- SENTENCE 1054 ---
Question 3 focuses on shifts in water quality due to climate drivers.

--- SENTENCE 1055 ---
Climate indicators include water temperature, ocean acidification and calcification rates, and sea level rise.

--- SENTENCE 1056 ---
Increases in water temperature cause coral bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease.

--- SENTENCE 1057 ---
Acidification can affect organism survival, growth, and reproduction.

--- SENTENCE 1058 ---
Sea level rise causes increased erosion.

--- SENTENCE 1059 ---
Question 4 assesses other biotic and abiotic stressors, individually or in combination, that may influence sanctuary water quality, but were not addressed in the above questions, such as turbidity and iron pollution from ship groundings.

--- SENTENCE 1060 ---
Human activities that adversely impact water quality are the focus of Question 5.

--- SENTENCE 1061 ---
These include terrestrial point source discharges, commercial and recreational vessel-based activities, and coastal development.

## <span id="page-83-1"></span>**Question 1: What is the eutrophic condition of sanctuary waters and how is it changing?

--- SENTENCE 1062 ---
Eutrophication has not been documented, or does not appear to have the potential to negatively affect ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 1063 ---
**Rationale:** Data on eutrophication are limited, but available data suggest that nitrogen, phosphorus, and chlorophyll *a* concentrations remain below recommended threshold levels in sanctuary waters.

--- SENTENCE 1064 ---
However, dissolved inorganic nitrogen may be increasing in Fagatele Bay based on the most recent data.

--- SENTENCE 1065 ---
Macroalgae cover was evaluated as a proxy for nutrients and has been variable over the reporting period, but remains low overall within sanctuary units.

--- SENTENCE 1083 ---

Quantitative data on eutrophication within NMSAS boundaries are limited.

--- SENTENCE 1084 ---
Data collection has been intermittent and focused on nearshore habitats, particularly streams, sandy shores, and coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 1085 ---
Fagatele Bay is the exception; its designation as a "pristine" watershed by the American Samoa Environmental Protection Agency (AS-EPA) made it an ideal control site for studies throughout the reporting period.

--- SENTENCE 1086 ---
Data for pelagic areas are limited to satellite-derived datasets and no recent data are available for mesophotic and deep-sea habitats.

--- SENTENCE 1087 ---
Recent modeling efforts suggest that DIN loading in Fagatele Bay and Fagalua/Fogama'a units are likely low compared to other coastal areas in Tutuila (Shuler & Comeros-Raynal, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 1088 ---
Fagatele Bay had the lowest nutrient concentration out of 28 watersheds sampled by Comeros-Raynal et al. (2017, 2019) throughout Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 1089 ---
Fagalua/Fogama'a, Aunu'u, Ta'u, Rose Atoll, and Swains Island were not included in the analysis.

--- SENTENCE 1090 ---
Overall, nutrient levels were below the AS-EPA water quality standard for embayments ("median not to exceed"), but recent nutrient measurements in Fagatele Bay were higher than previous studies, suggesting either fluctuating or increasing nutrient levels in the bay from land-based sources or perhaps other sources, such as submarine groundwater discharge (Whitall et al., 2022; Comeros-Raynal et al., 2021; Figure S.WQ.1.1).

--- SENTENCE 1091 ---
Workshop experts noted that discharge from the landfill and agricultural activities in the nearby watershed may be influencing nutrient dynamics within both Fagatele Bay and Fagalua/Fogama'a units and recommended continued monitoring of nutrients in these units.

--- SENTENCE 1092 ---
The high proportion of nitrate in DIN measurements from Fagatele Bay suggests these are possible sources of nitrogen enrichment.

--- SENTENCE 1093 ---
In 2010, NOAA's National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) collected and analyzed water samples from coral reef habitats around all of the islands in American Samoa (ESD, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 1094 ---
The results indicated that phosphate, nitrate, nitrite, and total nitrogen across all islands of American Samoa were below AS-EPA-recommended levels for open ocean waters (Figure S.WQ.1.2).

--- SENTENCE 1095 ---
However, these samples were limited to one point in time and no recent data are available, therefore it is not possible to determine any trends in open ocean nutrient levels.

!

--- SENTENCE 1096 ---
Comparison of Ridge to Reef (sampled in 2016) and National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS; sampled in 2019) nutrient data for Fagatele Bay (average +/- standard error [SE]).

--- SENTENCE 1097 ---
The R2R study did not evaluate HPO4, HSiO3, Urea, or total P. Source: Whitall et al., 2022; Comeros-Raynal et al., 2021

!

--- SENTENCE 1098 ---
Nutrient data collected in 2010 around all islands in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 1099 ---
Data have been converted to mg/L (average +/- standard deviation [SD]) to compare with AS-EPA standards.

--- SENTENCE 1100 ---
Source: ESD, 2020

Chlorophyll *a* is a useful indicator of eutrophication, as it measures the amount of primary production in the water column.

--- SENTENCE 1101 ---
Data on chlorophyll *a* concentrations in sanctuary units are sparse for most of the reporting period, so no trend data are available.

--- SENTENCE 1102 ---
Data from grab samples in 2010 and 2012 indicated that chlorophyll *a* levels were within the AS-EPA water quality standards for open coastal waters (ESD, 2020; Tuitele et al., 2018; Figure S.WQ.1.3).

--- SENTENCE 1103 ---
Since May 2019, chlorophyll *a* has been measured consistently by a sensor on the Moored Autonomous Partial Pressure of Carbon Dioxide (MAPCO2) buoy located in Fagatele Bay (Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory

--- SENTENCE 1104 ---
[PMEL], 2020; PacIOOS, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 1105 ---
The buoy has recorded low chlorophyll *a* levels throughout the year, with slightly higher values from October–May; however, these data have not been verified and are insufficient to evaluate long-term trends.

--- SENTENCE 1106 ---
No other *in situ* data are available for any of the other sanctuary units.

--- SENTENCE 1107 ---
Satellite monitoring of the waters around American Samoa indicates that chlorophyll *a* concentrations are generally low across the territory (<0.1 mg/m2), with some slight seasonal fluctuations (Figure S.WQ.1.4).

--- SENTENCE 1108 ---
Based on these limited data, chlorophyll *a* levels do not indicate eutrophication in sanctuary units.

!

--- SENTENCE 1109 ---
** Average chlorophyll *a* values (+/- SE) from grab samples at all islands in American Samoa in 2010 and 2012.

--- SENTENCE 1110 ---
All values are below the AS water quality standard of 0.25 μg/L for open ocean coastal waters (Tuitele et al., 2018).

--- SENTENCE 1111 ---
Source: ESD, 2020

!

--- SENTENCE 1112 ---
The NOAA Center for Satellite Applications and Research Ocean Color Science Team has created experimental data products to illustrate chlorophyll *a* concentrations using satellite-derived datasets.

--- SENTENCE 1113 ---
The long-term climatology indicates that chlorophyll *a* concentrations are low (approximately 0.03–1 mg m3) in the waters surrounding American Samoa, with some enrichment around populated islands.

--- SENTENCE 1114 ---
Source: NOAA Center for Satellite Applications and Research, 2022a, 2022b

Macroalgae are another indicator of eutrophication, as cover tends to increase with nutrient inputs.

--- SENTENCE 1115 ---
Local and federal monitoring programs have recorded low macroalgae abundances across all sanctuary units throughout the reporting period (Fenner, 2013b; MARC 2020; Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019; Coral Reef Advisory Group

--- SENTENCE 1116 ---
Some temporal fluctuations have been observed, including a drop in cover in 2018 (Figure S.WQ.1.5), but macroalgae cover has generally remained low (<10% on average) throughout the years.

--- SENTENCE 1117 ---
Benthic camera tows along the Tutuila insular shelf in 2002, 2004, and 2008 indicated that macroalgae was low in the upper and lower mesophotic zones, but higher (15–20%) in the 50–79 m depth zone (Bare et al., 2010).

--- SENTENCE 1118 ---
However, there was considerable variation across sites and these surveys have not been repeated, so this may not reflect current mesophotic conditions in NMSAS.

!

--- SENTENCE 1119 ---
Macroalgae cover in NMSAS units between 2015 and 2018.

--- SENTENCE 1120 ---
Image: Modified from Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019

### *Conclusion*

Quantitative data on eutrophication within NMSAS boundaries are limited.

--- SENTENCE 1121 ---
Data for Fagatele Bay are more robust and indicate that nutrient levels are below recommended thresholds, but may be increasing, likely due to the presence of a landfill and increased agriculture in the surrounding watershed.

--- SENTENCE 1122 ---
Macroalgae cover remains low within shallow coral reef habitats, and satellite data for chlorophyll *a* indicate low concentrations throughout the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 1123 ---
Quantitative *in situ* data are not available for pelagic, mesophotic, and deep-sea habitats, and experts recommended more frequent and expanded sampling across sanctuary units to address these gaps.

## <span id="page-89-0"></span>**Question 2: Do sanctuary waters pose risks to human health and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 1124 ---
One or more water quality indicators suggest the potential for human health impacts, but human health impacts have not been reported.

--- SENTENCE 1125 ---
There are currently no known human health risks from NMSAS waters; however, data are limited and no trend data are available.

--- SENTENCE 1126 ---
Contaminants were detected in Fagatele Bay, but only nickel concentrations exceeded toxicology screening levels.

--- SENTENCE 1127 ---
Coliform bacteria have been detected in Fagatele Bay and there is a sewage outfall in the Aunu'u Multipurpose Zone, but sanctuary units are not part of regular water sampling efforts, so any potential health impact is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1128 ---
No ciguatera poisoning has been reported from fish caught in the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 1129 ---

--- SENTENCE 1150 ---
|

Heavy metals, pesticides, bacteria, and harmful algal blooms can have detrimental impacts on human health through direct contact or bioaccumulation in organisms used for food.

--- SENTENCE 1151 ---
Some of these are linked to human activities through runoff, groundwater contamination, or sewer outfalls.

--- SENTENCE 1152 ---
Two known sources of potential contamination include the Futiga landfill, located north of the Fagatele Bay and Fagalua/Fogama'a units, and a sewage outfall on the western side of Aunu'u (see the Pressures chapter for more information).

--- SENTENCE 1153 ---
Incidents of ciguatera fish poisoning from *Gambierdiscus* blooms have been reported in American Samoa, but there is no clear link to human activities.

--- SENTENCE 1154 ---
As most of NMSAS has been perceived as "pristine," quantitative data on these indicators within sanctuary boundaries are very limited.

--- SENTENCE 1155 ---
The Futiga landfill has been used as a municipal waste disposal site since the 1960s.

--- SENTENCE 1156 ---
The landfill was recompacted in 2018 to extend its lifespan, but is nearing its capacity.

--- SENTENCE 1157 ---
The lack of a liner and leachate collection system has caused concern about potential contamination to adjacent waters.

--- SENTENCE 1158 ---
In 2019, NCCOS tested for the presence of contaminants in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1159 ---
They collected sediment samples at eight sites across the bay to screen for heavy metals (Figure S.WQ.2.1).

--- SENTENCE 1160 ---
Values were compared to known toxicity ratings originally assembled by Long et al. (1995).

--- SENTENCE 1161 ---
In total, 17 metals were detected, but only nickel was present in concentrations above the ERL value, indicating that it may be toxic to benthic infauna (Figure S.WQ.2.1).

--- SENTENCE 1162 ---
All values from Fagatele Bay were below values previously recorded from other sites in Tutuila (Whitall et al., 2022).

!

--- SENTENCE 1163 ---
The concentration of nickel in sediment samples taken from three sites in Fagatele Bay was above the ERL value, indicating possible toxicity to benthic infauna.

--- SENTENCE 1164 ---
At one site, the concentration was above the ERM value (51.6 μg/g), which may indicate toxicity to benthic infauna.

--- SENTENCE 1165 ---
Source: Whitall et al., 2022

To detect pesticides, hydrocarbon derivatives (PAHs), and pharmaceutical compounds, the same study deployed Continuous Low-Level Aquatic Monitoring samplers (CLAMs) at eight sites within Fagatele Bay (Figure S.WQ.2.2).

--- SENTENCE 1166 ---
CLAMs are *in situ* submersible field extraction units that are able to continuously sample by filtering water at a known flow rate.

--- SENTENCE 1167 ---
Results indicate that the vast majority of the 400 compounds tested were not detectable.

--- SENTENCE 1168 ---
However, 30 organic compounds were detected.

--- SENTENCE 1169 ---
None of these exceeded published LC50 values (where available), defined as the lethal concentration required to kill 50% of tested organisms.

--- SENTENCE 1170 ---
Of the compounds that were detected in Fagatele Bay, most were orders of magnitude below the LC50 values.

--- SENTENCE 1171 ---
However, LC50s are not available for nine of the detected PAHs and two of the detected organic compounds due to their water solubility or recent invention.

--- SENTENCE 1172 ---
While no immediate threats to human health were detected, these compounds may have sublethal effects (e.g., endocrine disruption).

--- SENTENCE 1173 ---
The fact that pesticides, PAHs, and pharmaceutical compounds were detected in Fagatele Bay is concerning and should be monitored (Whitall et al., 2022).

!

--- SENTENCE 1174 ---
In 2019, NCCOS collected water samples using CLAM devices at 8 sites in Fagatele Bay to evaluate the concentration of contaminants in the water.

--- SENTENCE 1175 ---
Thirty organic compounds were detected in low quantities.

--- SENTENCE 1176 ---
Source: Whitall et al., 2022

AS-EPA monitors popular recreational beaches around Tutuila for the presence of enterococci bacteria, which may indicate fecal contamination from animals or humans (Tuitele et al., 2018; Sunia et al., 2020; American Samoa Environmental Protection Agency

--- SENTENCE 1177 ---
However, none of their beach monitoring sites are within NMSAS boundaries.

--- SENTENCE 1178 ---
Monitoring sites in villages closest to the sanctuary (Leala-Taputimu Sliding Rock, Aunu'u Wharf, Ta'u Beach) generally have few advisories, but AS-EPA occasionally recommends avoiding swimming at

these sites (mostly Leala-Taputimu; Tuitele et al., 2018; Sunia et al., 2020; AS-EPA, 2021).

--- SENTENCE 1179 ---
AS-EPA's 2020 integrated monitoring report noted that Fagatele-Larson watershed was listed as impaired and was assigned a "Not Supporting (fair)" status for aquatic life in ocean shoreline waters in 2014 as a result of an "Undetermined NPS [nonpoint source] Stressor"; however, subsequent testing found the watershed was "Fully Supporting" (Sunia et al., 2020).

--- SENTENCE 1180 ---
In 2019, NCCOS analyzed water sampled at around 3 m depth at eight sites within Fagatele Bay and the inflowing stream for coliform bacteria and *E. coli*

--- SENTENCE 1181 ---
(Whitall et al., 2022).

--- SENTENCE 1182 ---
All samples tested positive for coliform bacteria and over half of the samples tested positive for *E. coli*, indicating that mammalian (e.g., bat, pig, human) wastes are entering the bay.

--- SENTENCE 1183 ---
However, this was a limited sampling effort and additional sampling is needed to evaluate whether these bacteria present a human health risk.

--- SENTENCE 1184 ---
Experts noted that a sewage outfall in the Aunu'u Multipurpose Zone may be a potential source of contamination.

--- SENTENCE 1185 ---
The wastewater collection system for the village consists of a wet well with a grinder pump, and untreated sewage is discharged through an ocean outfall in shallow water on a fringing coral reef.

--- SENTENCE 1186 ---
It was constructed by the American Samoa Power Authority to protect shallow groundwater resources impacted by septic tanks and leach fields.

--- SENTENCE 1187 ---
Surveys conducted prior to 2007 indicate that bacterial counts for the waters in the area around the sewage outfall met American Samoa water quality standards for recreational beaches, although the location and depth of the outfall indicate a potential for unacceptable bacterial levels along these beaches.

--- SENTENCE 1188 ---
In 2007, the AS-EPA and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency developed a wastewater facilities plan for the village and island of Aunu'u (AS-EPA, 2007), but it was not implemented due to other American Samoa Power Authority priorities.

--- SENTENCE 1189 ---
Ciguatera fish poisoning is caused by eating reef fish that are contaminated with ciguatoxin, a chemical produced by the dinoflagellate *Gambierdiscus toxicus*, which grows on algae that are eaten by herbivorous fish and bioaccumulates in larger fish through the food web.

--- SENTENCE 1190 ---
Ciguatera fish poisoning rarely causes death, but symptoms can last for months.

--- SENTENCE 1191 ---
It has been reported from Tutuila (Clemens, 1997)

--- SENTENCE 1192 ---
but there are limited data on the incidence of ciguatera in American Samoa and which species of fish or areas pose the greatest risk.

--- SENTENCE 1193 ---
No cases of ciguatera fish poisoning from fish caught in the sanctuary have been reported.

### *Conclusion*

Contaminants have been detected in Fagatele Bay, which poses some concern; however, levels are below documented thresholds for human health risks.

--- SENTENCE 1194 ---
Additional testing is necessary to determine if there is bacterial contamination of sanctuary waters, particularly Fagatele Bay, Fagalua/Fogama'a, and Aunu'u, based on identified threats.

--- SENTENCE 1195 ---
Human contact with pelagic and remote areas is limited, but risks should be evaluated in the future.

--- SENTENCE 1196 ---
## <span id="page-94-0"></span>**Question 3: Have recent, accelerated changes in climate altered water conditions and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 1197 ---
Climate related changes have caused measurable, but not severe, degradation in some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 1198 ---
Increasing sea surface temperatures have caused more frequent and more severe coral bleaching events.

--- SENTENCE 1199 ---
Ocean acidification is affecting water quality worldwide; however, aragonite saturation state and calcification rates have remained high in sanctuary units.

Climate change and ocean acidification are global pressures that are expected to increase sea surface and air temperatures, raise sea levels, make oceans more acidic, shift cyclone and rainfall patterns, and eventually impact oceanic currents, ocean stratification, and thermohaline circulation.

--- SENTENCE 1242 ---
The widespread effects of climate change are likely to affect all sanctuary waters from the surface to the deep sea, but shallow ecosystems, such as coral reefs, are expected to be the first affected.

--- SENTENCE 1243 ---
Satellite-derived data indicate a steady increase in SST across American Samoa over the last few decades (Coral Reef Watch, 2020; Figure S.WQ.3.1).

--- SENTENCE 1244 ---
Shallow coral reef habitats are particularly susceptible to rising temperatures as corals live very close to their upper thermal tolerances (Jokiel & Coles, 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1245 ---
Temperature increases of just 1–2°C above local averages persisting for several weeks can cause widespread coral bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 1246 ---
As water temperatures have increased, so have the frequency and intensity of bleaching events (Coral Reef Watch, 2020).

--- SENTENCE 1247 ---
Bleaching events were documented in American Samoa in 2015 (Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019), 2017, and 2020.

--- SENTENCE 1248 ---
*In situ* temperature measurements indicate that the timing and magnitude of temperature patterns are similar across all of the islands.

--- SENTENCE 1249 ---
However, mean temperatures at Swains Island are 0.4°C higher in the summer (Dec–Mar) and 0.8°C higher in the winter (Jul–Oct) than the other

islands and, in 2016, Swains Island experienced an unprecedented high water temperature of almost 31°C.

--- SENTENCE 1250 ---
Experts believe this was the cause of a staggering decline (>60%) in the number of *Pocillopora* coral colonies at Swains Island between 2015–2018 (Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019;

--- SENTENCE 1251 ---
Detailed data on bleaching prevalence and associated mortality in sanctuary units were not collected during these events.

!

--- SENTENCE 1252 ---
