### **Aircraft**

Between 1900–1950, American Samoa was under the administration of the Department of the Navy, and during the years of World War II, Tutuila supported a naval air station.

--- SENTENCE 2516 ---
As a consequence of intensive wartime training and patrols, 43 naval aircraft were recorded as having ditched or crashed into American Samoan waters between 1942–1944, mainly in the vicinity of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2517 ---
None of these aircraft have been located or identified in the sanctuary or territory.

--- SENTENCE 2518 ---
Tutuila may also be the site of one of the most famous commercial aircraft crashes in Pacific history.

--- SENTENCE 2519 ---
On January 12, 1939, Captain Edwin C. Musick, along with his six-man aircrew, suffered a fatal explosion and crashed into the ocean approximately 12 miles northwest of Pago Pago.

--- SENTENCE 2520 ---
Musick had inaugurated the Panamerican Flying Clipper service in the Pacific, the first transoceanic air link in the region.

--- SENTENCE 2521 ---
A 2019 deep-sea acoustic survey for the aircraft (Figure S.MH.14.3) was conducted by the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation and OET, but the site was not located (Matthews, 2020).

!

--- SENTENCE 2522 ---
The Sikorsky S42 is the type of flying boat aircraft flown by PanAmerican/Edwin C. Musick and lost north of Tutuila Island in 1939.

--- SENTENCE 2523 ---
Library of Congress

Contemporary losses can also have significant cultural impacts.

--- SENTENCE 2524 ---
In 2014, a father and son team (Babar and Haris Suleman) were attempting an around-the-world flight, when their Beech A36 Bonanza aircraft developed problems and crashed shortly after takeoff from Pago Pago.

--- SENTENCE 2525 ---
The father's body was never recovered (Barbash, 2014).

--- SENTENCE 2526 ---
### **Coastal Archaeological Sites/Features**

As of 2002, the American Samoa Historic Preservation Office's archaeological sites database maintained a record of 691 sites throughout the territory.

--- SENTENCE 2527 ---
As the largest and most populous island in American Samoa, there are numerous archaeological sites on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2528 ---
However, only a few are known within or adjacent to marine and coastal/shoreline locations.

--- SENTENCE 2529 ---
These include features such as whetstones, petroglyphs, grinding holes/bait cups (Figure S.MH.14.4), and certain archaeological sites of coastal villages.

!

--- SENTENCE 2530 ---
Foāga (grinding stone holes or bait cups) found at Fagatele Bay are indicative of early Samoan settlement in ancient times.

--- SENTENCE 2531 ---
Carved into the shoreline along the reef edge, the stone holes may have been used to sharpen basalt stone tools or to collect sea water to make sea salt.

--- SENTENCE 2532 ---
Photo: Hans Van Tilburg/NOAA

The 2010 article *Damage to Archaeological Sites on Tutuila Island (American Samoa)

--- SENTENCE 2533 ---
Following the 29 September 2009 Tsunami* (Addison et al., 2010) assessed post-tsunami impacts to shoreline cultural resource sites.

--- SENTENCE 2534 ---
More than fifty nearshore sites were identified during the survey.

--- SENTENCE 2535 ---
They ranged in size from whole coastal settlements (e.g., Fagafue, Aoloau Tuai) to single, isolated artifacts and included major lithic manufacture sites, exposed stratigraphy with cultural layers, and a variety of other archaeological remains.

--- SENTENCE 2536 ---
The authors found:

The presence of exposed stratigraphy with cultural strata at several locations around the island suggests that Tutuila's coasts are eroding and that archaeological deposits are being lost in coastal areas.

--- SENTENCE 2537 ---
Global climate change and sea-level rise should inspire a sense of urgency for the excavation and detailed study of these deposits before they are completely gone.

--- SENTENCE 2538 ---
In 2013, ONMS, along with partner agencies, conducted a multidisciplinary survey of Swains Island (Van Tilburg et al., 2013).

--- SENTENCE 2539 ---
The fieldwork involved three areas of inter-related research: 1) a geomorphology survey that revealed the previous channel (now a filled swale) leading into the brackish lake; 2) a maritime archaeology survey of the lake and nearshore marine locations that identified historic and prehistoric maritime heritage resources; and 3) a terrestrial archaeology survey on land that identified 19th-century historic and possible prehistoric cultural artifacts from previous habitation phases.

--- SENTENCE 2540 ---
The project also resulted in the 2014 documentary *Swains Island—One of the Last Jewels of the Planet* by the Ocean Futures Society.

--- SENTENCE 2541 ---
#### **Shoreline Pillboxes**

The remnants of numerous concrete pillboxes along the shoreline, as well as gun emplacements, bunkers, naval buildings, foundations, etc., are the more visible reminders of the World War II period in American Samoa (Kennedy et al., 2005).

--- SENTENCE 2542 ---
A National Register of Historic Places multiple property nomination for many of these World War II sites was prepared in 2005.

--- SENTENCE 2543 ---
Although outside of sanctuary boundaries, nearshore coastal pillbox sites are associated with the U.S. Marines and with the local Fitafita Samoan Marines (Figure S.MH.14.5).

--- SENTENCE 2544 ---
Individual pillboxes in the surf zone are subject to continuing erosion and change, and some have been knocked down, broken, or displaced.

--- SENTENCE 2545 ---
Still, these resources are robust, and even when impacted by erosion, may still be considered eligible for nomination to the National Register of Historic Places, as they are close enough to their original position and still retain their historic and educational value.

!

--- SENTENCE 2546 ---
** World War II pillbox defensive structures are located along the shorelines of Tutuila, where they are slowly being impacted by coastal erosion.

--- SENTENCE 2547 ---
Photo: Hans Van Tilburg/NOAA

### **Geocultural Features**

There are a number of legends and stories represented by natural features or specific locations within the coastal and marine context.

--- SENTENCE 2548 ---
Even specific locations underwater, such as freshwater springs or passages in the reef, can be associated with cultural folklore (Van Tilburg, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 2549 ---
Features of the landscape and seascape are visible touchstones of oral history.

--- SENTENCE 2550 ---
According to Volk et al. (1992):

These sites are of extraordinary significance to Samoan culture.

--- SENTENCE 2551 ---
Compared to all of the archaeological and historic sites that the [Historic Preservation Office] tries to protect, these sites are seen as the most significant to local residents.

--- SENTENCE 2552 ---
(p. 32)

Examples of geocultural locations include Turtle and Shark Cove, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

--- SENTENCE 2553 ---
No negative impacts, or obstacles to access these cultural locations, are apparent (see the heritage and sense of place discussion in the Ecosystem Services section, which describes geocultural locations in NMSAS).

#### **Other Types of Resources**

Other resources and topics that enhance our understanding of maritime heritage within the territory and advance possible topics for future research both within and beyond the boundaries of NMSAS include:

- Reported World War II–era disposal of lots of vehicles, equipment, and even ammunition over the reef at Faga'alu Bay the elementary school (outside NMSAS boundaries);
- Reports from fishermen about ammunition (unexploded ordnance, disposed military munitions) located on Taema Bank and also at deeper locations off the north side of Tutuila Island (outside NMSAS boundaries);
- Unexploded ordnance at Rose Atoll (within NMSAS boundaries);
- Deterioration of the Rose Atoll concrete monument (USFWS jurisdiction);
- Basalt stones/boulders recorded at Rose Atoll both by 19th-century observers and on recent surveys by archaeologists (outside NMSAS boundaries; Sachet, 1954; Pickering, 1876; Kramer, 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2554 ---
### *Conclusion*

Maritime heritage resources are the tangible and intangible properties (archaeological, cultural, historical resources) that capture our human connections to Great Lakes and ocean areas.

--- SENTENCE 2555 ---
Current ONMS knowledge of the nature, location, and significance of maritime heritage resources within NMSAS is limited.

--- SENTENCE 2556 ---
Significant data gaps exist for field assessments of submerged shipwrecks and aircraft, the updated condition of nearshore/coastal archaeological sites and features (since 2010), and the identification of geocultural locations, including associated folklore and Samoan place names.

--- SENTENCE 2557 ---
The most relevant information for addressing the condition of maritime heritage resources in the sanctuary comes from the existing desk-based assessment of heritage resources for the entirety of American Samoa, which includes the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2558 ---
Therefore, resources outside NMSAS boundaries were considered in order to estimate possible conditions of potential resources within the sanctuary itself.

--- SENTENCE 2559 ---
In general, the

collective condition of maritime heritage resources is fair, as many known sites are in somewhat degraded condition, even though many have not been subject to human impacts that might otherwise diminish their aesthetic, cultural, historical, archaeological, scientific, or educational value.

--- SENTENCE 2560 ---
Maritime heritage resources have been subjected, however, to damaging natural forces like erosion and high-energy shoreline events, which are also cause for concern regarding trends and future conditions.

--- SENTENCE 2561 ---
Resources like submerged shipwrecks and aircraft, which likely exist within the sanctuary, are presumed to be slowly degrading, primarily due to natural processes.

## <span id="page-181-0"></span>**Question 15: What are the levels of human activities that may adversely affect maritime heritage resources and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 2562 ---
Some potentially damaging activities may exist, but they have not been shown to degrade maritime heritage resource condition.

--- SENTENCE 2563 ---
This question addresses human activities that may have adverse impacts, and is not meant to consider deterioration primarily due to natural processes.

--- SENTENCE 2564 ---
Based on observations by participating experts, few activities, either within or adjacent to NMSAS boundaries, are known to have the potential for adverse impacts to maritime heritage resources.

--- SENTENCE 2565 ---
Additionally, experts agreed that this low level of adverse activity has not changed since the previous condition report.

### *Key Data Sets*

NMSAS is not subject to many human activities that adversely impact maritime heritage resources.

--- SENTENCE 2566 ---
Potential activities that could have adverse impacts include:

- Anchor damage to submerged historic properties;
- Dredging channels/dumping dredge spoils;
- Trawling/fishing impacts of nets and lines to submerged properties;
- Illegal salvage of or damage to submerged shipwrecks and aircraft;
- Nearshore development, including coastal armoring or landfill, harbor/breakwater, pipeline, or submarine cable infrastructure;
- Offshore development, including submarine pipelines or cables, or renewable energy sources like wind turbines;
- Obstruction of public or practitioner access to culturally significant locations/features;
- Obstruction of cultural viewsheds by nearshore development or development of offshore wind turbines;
- Indirect impacts (e.g., sedimentation from land runoff or development).

--- SENTENCE 2567 ---
There are no indications of permissible human activities that might adversely affect maritime heritage resources within the sanctuary, but some activities could have general impacts to areas outside or adjacent to sanctuary boundaries.

--- SENTENCE 2568 ---
Due to limited formal studies and reports, evidence supporting this question relies heavily on personal experience of subject matter experts.

### **Nearshore Activities and Development**

Sand removal, or sand "mining," may be a cause of increased coastal erosion, but it is not known to occur in the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2569 ---
Sand mining for traditional use has been ongoing for years in the Fatu ma Futi area (e.g., beautification of the front yard during ceremonial events).

--- SENTENCE 2570 ---
Over the years, American Samoa has also experienced severe erosion at Utulei Beach as a result of climate change.

--- SENTENCE 2571 ---
Potential erosion due to the removal of sand in public places is of great concern.

--- SENTENCE 2572 ---
Palm trees once standing along the shoreline are now falling into the ocean.

--- SENTENCE 2573 ---
An area on Aunu'u may possibly be mined for sand (across from the sanctuary boundary), but that has not been confirmed.

--- SENTENCE 2574 ---
Shoreline armoring could impact maritime heritage resources or locations, but there are no current plans proposed for the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2575 ---
When under threat of erosion, it is common to consider a seawall as the fastest and most effective way to stabilize the coastline.

--- SENTENCE 2576 ---
Seawalls often bring other problems, including the loss of the high-tide beach and acceleration of erosion on adjacent land (Romine & Fletcher, 2012).

### **Offshore Activities and Development**

There are no offshore development activities that may impact maritime heritage resources within NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 2577 ---
A fiber optic submarine cable was recently installed outside of sanctuary boundaries.

--- SENTENCE 2578 ---
This project required that a sidescan sonar survey be conducted to confirm that no historic properties were located within the area of potential effect, a requirement of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (TeleGeography, 2020).

#### **Access to Cultural Resources**

There are no known activities that might obstruct access to culturally significant locations or features (e.g., Turtle and Shark Cove).

### **Other Activities and Impacts**

In 2016, the longline fishing vessel *No. 1 Ji Hyun* grounded on the western reef of Aunu'u (Figure S.MH.15.1).

--- SENTENCE 2579 ---
No historic properties, like submerged shipwrecks or aircraft, are known to be present in the affected area, but the reef itself is culturally important to the community of Aunu'u as a viewshed and a location for fishing, gathering, subsistence, and traditional practices.

--- SENTENCE 2580 ---
The grounding assessment report (Peau, 2018) states: "This area is of ecological and cultural significance for local residents using hook-and-line, casting nets, spearfishing (nonscuba assisted), and other non-destructive fishing methods, including those traditionally used for sustenance and cultural purposes such as gleaning" (p. XXX).

--- SENTENCE 2581 ---
The 2016 grounding represents the one activity that has degraded a location with heritage significance within the sanctuary (this event and its impact to the reef ecosystem is discussed further in the State of Habitat and State of Living Resources sections).

--- SENTENCE 2582 ---
The grounding highlighted the need for greater response capabilities and supplies and to create clearer processes for accountability from vessel owners who ground within sanctuary waters (Weinberg, 2016).

!

--- SENTENCE 2583 ---
The fishing vessel *No. 1 Ji Hyun*, grounded on the western reef of Aunu'u (within NMSAS), April 2016.

--- SENTENCE 2584 ---
Photo: NOAA

### *Conclusion*

Current ONMS knowledge of the nature, location, and significance of maritime heritage resources within NMSAS is limited, and this data gap in recording and understanding tangible heritage resources and culturally significant locations within sanctuary boundaries affects the assessment of potential adverse impacts to those resources from human activities.

--- SENTENCE 2585 ---
Nevertheless, it is clear from NMSAS staff knowledge and the workshop discussion that the site and community place high priority on cultural traditions and practices, and that few human activities within American Samoa have obvious adverse impacts to heritage resources or locations.

--- SENTENCE 2586 ---
Due to limited formal studies and reports, this assessment relies heavily on the experience of subject matter experts.

--- SENTENCE 2587 ---
Based on their input, the status was rated as good/fair.

--- SENTENCE 2588 ---
Additionally, there was agreement that this low level of adverse activity has not changed since the previous condition report.

--- SENTENCE 2589 ---
## **State of Ecosystem Services**

<span id="page-184-0"></span>Ecosystem services are the benefits that humans receive from natural and cultural resources.

--- SENTENCE 2590 ---
Generally, the taxonomy of the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) is used in ONMS condition reports.

--- SENTENCE 2591 ---
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) was an initiative of the United Nations to assess ecosystem services, including cultural, provisioning, regulating, and supporting services.

--- SENTENCE 2592 ---
Categories of ecosystem services include "final" services, which are directly valued by people, and "intermediate" services, which are ecological functions that support final services (Boyd & Banzhaf, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 2593 ---
In ONMS condition reports, only final ecosystem services are rated, which is consistent with the anthropogenic focus of the reports and highlights priority management successes and challenges in sanctuaries.

--- SENTENCE 2594 ---
The complete definitions of ecosystem services considered by ONMS are included in Appendix B.

There are two categories of ecosystem services: intermediate and final.

--- SENTENCE 2595 ---
Ecosystem services that are evaluated in condition reports are final ecosystem services.

--- SENTENCE 2596 ---
Intermediate services support other ecosystem services, whereas a good/service must be directly enjoyed by a person to be considered a final ecosystem service.

--- SENTENCE 2597 ---
For example, nutrient balance leads to clearer water and higher visibility for snorkeling and scuba diving.

--- SENTENCE 2598 ---
Nutrient balance is an intermediate service that supports the final ecosystem service of non-consumptive recreation via snorkeling and scuba diving.

### **Thirteen final ecosystem services may be rated in ONMS condition reports**

#### *Cultural* (non-material benefits)

- 1.

--- SENTENCE 2599 ---
Consumptive recreation Recreational activities that result in the removal of or harm to natural or cultural resources
- 2.

--- SENTENCE 2600 ---
Non-consumptive recreation Recreational activities that do not result in intentional removal of or harm to natural or cultural resources
- 3. Science

--- SENTENCE 2601 ---
The capacity to acquire and contribute information and knowledge
- 4.

--- SENTENCE 2602 ---
The capacity to acquire and provide intellectual enrichment
- 5.

--- SENTENCE 2603 ---
Heritage Recognition of historical and heritage legacy and cultural practices
- 6. Sense of Place Aesthetic attraction, spiritual significance, and location identity

#### *Provisioning* (material benefits)

- 7.

--- SENTENCE 2604 ---
Commercial harvest The capacity to support commercial market demand for seafood products
- 8.

--- SENTENCE 2605 ---
The capacity to support non-commercial demand for food and utilitarian products
- 9.

--- SENTENCE 2606 ---
Water Providing water for human use by minimizing pollution, including nutrients, sediments, pathogens, chemicals, and trash
- 10.

--- SENTENCE 2607 ---
Ornamentals Resources collected for decorative, aesthetic, or ceremonial purposes
- 11.

--- SENTENCE 2608 ---
Biotechnology Medicinal and other products derived or manufactured from sanctuary animals or plants for commercial use
- 12.

--- SENTENCE 2609 ---
Energy Use of ecosystem-derived materials or processes for the production of energy

#### *Regulating* (buffers to change)

13.

--- SENTENCE 2610 ---
Coastal protection — Flow regulation that protects habitats, property, coastlines, and other features

Notably, some consider consumptive recreational fishing as a provisioning service, but it is included here as a cultural ecosystem service due to the emphasis on recreation.

--- SENTENCE 2611 ---
Additionally, it is possible that services categorized as provisioning may also yield cultural benefits and support cultural activities.

--- SENTENCE 2612 ---
Also, even though biodiversity was listed as an ecosystem service by the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005), ONMS decided to remove it, recognizing that biodiversity is an attribute of the ecosystem on which many final ecosystem services depend (e.g., recreation, harvest); therefore, it is addressed in the State section of this report.

--- SENTENCE 2613 ---
Lastly, although ONMS listed climate stability as an ecosystem service in 2015, it is no longer considered an ecosystem service in ONMS condition reports, because national marine sanctuaries are not large enough to influence climate stability (Fisher et al., 2008, 2009).

--- SENTENCE 2614 ---
For National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa (NMSAS), nine of the 13 final ecosystem services were rated during the 2020 workshops: non-consumptive recreation, consumptive recreation, science, education, heritage, sense of place, commercial harvest, subsistence harvest, and coastal protection.

--- SENTENCE 2615 ---
The other four ecosystem services were evaluated by staff, but were determined not to be applicable to the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2616 ---
## <span id="page-186-0"></span>*Ecosystem Services Indicators*

The status and trends of ecosystem services are best evaluated using a combination of three types of indicators: economic, non-economic, and resource.

--- SENTENCE 2617 ---
Economic indicators may include direct measures of use (e.g., person-days of recreation, catch levels) that result in spending, income, jobs, gross regional product, and tax revenues, or non-market economic values (the difference between what people pay to use a good/service and what they would be willing to pay).

--- SENTENCE 2618 ---
Non-economic indicators can be used to complement economic indicators and include importance-satisfaction ratings for natural and cultural resources, facilities and services for recreation uses, limits of acceptable change for resource conditions, social values and preferences, social vulnerability indicators, perceptions of resource conditions in the present and expectations for the future, and access to resources.

--- SENTENCE 2619 ---
Finally, resource indicators are considered in determining status and trend ratings for each ecosystem service.

--- SENTENCE 2620 ---
Resource indicators are used to determine if current levels of use are sustainable or are causing degradation to resources.

--- SENTENCE 2621 ---
If resources cannot support current levels of use, this may downgrade a rating that may otherwise be higher based on economic and non-economic indicators alone.

--- SENTENCE 2622 ---
Together, these three types of indicators are considered when assessing the status and trends of ecosystem services in national marine sanctuaries.

--- SENTENCE 2623 ---
## <span id="page-186-1"></span>*Non-Consumptive Recreation*

**Recreational activities that do not result in intentional removal of or harm to natural or cultural resources**

!

--- SENTENCE 2624 ---
The capacity to provide the ecosystem service is compromised, and existing management would require enhancement to enable acceptable performance.

--- SENTENCE 2625 ---
Though it is clear that both physical conditions and infrastructure limit access for non-consumptive recreation activities in the sanctuary, the levels of existing activities are not well understood or quantified.

--- SENTENCE 2626 ---
The improving trend reflects sanctuary and partner outreach and education activities that highlight recreational opportunities in the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2627 ---
These create interest among residents and tourists in using the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2628 ---
Non-consumptive recreational activities are those that do not result in the intentional removal of or damage to natural and heritage resources.

--- SENTENCE 2629 ---
In national marine sanctuaries, these include activities such as swimming, snorkeling, scuba diving, boating, beach recreation, and beach camping.

--- SENTENCE 2630 ---
Sanctuaries are directed to facilitate recreational activities to the extent compatible with resource protection.

--- SENTENCE 2631 ---
The goals of NMSAS include increasing awareness of responsible use in the sanctuary and minimizing user impacts.

--- SENTENCE 2632 ---
The status of non-consumptive recreation is fair, as non-consumptive recreation is limited in most of the NMSAS units due to the remote nature of and limited or challenging access to these areas.

--- SENTENCE 2633 ---
Direct impacts to sanctuary resources from non-consumptive recreation appear to be minimal.

--- SENTENCE 2634 ---
The trend is improving, as NMSAS has implemented efforts to improve access during the reporting period.

--- SENTENCE 2635 ---
To access Fagatele Bay, most of Fagalua/Fogama'a, the Aunu'u Research Zone, and Ta'u, visitors must either hike across rough terrain or access the site by boat.

--- SENTENCE 2636 ---
There are no facilities at the sites, and land access is controlled by the traditional landowners.

--- SENTENCE 2637 ---
Limited area for beach camping is available adjacent to the Fagalua/Fogama'a unit, and campers often swim and fish within the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2638 ---
Rowing, kayaking, and paddling in these areas are impractical due to access constraints and reef structure.

--- SENTENCE 2639 ---
Residents of Aunu'u can easily access the Aunu'u Multipurpose Zone, which abuts the southern side of the village; however, the waves along this coast can be treacherous, making shore access to deeper waters dangerous at times.

--- SENTENCE 2640 ---
Visitors may access Aunu'u via a ferry from Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2641 ---
Access to Rose Atoll and Swains Island is restricted and requires a lengthy boat trip, making recreational access impractical.

--- SENTENCE 2642 ---
The remote nature of the units also makes it difficult to evaluate visitor use; therefore, no data are available to directly assess this service at Rose Atoll or Swains Island.

--- SENTENCE 2643 ---
Although there are no studies available that look specifically at non-consumptive recreational activities within the sanctuary itself, there have been studies that analyze marine-related activities and uses of the waters in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 2644 ---
For example, the National Coral Reef Monitoring Program conducted a socioeconomic survey in 2014 (Levine et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 2645 ---
The survey found that the most common non-consumptive recreational activities occurring in American Samoa were swimming, beach recreation, and beach camping (primarily at Fagalua/Fogama'a).

--- SENTENCE 2646 ---
Among residents of American Samoa surveyed (n = 448), 47% reported swimming more than once per month, 21% reported participating in beach recreation at least once in the past month, and 16% reported beach camping more than once per month.

--- SENTENCE 2647 ---
Less common activities included snorkeling, diving, boating, canoeing, and surfing (Levine, et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 2648 ---
Outside of this survey, there is little evidence or documentation of visitation to NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 2649 ---
In 2007, a trail leading from the ridge to the beach adjacent to Fagatele Bay was constructed to increase access.

--- SENTENCE 2650 ---
Public access to the beaches, and consequently the water, is under the purview of the village or individual families that reside adjacent to the water and public places, and one must obtain permission or approval for access.

--- SENTENCE 2651 ---
In some places, landowners charge an access fee (that does not go to NMSAS).

--- SENTENCE 2652 ---
These families are the caretakers of these special places and help to maintain and safeguard them for current and future generations.

--- SENTENCE 2653 ---
Sign-in sheet data maintained by landowners showed that 297 individuals visited Fagatele Bay in 2010 (Cheng & Gaskin, 2011).

--- SENTENCE 2654 ---
Data are not available for other years.

--- SENTENCE 2655 ---
The only available data regarding the number of snorkeling trips by visitors are from 2004, when roughly 2,750 snorkel trips were taken in Fagatele Bay (Spurgeon et al., 2004).

--- SENTENCE 2656 ---
Data regarding diving activities are also limited, but the same report found that in 2004, there were 15 active divers living in American Samoa and they completed a total of approximately 450 dives in the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2657 ---
In a more recent study, 70% of American Samoa residents surveyed reported that they never went snorkeling, and 93% reported that they never went diving (Levine et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 2658 ---
Five percent of respondents reported snorkeling four or more times a month and 2% reported diving four or more times a month.

--- SENTENCE 2659 ---
Humpback whales can be seen in the waters of American Samoa from mid-July–November, although exact arrival and departure times vary from year to year.

--- SENTENCE 2660 ---
There were no commercial whale watching operators in American Samoa from 1991–1998, but in 2005 and 2008, a

#### State of Ecosystem Services

minimal amount of commercial whale watching may have occurred (O'Connor et al., 2009).

--- SENTENCE 2661 ---
Anecdotally, experts at the workshop noted they were unaware of any current commercial whale watching operations.

--- SENTENCE 2662 ---
However, it is possible that those on cruise ships, yachts, or along the shore engage in whale watching, but there is no information on these user groups relative to wildlife viewing.

--- SENTENCE 2663 ---
Pago Pago Harbor is one of the deepest harbors in the Pacific and is an increasingly popular stop for cruise ships.

--- SENTENCE 2664 ---
The number of cruise ships visiting American Samoa has increased since 2006, and has more than doubled from six in 2006 to 14 in 2017 (Table App.F.1).

--- SENTENCE 2665 ---
Each ship carries hundreds to thousands of passengers.

--- SENTENCE 2666 ---
Cruise ship passengers generally disembark for a single day before traveling to the next destination.

--- SENTENCE 2667 ---
Cruise ship arrivals were canceled from December 2019–February 2020 due to a measles epidemic in neighboring Samoa, and ceased in March 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

--- SENTENCE 2668 ---
Arrivals by yachts vary from year to year, with a low of 50 arrivals in 2009 and a peak of 113 in 2011 (ASDOC, 2016, 2018).

--- SENTENCE 2669 ---
The number of tourist arrivals by plane has also varied (ASDOC, 2016, 2018; Table App.F.2).

--- SENTENCE 2670 ---
During the study period, arrivals peaked at roughly 7,500 in 2007, then declined until 2015.

--- SENTENCE 2671 ---
Arrivals increased in 2016 and 2017 with 2,501 and 5,579 arrivals, respectively.

--- SENTENCE 2672 ---
Tourism is limited, and the majority of tourist arrivals are from the U.S. and New Zealand.

--- SENTENCE 2673 ---
Tourists frequently visit the nearby National Park of American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 2674 ---
From 2008–2018, there was a steady increase in the number of visitors to the park (National Park Service, 2022; Figure ES.NCR.1).

--- SENTENCE 2675 ---
Visitors include both tourists and local residents.

--- SENTENCE 2676 ---
A notable peak in visitation occurred in 2017, with roughly 70,000 visitors entering the park.

--- SENTENCE 2677 ---
Although these data sources provide information on the total number of visitors to the island, it is unclear how many actually visit the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2678 ---
Cruise, yacht, and airplane arrivals abruptly ended in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the amount of time it will take for visitation to return to pre-pandemic levels is unclear.

Arrivals and departures by vessel type are shown in Table App.

Educational programs implemented by NMSAS have likely increased awareness of, and perhaps visitation and recreation within, the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2685 ---
NMSAS has also supported efforts to increase awareness around ocean swimming and science.

--- SENTENCE 2686 ---
From 2011–2015, the Ocean Swimming/Ocean Science course, which included swimming instruction, offered one credit to participating Samoana High School students.

--- SENTENCE 2687 ---
The total number of students who took the course from 2012– 2015 was 160 (50 students in 2012, 50 students in 2013, 30 students in 2014, and 30 students in 2015).

--- SENTENCE 2688 ---
In the summer season, the Ocean Star course offered elementary school students the opportunity to learn about coral reefs and swimming.

--- SENTENCE 2689 ---
Thirty-five students participated in 2013, 35 participated in 2014, and 40 participated in 2015.

--- SENTENCE 2690 ---
A more complete list of educational programs is provided in the Education ecosystem service section.

--- SENTENCE 2691 ---
Because of these outreach efforts, awareness of the various locations within the sanctuary has increased, which could possibly result in increased visitation.

--- SENTENCE 2692 ---
Despite increased awareness, access to many sanctuary sites remains challenging.

--- SENTENCE 2693 ---
NMSAS does not have the ability to improve infrastructure related to accessing the marine environment, since the surrounding lands are either community-owned or privately owned.

--- SENTENCE 2694 ---
Anchoring is prohibited in all sanctuary units, and NMSAS has not maintained mooring buoys during the study period, which may limit boat access.

--- SENTENCE 2695 ---
There is a limited number of for-hire and tour businesses that take snorkelers and boaters out to NMSAS units in Tutuila, including Aunu'u and Fagatele Bay, but the industry is not well developed.

--- SENTENCE 2696 ---
These businesses have begun taking a limited number of visitors to the Ta'u unit to snorkel or dive around the large *Porites* colonies there.

--- SENTENCE 2697 ---
The lack of access and limited capacity to provide this service may restrict non-consumptive use of the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2698 ---
The condition of natural resources is likely not significantly affected by non-consumptive recreation and, therefore, did not influence this rating.

--- SENTENCE 2699 ---
As described in the State of Water Quality section, the status of water quality is good.

--- SENTENCE 2700 ---
According to the American Samoa Environmental Protection Agency (AS-EPA), the open coastal waters in Fagatele Bay, Ta'u, and Aunu'u fully support recreational use.

--- SENTENCE 2701 ---
Coral communities remain robust, though they may be experiencing impacts from climate change.

--- SENTENCE 2702 ---
Antarctic humpback whales continue to journey to American Samoa for calving and breeding, with high densities observed near Fagatele Bay and Aunu'u.

--- SENTENCE 2703 ---
Lastly, relatively low fish biomass, particularly for larger parrotfish, groupers, and sharks, is unrelated to non-consumptive recreation.

### **Conclusion**

Although there have been no studies specific to non-consumptive recreation in NMSAS, there have been studies of participation rates across the entire region.

--- SENTENCE 2704 ---
This proxy data show that swimming and beach recreation are some relatively common activities in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 2705 ---
Although the number of cruise ship arrivals increased, the number of overall tourist arrivals to American Samoa decreased from 2007–2015 (although there have been some increases in recent years).

--- SENTENCE 2706 ---
Visitation to the National Park of American Samoa has increased since 2008, with peak visitation occurring in 2017 (Figure ES.NCR.1).

--- SENTENCE 2707 ---
Yet, despite increasing awareness of the sanctuary and the recreational opportunities available, a lack of infrastructure to promote access continues to be a limiting factor.

--- SENTENCE 2708 ---
Expert opinion, along with measurable proxy indicators, led to a status rating of fair with an improving trend.

--- SENTENCE 2709 ---
## <span id="page-190-0"></span>*Consumptive Recreation*

**Recreational activities that result in the removal of or harm to natural or cultural resources**

!

--- SENTENCE 2710 ---
The capacity to provide the ecosystem service is compromised, but performance is acceptable.

--- SENTENCE 2711 ---
The status of good/fair was based primarily on the fact that recreational opportunities have not been significantly reduced by changes in resource availability or access restrictions.

--- SENTENCE 2712 ---
The expansion of NMSAS restricted fishing access at two sites, but likely had minimal impact on recreational fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2713 ---
People were still able to access resources, and NMSAS worked to increase awareness of responsible recreational fishing practices.

--- SENTENCE 2714 ---
Consumptive recreation in the sanctuary likely decreased after the expansion in 2012, then increased after subsequent outreach to enhance recreational fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2715 ---
There are insufficient data to determine the extent of these changes; therefore, the ratings for this service are based primarily upon expert opinion.

--- SENTENCE 2716 ---
Consumptive recreation is a term used to describe recreational activities that may result in the death of or disturbance to wildlife, or the destruction of natural habitats.

--- SENTENCE 2717 ---
In many places, this includes recreational fishing, sport fishing, and beachcombing.

--- SENTENCE 2718 ---
Within the National Marine Sanctuary System, sites try to balance access to these activities with resource protection to

#### State of Ecosystem Services

maintain this ecosystem service.

--- SENTENCE 2719 ---
Evaluating this service in the Pacific Islands is difficult, as island communities rely on fishing for subsistence and do not view it as a recreational activity.

--- SENTENCE 2720 ---
The National Coral Reef Monitoring Program found that in American Samoa, 24% of survey respondents reported fishing "for fun" on either "frequent[ly]" or "sometimes," but this was almost always coupled with other reasons, including food provision or fulfilling cultural obligations (Levine et al., 2016).

--- SENTENCE 2721 ---
When residents fish, it is primarily to support their families and communities, which is discussed further in the subsistence harvest section.

--- SENTENCE 2722 ---
Due to the traditional marine tenure system, residents usually fish in their home village and do not require a license, special gear, or for-hire operations.

--- SENTENCE 2723 ---
This makes it difficult to track fishing activities in the territory, so data to assess the level of consumptive recreation as a stand-alone activity are limited.

--- SENTENCE 2724 ---
Non-residents (e.g., tourists or contract workers) may engage in recreational fishing activities; however, opportunities are limited, as only a few companies offer charter fishing services, and cruise ship tourists usually do not have enough time to engage in fishing activities during their short (<12 hours) visit to the island.

--- SENTENCE 2725 ---
Experts noted that they observed little recreational fishing, even by visitors to the island.

--- SENTENCE 2726 ---
Fishing tournaments (Figure ES.CR.1) are one of the few truly recreational fishing activities in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 2727 ---
Therefore, consumptive recreation is likely a small portion of total fishing when compared to commercial and subsistence harvests.

--- SENTENCE 2728 ---
What is known about the level of recreational fishing effort is summarized below.

--- SENTENCE 2729 ---
During the expansion process, NMSAS worked with village councils to evaluate fisheries regulations for each unit.

--- SENTENCE 2730 ---
The Futiga Village Council requested that fishing activity be restricted in Fagatele Bay and in Aunu'u, and that some fishing be allowed within the research zone of the Aunu'u unit.

--- SENTENCE 2731 ---
Fagatele Bay is now a no-take marine protected area, and only surface fishing for pelagic species is allowed in the Aunu'u Research Zone.

--- SENTENCE 2732 ---
These units are difficult to access for fishing, requiring either a boat or a hike across rough terrain.

--- SENTENCE 2733 ---
Fishing is allowed in the Aunu'u Multiple Use Zone, which is the only NMSAS unit that is close to a village and is considered an important fishing ground.

--- SENTENCE 2734 ---
In 2013, NOAA Fisheries designated a 22-km no-take zone around Rose Atoll; however, recreational fishing is allowed in this zone with a permit.

--- SENTENCE 2735 ---
Fishing access was not altered in Fagalua/Fogama'a, Ta'u, or Swains Island.

--- SENTENCE 2736 ---
The sanctuary expansion may have affected consumptive recreation by restricting fishing in Fagatele Bay and the Aunu'u Research Zone, but the estimated impact was minimal due to the location of and access constraints associated with these sites (ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 2737 ---
Residents were also confused about fishing access after the expansion, which may have curtailed activity immediately after the expansion.

--- SENTENCE 2738 ---
To counter this and to correct misperceptions related to the new units, NMSAS conducted outreach to educate the public about fishing access in the sanctuary, and hosts an annual fishing tournament to encourage pelagic fishing (Figure ES.CR.1).

!

--- SENTENCE 2739 ---
** Participants at the 2019 Fagota Mo Taeao Open Fishing Tournament.

--- SENTENCE 2740 ---
Photo: Nerelle Que/NOAA

Tourism is still limited in American Samoa, but cruise ship visits have increased over the reporting period, doubling from six in 2006 to 14 in 2017 (see Table App.F.1).

--- SENTENCE 2741 ---
Each ship carries hundreds of visitors.

--- SENTENCE 2742 ---
Pago Pago Harbor is one of the deepest harbors in the Pacific, making it an ideal stop for cruise ships and yachts.

--- SENTENCE 2743 ---
Although this may change in the future, at present, tourists do not appear to engage in consumptive recreation (see Table App.F.2).

--- SENTENCE 2744 ---
Cruise ships often arrive after peak fishing hours and do not stay long enough for passengers to engage in fishing charters.

--- SENTENCE 2745 ---
Also, due to the limited tourism market, there are only a few for-hire operations that take visitors to the sanctuary on tours.

--- SENTENCE 2746 ---
These businesses must rely on other activities (e.g., inter-island transport, commercial diving, etc.) throughout the year to sustain operations.

--- SENTENCE 2747 ---
Companies that coordinate cruise ship visits in American Samoa do not promote many waterbased recreation tours due to the lack of companies able to provide these tours.

--- SENTENCE 2748 ---
There are no fishing, whale watching, or island cruises listed as tour options for any of the ships.

--- SENTENCE 2749 ---
Yachts often visit for longer periods and may engage in consumptive recreation activities during their stay, or during transit before or after their visit to Pago Pago.

--- SENTENCE 2750 ---
However, there are no data on fishing from yachts, including whether yachters fish within the sanctuary; any activity is believed to be minimal.

--- SENTENCE 2751 ---
Workshop experts noted that the National Park of American Samoa is a more established destination for tourists, with well-developed terrestrial access and the Ofu ranger station located close to the Ofu airport.

--- SENTENCE 2752 ---
The park also tracks visitor use.

--- SENTENCE 2753 ---
These data may be helpful for evaluating this service in the future, as it is possible that the same visitors that use the park also recreate in NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 2754 ---
However, more research would be needed to confirm this.

--- SENTENCE 2755 ---
A full discussion of cruise ship, yacht, and other tourist arrivals is provided in the nonconsumptive recreation section (ASDOC, 2016, 2018).

--- SENTENCE 2756 ---
The annual Fagota Mo Taeao Open Fishing Tournament, started in 2016, is hosted by the Sanctuary Advisory Council Fishing Committee, and is co-managed by NMSAS and the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR).

--- SENTENCE 2757 ---
The purpose of the tournament is to increase awareness of sustainable fishing practices in the sanctuary and bring traditional fishers and recreational anglers together.

--- SENTENCE 2758 ---
It is open to both residents and non-residents.

--- SENTENCE 2759 ---
The tournament receives extensive local sponsorship and provides donations of fish to a local charity.

--- SENTENCE 2760 ---
The tournament supports and is supported by local communities.

--- SENTENCE 2761 ---
Prizes are awarded to the three heaviest fish caught in six different species categories, and awards are also provided for outstanding sportsmanship and participation.

--- SENTENCE 2762 ---
In 2019, the two-day tournament had a total of 96 boats, including 80 local alia registered.

--- SENTENCE 2763 ---
The youngest recreational angler participating in the tournament was nine years old.

--- SENTENCE 2764 ---
The number of reported catches has increased since the tournament's inception.

--- SENTENCE 2765 ---
The most commonly kept fish caught were yellowfin, dogtooth, and skipjack tuna.

--- SENTENCE 2766 ---
Participants reported some catches from both Aunu'u and Ta'u, but most were from outside of the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2767 ---
### **Conclusion**

There is limited evidence related to consumptive recreation within NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 2768 ---
At present, the majority of those who benefit from consumptive recreation in American Samoa are local residents.

--- SENTENCE 2769 ---
However, residents generally do not engage in fishing solely for recreational purposes, but do so in conjunction with other responsibilities, such as providing food.

--- SENTENCE 2770 ---
Tourists arriving via cruise ships, yachts, and other means have not been significant participants in these activities, and are not useful indicators for this service at this time.

## <span id="page-193-0"></span>*Science*

**

--- SENTENCE 2771 ---
The capacity to acquire and contribute information and knowledge**

!

--- SENTENCE 2772 ---
Demand for the service is not fully met, but performance is acceptable and may not warrant enhanced management.

--- SENTENCE 2773 ---
Science activity has been increasing at NMSAS throughout the reporting period and current levels are rated as good/fair.

--- SENTENCE 2774 ---
During this time, research activities, publications, science capacity, and partnerships have all increased.

--- SENTENCE 2775 ---
Experts noted that there are still limitations due to the lack of access to large research vessels and science staff capacity, and the program will need more support in the future, given the substantial expansion of the sanctuary in 2012.

--- SENTENCE 2776 ---
The incorporation of traditional knowledge and more student programs were highlighted as areas for future improvement.

--- SENTENCE 2777 ---
Science as an ecosystem service is defined as the capacity to acquire and contribute information and knowledge.

--- SENTENCE 2778 ---
This information and knowledge can come in many forms, from quantitative data on ecological parameters such as fish biomass and coral cover to traditional knowledge about seasonal trends and cycles.

--- SENTENCE 2779 ---
Science services often involve scientists, but can also be generated by students and community members.

--- SENTENCE 2780 ---
The information generated from these programs feeds directly into the adaptive management process at NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 2781 ---
Science capacity at NMSAS falls into three main categories: science conducted by sanctuary staff, science conducted by research partners, and science conducted by students and the community.

--- SENTENCE 2782 ---
NMSAS had limited scientific capacity during this reporting period, but has recently

#### State of Ecosystem Services

added a full-time research coordinator, a research scientist, and a marine operations coordinator to support scientific field operations.

--- SENTENCE 2783 ---
The lack of NMSAS science capacity limited sanctuary-led research activities in the past, but NMSAS has acquired funding and technical capacity to initiate a research program that includes long-term coral reef monitoring, which began in 2020.

--- SENTENCE 2784 ---
The program will address the priorities established in the marine conservation science and climate change action plans within the NMSAS management plan, including monitoring, characterization, climate science, and improving public science outreach (ONMS, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 2785 ---
Most of the science conducted at NMSAS from 2007 to 2020 was implemented by partner organizations, including the ONMS Maritime Heritage Program, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Pacific Island Fisheries Science Center Ecosystem Services Division, NOAA National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science, NOAA Coral Reef Conservation Program (CRCP), NOAA Ocean Exploration, NOAA Ocean Acidification Program (OAP), American Samoa Historic Preservation Office, the Bishop Museum, the Ocean Exploration Trust (OET), XL Catlin Seaview Survey, the Ocean Futures Society, agencies associated with the American Samoa Coral Reef Advisory Group, and a number of academic institutions.

--- SENTENCE 2786 ---
Projects include shallow coral reef monitoring, ocean acidification monitoring, mesophotic reef characterization and exploration, bathymetric mapping, deep-sea exploration, targeted research on contaminants and coral disease, and archaeological and social science research to evaluate maritime heritage resources.

--- SENTENCE 2787 ---
NMSAS has tracked the effort and outcomes of these projects.

--- SENTENCE 2788 ---
Figure ES.S.1 illustrates the increase in scientific permits within NMSAS since 2007.

--- SENTENCE 2789 ---
Prior to 2007, the highest number of permits in any given year was three, but this increased to nine in 2018.

--- SENTENCE 2790 ---
This activity decreased slightly in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, but is expected to increase as travel resumes.

--- SENTENCE 2791 ---
Figure ES.S.2 shows the number of publications related to NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 2792 ---
Publications have increased since 2007, with seven publications specific to NMSAS and over 30 publications related to sanctuary units in some way.

--- SENTENCE 2793 ---
Major partner efforts include the American Samoa Reef Assessment and Monitoring Program cruises, funded by CRCP in 2008, 2010, 2012, 2015, and 2018 (Brainard et al., 2008; CREP, 2016; Vargas-Ángel et al., 2019), which collected data on shallow coral reef ecosystems (0–30 m) around all the islands within the territory using a stratified random sampling design.

--- SENTENCE 2794 ---
This program is now part of the National Coral Reef Monitoring Program and monitors benthic habitat, coral demographics, fish biomass and diversity, and oceanographic parameters.

--- SENTENCE 2795 ---
Later cruises increased sampling in NMSAS units to improve data availability for the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2796 ---
Divers from Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, the National Park of American Samoa, the University of Hawai'i, and the Bishop Museum conducted exploration dives in Fagatele Bay, Fagalua/Fogama'a, and Aunu'u using rebreathers from 2015–2018.

Another significant effort was the Campaign to Address Pacific Monument Science, Technology, and Ocean Needs (CAPSTONE) project conducted aboard *Okeanos Explorer* in 2017.

--- SENTENCE 2800 ---
This project assessed deep-sea habitats within NMSAS as part of its exploration efforts, and data are publicly accessible via the NOAA Deep-Sea Coral Research and Technology Program portal and a number of publications, including Kennedy et al. (2019) and Amon et al. (2020).

--- SENTENCE 2801 ---
The ship is well equipped for outreach and conducted telepresence activities for the local community.

--- SENTENCE 2802 ---
This was followed by OET's 2019 cruise aboard the exploration vessel *Nautilus*, which was telepresence enabled and included local agency staff and students as part of the science team (OET, 2019).

--- SENTENCE 2803 ---
Also in 2019, a Moored Autonomous Partial Pressure of Carbon Dioxide (MAPCO2) buoy was installed in Fagatele Bay to monitor ocean acidification and general oceanographic conditions as part of a partnership between NMSAS, OAP, and CRCP.

--- SENTENCE 2804 ---
The buoy transmits real-time data, which are available at the Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory and Pacific Islands Ocean Observing System websites.

--- SENTENCE 2805 ---
NMSAS also supports capacity building and stakeholder engagement through internships in partnership with Kupu and through the NOAA Hollings Scholarship Program, NOAA Dr. Nancy Foster Scholarship Program, and NOAA Experiential Research and Training Opportunities.

--- SENTENCE 2806 ---
NMSAS provides science information to the public through its visitor center (the Tauese P.F. Sunia Ocean Center or "Ocean Center") and education and outreach programs.

--- SENTENCE 2807 ---
Workshop experts noted that science capacity at NMSAS is limited by a lack of access to vessels capable of supporting operations at Swains Island and Rose Atoll, the limited staff capacity at NMSAS for scientific operations, the lack of entry-level positions for emerging local scientists, and the lack of dedicated lab space, research facilities, and affordable housing for visiting researchers.

--- SENTENCE 2808 ---
They noted that science capacity in NMSAS has increased, but given the expansion of the sanctuary in 2012, more support is required to meet monitoring and conservation science needs.

--- SENTENCE 2809 ---
The NOAA ship *Hi'ialakai* was decommissioned in 2020, leaving a substantial gap in access to remote sites that needs to be addressed.

--- SENTENCE 2810 ---
In addition, experts recommended incorporating more traditional knowledge into sanctuary science activities and expanding opportunities for student engagement.

### **Conclusion**

Science is an important ecosystem service for NMSAS and science activity has increased throughout the reporting period.

--- SENTENCE 2811 ---
The service was rated as good/fair.

--- SENTENCE 2812 ---
Research activities, publications, science capacity, and partnerships have all increased during the reporting period.

--- SENTENCE 2813 ---
NMSAS has successfully worked with partners to support research cruises to study shallow coral reef and deep-sea ecosystems, explore mesophotic systems, investigate contaminants in Fagatele Bay, and install a buoy to monitor ocean acidification in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2814 ---
College interns and fellows have supported science efforts, and staff have incorporated science into education and outreach programs.

--- SENTENCE 2815 ---
Experts noted that there are still limitations due to a lack of vessel access and science staff capacity, and suggested that the NMSAS science program would benefit from more support.

--- SENTENCE 2816 ---
The incorporation of traditional knowledge and additional student programs were also highlighted as targets for improvement.

## <span id="page-197-0"></span>*Education*

#### **The capacity to acquire and provide educational programs**

!

--- SENTENCE 2818 ---
The capacity to provide the ecosystem service has remained unaffected or has been restored.

--- SENTENCE 2819 ---
Education programs have strengthened the NMSAS mission to restore and protect marine ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2820 ---
NMSAS has a very robust education program that includes: pre-K through higher education programs for teachers and students that reach an average of over 3500 students and 100 teachers yearly; immersive summer programs that have reached over 850 participants; a wide range of community outreach events; and a well-regarded visitor center that serves both the local community and tourists—approximately 58,000 individuals have toured the center to date.

--- SENTENCE 2821 ---
The number of programs has expanded during the reporting period with new offerings added each year.

--- SENTENCE 2822 ---
Education is the process by which individuals develop their knowledge, values, and skills.

NMSAS provides unique opportunities that attract educators at many levels for both formal and informal education.

--- SENTENCE 2869 ---

--- SENTENCE 2870 ---
