## <span id="page-237-0"></span>*Accelerated Climate Change*

The 2007 condition report recognized that rising ocean temperatures associated with climate change were a growing pressure on the coral reef ecosystems in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3408 ---
Further assessments have clearly indicated that rising temperatures are just one component of climate change.

--- SENTENCE 3409 ---
Sea level rise, ocean acidification, changes in storm intensity, and rainfall will also affect the sanctuary's ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 3410 ---
In 2011, ONMS developed a climate profile for Fagatele Bay (Cheng & Gaskin, 2011).

--- SENTENCE 3411 ---
The report compiled existing information on climate change and potential impacts on Fagatele Bay, including its ecosystems, ecosystem services, and maritime heritage

#### Response to Pressures

resources.

--- SENTENCE 3412 ---
As part of the management review and expansion, ONMS developed a Climate Change Action Plan that guides the sanctuary's response to climate change pressures.

--- SENTENCE 3413 ---
Efforts described in the action plan aim to understand and characterize climate change drivers and impacts in the sanctuary, suggest "green" sanctuary operations, identify habitats vulnerable and resilient to climate change, conduct and prioritize climate change research and monitoring, and promote public awareness about the problem.

--- SENTENCE 3414 ---
As part of these efforts, NMSAS conducted initial assessments of greenhouse gas emissions for sanctuary operations and initiated efforts to reduce emissions.

--- SENTENCE 3415 ---
In 2016, NMSAS partnered with the National Marine Sanctuary Foundation and Eco Adapt to conduct a rapid vulnerability assessment and develop of adaptation strategies for NMSAS and the territory.

--- SENTENCE 3416 ---
This effort included two workshops and resulted in a report (Score, 2017).

--- SENTENCE 3417 ---
This was an important first step to evaluate climate threats and vulnerabilities to marine resources.

--- SENTENCE 3418 ---
Adaptation strategies were developed for ten focal resources.

--- SENTENCE 3419 ---
In order to evaluate climate change effects, NMSAS has worked to increase the site's conservation science program.

--- SENTENCE 3420 ---
In 2019, a Moored Autonomous Partial Pressure of Carbon Dioxide (MAPCO2) buoy was installed in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3421 ---
The sensors on this buoy monitor ocean acidification and are part of a national array of moored carbon dioxide buoys across the Pacific, Atlantic, and Caribbean.

--- SENTENCE 3422 ---
The buoy is funded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)

--- SENTENCE 3423 ---
Ocean Acidification Program and involves many partners, including NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program, Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory, Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory, Coral Reef Conservation Program, Pacific Integrated Ocean Observing System (PacIOOS), and NMSAS.

--- SENTENCE 3424 ---
In 2020, NMSAS initiated an annual monitoring program for coral reefs in Fagatele, Fagalua/Fogama'a, Aunu'u, and Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 3425 ---
The program is monitoring key indicators such as coral cover, demographics, and diversity; fish biomass and species richness; and macroinvertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 3426 ---
ONMS also worked with NOAA Ocean Exploration and the Ocean Exploration Trust to conduct deep-sea expeditions in 2017 and 2019, respectively.

--- SENTENCE 3427 ---
These expeditions collected valuable information on deep-sea habitats in the sanctuary, providing a baseline for evaluating changes in deep-sea fauna and habitats in the future.

--- SENTENCE 3428 ---
Ocean literacy programs hosted by NMSAS have included outreach efforts to raise awareness of climate change impacts in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 3429 ---
A full list of these activities is included in the Ecosystem Services section on education.

--- SENTENCE 3430 ---
These programs extended far beyond American Samoa, and included media partnerships with Jean-Michel Cousteau and the Ocean Futures Society to create a film about Swains Island; the XL Catlin Seaview Survey to create virtual reality imagery that is used in tours and resulted in an iconic coral bleaching photo at Fatumafuti; and the South Florida PBS program Changing Seas.

--- SENTENCE 3431 ---
These efforts reached global audiences and helped raise awareness of the threat climate poses to these special places.

--- SENTENCE 3432 ---
In 2020, ONMS completed a NMSAS Climate Change Impacts Profile and created a Sanctuary Advisory Council Climate Change Working Group to provide input on NMSAS climate change efforts (ONMS, 2020a).

## <span id="page-239-0"></span>*Fishing*

Fishing is an integral part of Samoan culture, but it also can impair ecosystem functions and resilience if not properly managed.

--- SENTENCE 3433 ---
For many years, scientists have noted that fish populations in Fagatele Bay are lower than they should be, and the 2007 condition report documented the use of destructive fishing practices, including dynamite fishing, within the bay (National Marine Sanctuary Program, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 3434 ---
As part of the management review and expansion, NMSAS worked with local communities to evaluate management options.

--- SENTENCE 3435 ---
In the end, fishing activities in Fagatele Bay and the Aunu'u Research Zone were restricted to improve fish biomass (Table R.1; Table R.2).

--- SENTENCE 3436 ---
The Resource Protection and Enforcement Action Plan was developed during the expansion to guide efforts to improve compliance with fisheries restrictions and improve enforcement.

--- SENTENCE 3437 ---
Efforts included the production and dissemination of outreach materials to alert the fishing community of the new sanctuary regulations and improved partnership with the NOAA Fisheries Office of Law Enforcement and DMWR Law Enforcement through their Joint Enforcement Agreement.

--- SENTENCE 3438 ---
DMWR conducts regular patrols of sanctuary areas to support compliance with sanctuary regulations.

--- SENTENCE 3439 ---
In 2016, NMSAS and partners initiated an annual fishing tournament to improve communication with the local fishing community and encourage pelagic fishing as a way to reduce pressures on reef fish populations.

--- SENTENCE 3440 ---
In 2020, NMSAS initiated efforts to improve monitoring of reef fish communities in the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3441 ---
## <span id="page-239-1"></span>*Coastal Development and Nearshore Construction*

As noted in the State section, land use changes can have detrimental impacts to sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 3442 ---
NMSAS does not have regulatory oversight over coastal development, but actively participates in the Coral Reef Advisory Group to support efforts to improve watershed management and has collaborated with ASDOC on coastal planning near sanctuary areas.

--- SENTENCE 3443 ---
Some development is necessary to maintain vital services for local communities.

--- SENTENCE 3444 ---
This includes the need for improved vessel access to Swains Island.

--- SENTENCE 3445 ---
During the expansion, ONMS worked with the island's owners, the Jennings family, to establish boundaries for the sanctuary that would take these needs into account, while protecting the island's marine ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 3446 ---
## <span id="page-239-2"></span>*Nonpoint Source Pollution*

Most sanctuary areas are considered pristine, located away from development and dense human settlements.

--- SENTENCE 3447 ---
However, they are not immune from contamination.

--- SENTENCE 3448 ---
The Resource Protection and Enforcement Action Plan includes a strategy to facilitate research on land-based sources of pollution and develop outreach materials.

--- SENTENCE 3449 ---
NMSAS worked cooperatively with researchers at the American Samoa Environmental Protection Agency (AS-EPA), NOAA National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science, and other organizations to assess land-based pollution and contaminants in Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3450 ---
The results of these efforts were shared at the expert workshops and are incorporated into the State section of this report.

--- SENTENCE 3451 ---
These projects provide important information about nonpoint source pollution in the sanctuary and lay the groundwork for future

management efforts.

--- SENTENCE 3452 ---
Information about land-based sources of pollution are also included in ocean literacy efforts discussed in the Ecosystem Services section on education.

--- SENTENCE 3453 ---
## <span id="page-240-0"></span>*Point Source Pollution*

Point source pollution sources are limited to the Aunu'u sewage outfall, located in Aunu'u Zone A, and discharges from vessels passing through the Muliāva unit.

--- SENTENCE 3454 ---
In 2007, AS-EPA and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency developed a wastewater facilities plan for the village and island of Aunu'u (AS-EPA, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 3455 ---
NMSAS encouraged AS-EPA to implement this plan, but it is a low priority due to the lack of detectable human health impairments.

## <span id="page-240-1"></span>*Marine Debris*

Completely preventing marine debris from entering sanctuary boundaries is virtually impossible, as debris comes from a mix of ocean-based and land-based sources.

--- SENTENCE 3456 ---
NMSAS implements a marine debris strategy, described in the Resource Protection and Enforcement Action Plan, through routine monitoring of marine debris via towed snorkel and beach surveys.

--- SENTENCE 3457 ---
This has allowed sanctuary staff to evaluate and minimize marine debris within the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3458 ---
Through these efforts, abandoned nets, a tire, a damaged drifter drogue, ropes, buoys, and many smaller debris items were removed from coral reef areas in Fagalua and Fagatele Bay, and beach cleanups were conducted at multiple sites.

--- SENTENCE 3459 ---
NMSAS has supported internships focused on marine debris and the topic is included in ocean literacy programs and many of the other education and outreach efforts listed in the Ecosystem Services section on education.

--- SENTENCE 3460 ---
## <span id="page-240-2"></span>*Vessel Groundings*

The Resource Protection and Enforcement Action Plan also includes a strategy to minimize damage through coordinated emergency preparedness and contingency planning.

--- SENTENCE 3461 ---
These strategies were implemented when a fishing vessel grounded on the reef in the Aunu'u unit in 2016.

--- SENTENCE 3462 ---
NMSAS worked with the U.S. Coast Guard and others to immediately respond to the grounding and removed the vessel under the authority of the NMSA as quickly as possible.

--- SENTENCE 3463 ---
Similar groundings in other areas have lingered for many years, compounding the damage to fragile reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 3464 ---
Lessons learned from this response have been incorporated into response strategies.

--- SENTENCE 3465 ---
NMSAS also obtained funding to support capacity-building for coral restoration activities and a pilot coral nursery that should facilitate improved mitigation for future events.

--- SENTENCE 3466 ---
## <span id="page-240-3"></span>*Visitation*

Due to the remote location of NMSAS management areas, even on the main island of Tutuila, visitation numbers are thought to be low.

--- SENTENCE 3467 ---
However, visitors can cause physical damage, leave marine debris, or introduce invasive species or disease from other locations.

--- SENTENCE 3468 ---
NMSAS has developed education and outreach programs to encourage responsible use of the sanctuary, including ocean etiquette and student interpretation tour training.

--- SENTENCE 3469 ---
In 2015, NMSAS initiated the annual Get Into Your Sanctuary program, which is now conducted nationwide.

--- SENTENCE 3470 ---
Signs were maintained along the Fagatele Bay access trail to educate visitors about sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 3471 ---
Visitors are also encouraged to visit the Ocean Center to learn more about sanctuary resources

and visitation guidelines.

--- SENTENCE 3472 ---
NMSAS has continuously improved outreach capacity during the reporting period.

--- SENTENCE 3473 ---
This includes Science on a SphereⓇ, SOS ExplorerⓇ (a flat screen version of Science on a SphereⓇ), and outdoor signage.

--- SENTENCE 3474 ---
In addition, NMSAS has created radio, television, and social media content to remind the community and visitors to care for sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 3475 ---
In 2013–2014, NMSAS and the National Park of American Samoa partnered to conduct a tour guide training program to enhance interpretation and resource protection capacity.

## <span id="page-241-0"></span>*Nuisance Species Outbreaks*

From 2011–2017, CoTS (*Acanthaster planci*) populations increased rapidly, threatening corals around the island of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3476 ---
CoTS were observed in low numbers at Fagatele Bay and Aunu'u.

--- SENTENCE 3477 ---
More were observed in Fagalua/Fogama'a and along the Vaitogi coastline just outside of the sanctuary, however these numbers were much lower than northern sites, where thousands of starfish were observed.

--- SENTENCE 3478 ---
Sites on the north side of the island were severely infested, and efforts were undertaken by the National Park of American Samoa to stop the outbreak through diver interventions (NPS, 2014).

--- SENTENCE 3479 ---
The National Park of American Samoa estimated that over 25,000 CoTS were culled using injections of sodium bisulfite or ox bile salts.

--- SENTENCE 3480 ---
As part of this effort, NMSAS brought rebreather dive teams to American Samoa in 2014 and 2015 to implement control measures during the "CoTS Blitz."

--- SENTENCE 3481 ---
Sanctuary divers surveyed 29 miles of reef, spent 307 hours underwater, and culled over 1,600 sea stars during this effort.

--- SENTENCE 3482 ---
NMSAS has continued to monitor CoTS as part of its resource protection program and is prepared to implement control measures should an outbreak be observed within the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3483 ---
## <span id="page-241-1"></span>*Research Activities*

The NMSAS science program has grown with the sanctuary, and research is encouraged within the sanctuary units.

--- SENTENCE 3484 ---
Projects often require the installation of scientific instruments, markers, or buoys.

--- SENTENCE 3485 ---
NMSAS carefully reviews permit applications and requires researchers to implement best practices to avoid damage to sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 3486 ---
Permitted activities included the placement of two oceanographic buoys, the MAPCO2 buoy in Fagatele Bay and the PacIOOS wave buoy in the Aunu'u Research Zone; a climate station in Fagatele Bay with oceanographic instruments and settlement structures; an ecological acoustic recorder in Fagatele Bay; monitoring markers; and contaminant and sediment monitoring devices.

--- SENTENCE 3487 ---
No significant damage has been observed from these research activities.

--- SENTENCE 3488 ---
In response to the outbreak of stony coral tissue loss disease in the Caribbean, NMSAS initiated decontamination procedures for staff, partners, and outside researchers in 2020 to minimize the potential transfer of invasive species and diseases.

--- SENTENCE 3489 ---
Gear must now be decontaminated between islands.

--- SENTENCE 3490 ---
# <span id="page-242-0"></span>*A Statement from National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa Superintendent Atuatasi Lelei Peau*

A lot has changed since the release of the Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary Condition Report in 2007.

--- SENTENCE 3491 ---
In 2012, the sanctuary expanded, becoming National Marine Sanctuary of American Samoa (NMSAS), and is now the largest sanctuary in the National Marine Sanctuary System.

--- SENTENCE 3492 ---
In addition, the condition report process has been improved to evaluate the resources in the sanctuary and the ecosystem services that the sanctuary provides to our local community.

--- SENTENCE 3493 ---
This report is an essential step in our management process and will help us chart our next steps forward.

--- SENTENCE 3494 ---
An important component of this report was the participation of our traditional leaders, scientists, local stakeholders, and partners.

--- SENTENCE 3495 ---
Over 130 experts provided their time and knowledge to assist NMSAS with this endeavor by attending our expert workshops and reviewing the draft report.

--- SENTENCE 3496 ---
I am grateful for their contributions.

--- SENTENCE 3497 ---
These experts distilled a tremendous amount of data to provide the status and trend ratings included in this report for water quality, habitat, living resources, maritime heritage resources, and ecosystem services.

--- SENTENCE 3498 ---
A particular highlight of this process was the inclusion of our traditional leaders' perspectives on the sanctuary and its value to American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 3499 ---
These traditional chiefs reinforced the significance NMSAS has placed on Samoan culture at the forefront of our mission, programs, and activities.

--- SENTENCE 3500 ---
They praised our efforts in developing and delivering programs and activities that benefit the community.

--- SENTENCE 3501 ---
We appreciate their participation in the workshops and review of the draft document to ensure the information was accurate and reflective of their opinions.

--- SENTENCE 3502 ---
I hope the condition report reflects and respects the unique setting of this sanctuary and the special relationship between the Samoan people and our natural environment.

--- SENTENCE 3503 ---
The report process revealed that water quality and habitat throughout NMSAS remain in good condition.

--- SENTENCE 3504 ---
The coral reef habitat in Fagatele Bay and giant *Porites* corals in Ta'u remain bright spots of resilience in a changing world.

--- SENTENCE 3505 ---
The findings suggest that protected resources, like sea turtles and humpback whales, have seen modest improvements in status, but are still at risk.

--- SENTENCE 3506 ---
However, reef fish communities, including sharks, large parrotfish, bottom fish, and iconic species, like the hump head wrasse and bump head parrotfish, are still below the levels recommended for ecosystem resilience around populated islands, and giant clam populations have declined significantly over time.

--- SENTENCE 3507 ---
In addition, acute events such as vessel groundings, the 2009 tsunami, and tropical cyclones have challenged the sanctuary's resilience, damaging coral reefs and subjecting maritime heritage resources to high-energy shoreline events.

--- SENTENCE 3508 ---
Although the coral reef habitat in NMSAS remains vibrant, coral bleaching events linked to climate change caused significant temporary declines in coral cover on reefs throughout American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 3509 ---
In addition, sea level rise coupled with rapid subsidence is affecting shorelines and coastal resources throughout the sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3510 ---
Climate impacts were noted across many sections of this report, from water quality, habitat, and living resources to ecosystem services

such as coastal protection, fishing, and sense of place.

--- SENTENCE 3511 ---
This is a significant threat to the sanctuary and will certainly be a major focus of future management efforts.

--- SENTENCE 3512 ---
In addition to supporting the Moored Autonomous Partial Pressure of Carbon Dioxide buoy in Fagatele Bay, in 2021, the NMSAS Advisory Council established a climate change working group, and we are taking steps to designate NMSAS as an Office of National Marine Sanctuaries (ONMS) Sentinel Site for climate change.

--- SENTENCE 3513 ---
Next, we plan to use the information gathered in this report to conduct vulnerability assessments to improve management objectives to maintain resilience and develop adaptation strategies.

--- SENTENCE 3514 ---
Despite these impacts, the sanctuary continues to provide valuable ecosystem services to American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 3515 ---
Our education programs have improved ocean literacy, reaching tens of thousands through tours of the Tauese P.F. Sunia Ocean Center, school visits, and innovative programs at the sanctuary sites.

--- SENTENCE 3516 ---
Our outreach efforts have reached beyond our borders through social media, films, and documentaries that reached international audiences.

--- SENTENCE 3517 ---
Subsistence harvest and consumptive recreation services were rated as good/fair, but access to nonconsumptive recreational activities remains a concern.

--- SENTENCE 3518 ---
We hope to improve the visitor experience in the future and have been working with our local government partners and traditional landowners to discuss options.

--- SENTENCE 3519 ---
NMSAS has made strides to improve its conservation science program, but the report highlighted numerous data gaps that we will need to address in the coming years.

--- SENTENCE 3520 ---
These include information about socioeconomic indicators, such as visitor use, community perceptions, and fishing pressure, and biophysical indicators, such as water quality; improved fish, sea turtle, seabird, and marine mammal data; connectivity; and climate change processes.

--- SENTENCE 3521 ---
The dearth of information about the sanctuary's mesophotic coral ecosystems, deep-sea habitats, and open ocean areas remains a significant challenge but a difficult one to address.

--- SENTENCE 3522 ---
Access to our remote sites remains limited, as NOAA ship capacity in the region declined with the decommissioning of the NOAA ship *Hiʻialakai* in 2020.

--- SENTENCE 3523 ---
We hope to continue to improve our science program and develop new partnerships to increase our capability to fill these pressing data requirements.

--- SENTENCE 3524 ---
This condition report provides a foundation for our next management plan.

--- SENTENCE 3525 ---
I look forward to engaging the public in the management plan review process and will continue to seek guidance from our Sanctuary Advisory Council members, community, and traditional leaders on our next steps forward.

--- SENTENCE 3526 ---
The findings presented in this report draw on the efforts, knowledge, and expertise of dozens of individuals, Sanctuary Advisory Council members, and local and federal agency partners that provided us with data sets, participated in expert workshops, and reviewed earlier drafts.

--- SENTENCE 3527 ---
We greatly appreciate and value the input that was provided.

--- SENTENCE 3528 ---
Special recognition and fa'afetai tele to the NMSAS team in collaboration with the ONMS Science and Heritage Division for your commitment and dedication to the condition report process.

--- SENTENCE 3529 ---
We are grateful for their contributions and diligence in ensuring the continued success of this project.

--- SENTENCE 3530 ---
"Fa'afetai i le tapuaiga maualuga a le komiti fa'afoe

--- SENTENCE 3531 ---
ina ua mae'a le galuega sa fau ao fau po.

--- SENTENCE 3532 ---
A lea ua a'e ma le manuia le faiva o le ofisa.

--- SENTENCE 3533 ---
O le fa'amoemoe ua taunu'u o le laau lea o le soifua."

--- SENTENCE 3534 ---
We congratulate and celebrate them, like the fishermen returning from the sea with bounty in their nets.

--- SENTENCE 3535 ---
Respectfully,

Atuatasi Lelei Peau

i tausaga o i luma.

--- SENTENCE 3600 ---
E aofia ai faamatalaga tau faailo o le tamaoaiga ma le soifua laulelei o tagata, e pei o mea e faaaoga e tagata asiasi, manatu o le lautele/alālafaga, malosi mo fagotaga, ma faailo tau aafiaga o tagata i le natura o mea e pei o le tulaga lelei o le vai, faasiliga

--- SENTENCE 3601 ---
i i'a, laumei, manu felelei, faamaumauga tau meaola o le gataifale; fesootaiga; ma faagasologa o suiga o le tau.

--- SENTENCE 3602 ---
O le lē lava o faamatalaga ma tusitusiga e uiga i ekosisitema a'au 'amu mesofoti, o nofoaga i le sami loloto, ma vaega sa'oloto o le vasa, o ni tulaga o lo'o avea pea ma lu'itau,

--- SENTENCE 3603 ---
ma e le faigofie foi ona fai

--- SENTENCE 3604 ---
atu i ai se tali.

--- SENTENCE 3605 ---
O loo faaitiitia pea avanoa e fesootai atu ai i a matou nofoaga maotua, talu ai ua faaitiitia avanoa o le vaa o le

--- SENTENCE 3606 ---
i le itulagi ina ua toe faafo'i le vaa *Hi'ialakai* a le NOAA i le 2020.

--- SENTENCE 3607 ---
O loo iai le faamoemoe e toe faaleleia le polokalama faasaienisi, ma atia'e nisi paaga fou e siitia ai le mafai ona tali

--- SENTENCE 3608 ---
atu i faamaumauga matuā moomia.

--- SENTENCE 3609 ---
O lenei ripoti o loo tuuina atu ai se faavae mo la tatou fono a ta'ita'i e sosoo ai.

--- SENTENCE 3610 ---
Ua ou fiafia lava o le a galulue faatasi ma le lautele e iloilo le fuafuaga faataatia a le taupulega, ma o le a faaauau pea le saili

--- SENTENCE 3611 ---
atu i se fautuaga mai sui o le Fono Faufautua o le Faasao, tagata lautele, ma ta'ita'i faaleaganuu aua le aga'i i luma.

--- SENTENCE 3612 ---
O su'esu'ega o loʻo tuʻuina atu i lenei ripoti e faʻatatau i taumafaiga, malamalama'aga, ma tomai o le toʻatele o tagata ta'ito'atasi, sui o le Fono Faufautua o le Faʻasao, ma paʻaga o ofisa faʻalotoifale ma feterale na tuʻuina mai faʻamaumauga, auai i a'oa'oga, ma iloiloina ripoti ua mavae.

--- SENTENCE 3613 ---
Matou te matua fa'afetaia

--- SENTENCE 3614 ---
ai ma fa'atauaina finagalo na fa'aalia.

--- SENTENCE 3615 ---
E fa'apitoa se fa'afetai tele i le vaega o le NMSAS lea sa galulue

--- SENTENCE 3616 ---
fa'atasi ma le Vaega o Saienisi ma Tu'ufa'asolo a le ONMS mo lo outou

--- SENTENCE 3617 ---
felagolagoma'i i le faiga o le ripoti o tulaga.

--- SENTENCE 3618 ---
E lagona la matou fa'agae'etia ona o lo outou sao ma le filigā

--- SENTENCE 3619 ---
ina ia fa'amautinoa le fa'aauau pea o le manuia o lenei poloketi.

--- SENTENCE 3620 ---
"Fa'afetai i le tapuaiga maualuga a le komiti fa'afoe

--- SENTENCE 3621 ---
ina ua mae'a le galuega sa fau ao fau po.

--- SENTENCE 3622 ---
A lea ua a'e ma le manuia le faiva o le ofisa.

--- SENTENCE 3623 ---
O le fa'amoemoe ua taunu'u o le laau lea o le soifua.

--- SENTENCE 3624 ---
"

E momoli atu ai le faamalo ma patipatia i latou, e pei o tautai ua taliu i uta ua mau o latou upega.

--- SENTENCE 3625 ---
Ma le ava tele,

Atuatasi Lelei Peau

# <span id="page-274-0"></span>**Appendix A:

--- SENTENCE 4456 ---
Questions and Rating Schemes for State of Sanctuary Resources**

The purpose of this rating scheme is to clarify the questions and possible responses used to report the condition of sanctuary resources in condition reports for all national marine sanctuaries.

--- SENTENCE 4457 ---
ONMS and subject matter experts used this guidance, as well as their own understanding of the condition of resources, to make judgments about the status and trends of sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 4458 ---
The questions derive from the National Marine Sanctuary System's mission, and a system-wide monitoring framework developed to ensure the timely flow of data and information to those responsible for managing and protecting resources in the ocean and coastal zone, and to those that use, depend on, and study sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 4459 ---
The questions are being used to guide ONMS and its partners at each of the sanctuary system's 14 units in the development of periodic sanctuary condition reports.

--- SENTENCE 4460 ---
Evaluations of status and trends were based on interpretation of quantitative and, when necessary, non-quantitative assessments and observations of scientists, managers, and users.

--- SENTENCE 4461 ---
In 2012, ONMS led an effort to review and edit the set of questions and their possible responses that were developed for the first round of condition reports (drafted between 2007 and 2014)

--- SENTENCE 4462 ---
(National Marine Sanctuary Program, 2004).

--- SENTENCE 4463 ---
The questions that follow are revised and improved versions of those original questions.

--- SENTENCE 4464 ---
Although all questions have been edited to some degree, both in their description and status ratings, the nature and intent of most questions have not changed.

--- SENTENCE 4465 ---
Five questions, however, are either new or are significantly altered and therefore, are not directly comparable to the original questions.

--- SENTENCE 4466 ---
For these, a new baseline will need to be established.

-

--- SENTENCE 4467 ---
Among the Water Quality questions, one was added on climate change.

--- SENTENCE 4468 ---
This was necessary to address the constantly increasing awareness and attention to the issue following the original design of the condition report process, which began in 2002.

--- SENTENCE 4469 ---
It also removed the need to combine climate change discussions with other questions.

--- SENTENCE 4470 ---
- Two Habitat Quality questions were combined due to feedback received during the development of the first round of reports.

--- SENTENCE 4471 ---
A single question regarding the "integrity of major habitat types" has been created and combines prior questions that separately inquired about non-biogenic and biogenic habitats.

--- SENTENCE 4472 ---
Our experience showed that species constituting biogenic habitat (e.g., kelp, corals, seagrass, etc.) were considered adequately within questions about living resources, and need not be covered twice in the reports.
-

--- SENTENCE 4473 ---
Among the Living Resource Quality questions, one used in the first round of condition reports was removed entirely.

--- SENTENCE 4474 ---
It asked about "the status of environmentally sustainable fishing."

--- SENTENCE 4475 ---
It was removed for a variety of reasons—it was the only question focused on a single, specific human activity and because fishing activity discussions were already included in the question regarding "human activities that may influence living resource

quality."

--- SENTENCE 4476 ---
In addition, living resource quality that would provide a basis for judgment for this question was typically considered as part of other living resource questions, and need not be covered twice.

--- SENTENCE 4477 ---
Another change to the Living Resource Quality questions pertains to the question about the "health of key species" which was previously addressed in a single question, but is now split into two.

--- SENTENCE 4478 ---
The first asks specifically about the status of "keystone and foundation" species, the second about "other focal species."

--- SENTENCE 4479 ---
In either case, the health of any species of interest can be considered in judgment of status and trends.

--- SENTENCE 4480 ---
• One of the initial maritime archaeology questions addressed potential environmental hazards presented by heritage resources like shipwrecks.

--- SENTENCE 4481 ---
While the assessment of such threats is important, it was decided that the question should actually address environmental hazards in general rather than apply specifically to historic maritime properties.

--- SENTENCE 4482 ---
Therefore, the question was removed from the maritime heritage resources section of the report and the subject is discussed in the context of other questions.

--- SENTENCE 4483 ---
Ratings for a number of questions depend on judgments of the "ecological integrity" within a national marine sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 4484 ---
This is because one of the foundational principles behind the establishment of sanctuaries is to protect ocean ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 4485 ---
The term ecological integrity is used to imply "the presence of naturally occurring species, populations and communities, and ecological processes functioning at appropriate rates, scales, and levels of natural variation, as well as the environmental conditions that support these attributes" (modified from the National Park Service's Vital Signs Monitoring Program).

--- SENTENCE 4486 ---
Sanctuaries have ecological integrity when they have their native components intact, including abiotic components (i.e., the physical forces and chemical elements, such as water), biotic elements (such as habitats), biodiversity (i.e., the composition and abundance of species and communities), and ecological processes (e.g., competition, predation, symbioses).

--- SENTENCE 4487 ---
For purposes of this report, the level of integrity that is judged to exist is based on the extent to which humans have altered specific components of the system, and the effect of that change on the ability of an ecosystem to resist continued change and recover from it.

--- SENTENCE 4488 ---
The statements for many questions are intended to reflect this judgment.

--- SENTENCE 4489 ---
Reference is made in the rating system to "near-pristine" conditions, for which this report would imply a status as near to an unaltered ecosystem as can reasonably be presumed to exist, recognizing that there are virtually no ecosystems on Earth completely free from human influence.

--- SENTENCE 4490 ---
Not all questions, however, use ecological integrity as a basis for judgment.

--- SENTENCE 4491 ---
One focuses on the impacts of water quality factors on human health.

--- SENTENCE 4492 ---
Two questions rate the status of keystone and key species compared with that expected in an unaltered ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 4493 ---
One rates maritime heritage resources based on their historical, archaeological, scientific, and educational value.

--- SENTENCE 4494 ---
Finally, four ask specifically about the levels of ongoing human activities (i.e., Pressures) that could affect resource condition.

--- SENTENCE 4495 ---
During workshops in which status and trends are rated, subject matter experts discuss each question and available data, literature (e.g., published scientific studies, reports), and experience associated with the topic.

--- SENTENCE 4496 ---
They then discuss the statements provided as options for judgments about status; these statements have been customized for each question.

--- SENTENCE 4497 ---
Once a particular statement is agreed upon, a color code and status rating (e.g., good, fair, poor) is

assigned.

--- SENTENCE 4498 ---
Experts can also decide that the most appropriate rating is "N/A" (i.e., the question does not apply), "Undetermined" (i.e., resource status is undetermined due to a paucity of relevant information), or "Mixed" (i.e., resource status across a number of indicators is mixed).

--- SENTENCE 4499 ---
A subsequent discussion is then held about the trend.

--- SENTENCE 4500 ---
Conditions are determined to be improving, remaining the same, or worsening in comparison to the results found in the first round of condition reports.

--- SENTENCE 4501 ---
Symbols used to indicate trends are the same for all questions: "**▲**"—conditions appear to be improving; "**▬**"—conditions do not appear to be changing; "**▼**" conditions appear to be worsening; " " —conditions appear to be mixed; and "**?**"—trend is undetermined.

--- SENTENCE 4502 ---
## *Water Quality*

#### **1.

--- SENTENCE 4503 ---
What is the eutrophic condition of sanctuary waters and how is it changing?

--- SENTENCE 4504 ---
**

Eutrophication is the accelerated production of organic matter, particularly algae, in a water body.

--- SENTENCE 4505 ---
It is usually caused by an increase in the amount of nutrients (largely nitrogen and phosphorus) being discharged to the water body.

--- SENTENCE 4506 ---
As a result of accelerated algal production, a variety of interrelated impacts may occur, including nuisance and toxic algal blooms, depleted dissolved oxygen, and loss of submerged aquatic vegetation (Bricker et al., 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4507 ---
Indicators commonly used to detect eutrophication and associated problems include nutrient concentrations, chlorophyll content, rates of water column or benthic primary production, benthic algae cover, algae bloom frequency and intensity, oxygen levels, and light penetration.

--- SENTENCE 4508 ---
Eutrophication of sanctuary waters can impact the condition of other sanctuary resources.

--- SENTENCE 4509 ---
Nutrient enrichment often leads to plankton and/or algae blooms.

--- SENTENCE 4510 ---
Blooms of benthic algae can affect benthic communities directly through space competition.

--- SENTENCE 4511 ---
Indirect effects of overgrowth and other competitive interactions (e.g., accumulation of algal-sediment mats) often lead to shifts in dominance in the benthic assemblage, oxygen depletion, etc.

--- SENTENCE 4512 ---
Disease incidence and frequency can also be affected by algae competition and changes in the chemical environment along competitive boundaries.

--- SENTENCE 4513 ---
Blooms can also affect water column conditions, including light penetration and plankton availability, which can alter pelagic food webs.

--- SENTENCE 4514 ---
HABs, some of which are exacerbated by eutrophic conditions, often affect other living resources, as biotoxins are consumed or released into the water and air, or decomposition depletes oxygen concentrations.

--- SENTENCE 4515 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                     |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Good

--- SENTENCE 4516 ---
| Eutrophication has not been documented, or does not appear to have the<br>potential to negatively affect ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4517 ---
|
| Good/Fair | Eutrophication is suspected and may degrade some attributes of ecological<br>integrity, but has not yet caused measurable degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4518 ---
|
| Fair      | Eutrophication has caused measurable but not severe degradation in some<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4519 ---
|
| Fair/Poor | Eutrophication has caused severe degradation in some but not all attributes of<br>ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4520 ---
| Eutrophication has caused severe degradation in most if not all attributes of<br>ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4521 ---
Do sanctuary waters pose risks to human health and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4522 ---
**

Human health concerns are generally aroused by evidence of contamination (usually bacterial or chemical) in bathing waters or seafood intended for consumption.

--- SENTENCE 4523 ---
They also arise when harmful algal blooms are reported or when cases of respiratory distress or other disorders attributable to harmful algal blooms increase dramatically.

--- SENTENCE 4524 ---
Any of these conditions should be considered in the course of judging the risk to humans posed by waters in a marine sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 4525 ---
Some sanctuaries may have access to specific information about beach closures and seafood contamination.

--- SENTENCE 4526 ---
In particular, beaches may be closed when criteria for water safety are exceeded.

--- SENTENCE 4527 ---
Shellfish harvesting and fishing may be prohibited when contaminant or biotoxin loads or infection rates exceed certain levels.

--- SENTENCE 4528 ---
Alternatively, seafood advisories may also be issued, recommending that people avoid or limit intake of particular types of seafood from certain areas (e.g., when ciguatera poisoning is reported).

--- SENTENCE 4529 ---
Any of these conditions, along with changing frequencies or intensities, can be important indicators of human health problems and can be characterized using the descriptions below.

--- SENTENCE 4530 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                      |
|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Good      | Water quality does not appear to have the potential to negatively affect human<br>health.

--- SENTENCE 4531 ---
|
| Good/Fair | One or more water quality indicators suggest the potential for human health<br>impacts but human health impacts have not been reported.

--- SENTENCE 4532 ---
|
| Fair      | Water quality problems have caused measurable human impacts, but effects are<br>localized and not widespread or persistent.

--- SENTENCE 4533 ---
|
| Fair/Poor | Water quality problems have caused severe impacts that are either widespread or<br>persistent.

--- SENTENCE 4534 ---
|
| Poor      | Water quality problems have caused severe, persistent, and widespread human<br>impacts.

--- SENTENCE 4535 ---
Have recent, accelerated changes in climate altered water conditions and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4536 ---
**

The purpose of this question is to capture shifts in water quality, and associated impacts on sanctuary resources, due to climate change.

--- SENTENCE 4537 ---
Though temporal changes in climate have always occurred on Earth, evidence is strong that changes over the last century have been accelerated by human activities.

--- SENTENCE 4538 ---
Indicators of climate change in sanctuary waters include water temperature, acidity, sea level, upwelling intensity and timing, storm intensity and frequency, changes in erosion and sedimentation patterns, and freshwater delivery (e.g., rainfall patterns).

--- SENTENCE 4539 ---
Climate-related changes in one or more of these indicators can impact the condition of habitats, living resources, and maritime archaeological resources in sanctuaries.

--- SENTENCE 4540 ---
Increasing water temperature has been linked to changing growth rates, reduced disease resistance, and disruptions in symbiotic relationships (e.g., bleaching on coral reefs), and changes in water temperature exposure may affect a species' resistance or the capacity to adapt to disturbances.

--- SENTENCE 4541 ---
Acidification can affect the survival and growth of organisms throughout the food web, as well as the persistence of skeletal material after death (through changes in rates of dissolution and bioerosion).

--- SENTENCE 4542 ---
Recent findings also suggest acidification impacts at sensory and behavioral levels, which can alter vitality and species interactions.

--- SENTENCE 4543 ---
Sea level change alters habitats, as well as their use and persistence.

--- SENTENCE 4544 ---
Variations in the timing and intensity of upwelling is known to change water quality through factors such as oxygen content and nutrient flow, further disrupting food webs and the natural functioning of ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 4545 ---
Changing patterns and intensities of storms alter community resistance and resilience within ecosystems that have, over long periods of time, adapted to such disturbances.

--- SENTENCE 4546 ---
Altered rates and volumes of freshwater delivery to coastal ecosystems affects salinity and turbidity regimes and can disrupt reproduction, recruitment, growth, disease incidence, phenology, and other important processes.

--- SENTENCE 4547 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                                        |
|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Good      | Climate-related changes in water conditions have not been documented or do not<br>appear to have the potential to negatively affect ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4548 ---
|
| Good/Fair | Climate-related changes are suspected and may degrade some attributes of<br>ecological integrity, but have not yet caused measurable degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4549 ---
|
| Fair      | Climate-related changes have caused measurable but not severe degradation in<br>some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4550 ---
|
| Fair/Poor | Climate-related changes have caused severe degradation in some but not all<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4551 ---
|
| Poor      | Climate-related changes have caused severe degradation in most if not all<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4552 ---
Are other stressors, individually or in combination, affecting water quality, and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4553 ---
**

The purpose of this question is to capture shifts in water quality due to anthropogenic stressors not addressed in other questions.

--- SENTENCE 4554 ---
For example, localized changes in circulation or sedimentation resulting from coastal construction or dredge spoil disposal can affect light penetration, salinity regimes, oxygen levels, productivity, waste transport, and other aspects of water quality that in turn influence the condition of habitats and living resources.

--- SENTENCE 4555 ---
Human inputs, generally in the form of contaminants from point or nonpoint sources, including fertilizers, pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and sewage, are common causes of environmental degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4556 ---
When present in the water column, any of these contaminants can affect marine life by direct contact or ingestion, or through bioaccumulation via the food chain.

--- SENTENCE 4557 ---
(Note: Over time, accumulation in sediments can sequester and concentrate contaminants.

--- SENTENCE 4558 ---
Their effects may manifest only when the sediments are resuspended during storm or other energetic events.

--- SENTENCE 4559 ---
In such cases, reports of status should be made under in the habitat/contaminants question.)

--- SENTENCE 4565 ---
What are the levels of human activities that may adversely influence water quality and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4566 ---
**

Among the human activities in or near sanctuaries that affect water quality are those involving direct discharges and spills (vessels, onshore and offshore industrial facilities, public wastewater facilities), those that contribute contaminants to groundwater, stream, river, and water control discharges (agriculture, runoff from impermeable surfaces through storm drains, conversion of land use), and those releasing airborne chemicals that subsequently deposit via particulates at sea (vessels, land-based traffic, power plants, manufacturing facilities, refineries).

--- SENTENCE 4567 ---
In addition, dredging and trawling can cause resuspension of contaminants in sediments.

--- SENTENCE 4568 ---
Many of these activities can be controlled through management actions in order to limit their impact on protected resources.

## *Habitat*

#### **6.

--- SENTENCE 4580 ---
What is the integrity of major habitat types and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4581 ---
**

Ocean habitats can be categorized in many different ways, including water column characteristics, benthic assemblages, substrate types, and structural character.

--- SENTENCE 4582 ---
There are intertidal and subtidal habitats.

--- SENTENCE 4583 ---
The water column itself is one habitat type (Federal Geographic Data Committee, 2012).

--- SENTENCE 4584 ---
There are habitats composed of substrates formed by rocks or sand that originate from purely physical processes.

--- SENTENCE 4585 ---
And, there are certain animals and plants that create, in life or after their death, substrates that attract or support other organisms (e.g., corals, kelp, beach wrack, drift algae).

--- SENTENCE 4586 ---
These are commonly called biogenic habitats.

--- SENTENCE 4587 ---
Regardless of the habitat type, change and loss of habitat is of paramount concern when it comes to protecting marine and terrestrial ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 4588 ---
Of greatest concern to sanctuaries are changes to habitats caused, either directly or indirectly, by human activities.

--- SENTENCE 4589 ---
Human activities like coastal development alter the distribution of habitat types along the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 4590 ---
Changes in water conditions in estuaries, bays, and nearshore waters can negatively affect biogenic habitat formed by submerged aquatic vegetation.

--- SENTENCE 4591 ---
Intertidal habitats can be affected for long periods by oil spills or by chronic pollutant exposure.

--- SENTENCE 4592 ---
Marine debris, such trash and lost fishing gear, can degrade the quality of many different marine habitats including beaches, subtidal benthic habitats, and the water column.

--- SENTENCE 4593 ---
Sandy seafloor and hard bottom habitats, even rocky areas several hundred meters deep, can be disturbed or destroyed by certain types of fishing gear, including bottom trawls, shellfish dredges, bottom longlines, and fish traps.

--- SENTENCE 4594 ---
Groundings, anchors, and irresponsible diving practices damage submerged reefs.

--- SENTENCE 4595 ---
Cables and pipelines disturb corridors across numerous habitat types and can be destructive if they become mobile.

--- SENTENCE 4596 ---
Integrity of biogenic habitats depends on the condition of particular living organisms.

--- SENTENCE 4597 ---
Coral, sponges, and kelp are well known examples of biogenic habitat-forming organisms.

--- SENTENCE 4598 ---
The diverse assemblages residing within these habitats depend on and interact with each other in tightly

linked food webs.

--- SENTENCE 4599 ---
They may also depend on each other for the recycling of wastes, hygiene, and the maintenance of water quality.

--- SENTENCE 4600 ---
Other communities that are dependent on biogenic habitat include intertidal communities structured by mussels, barnacles, and algae and subtidal hardbottom communities structured by bivalves, corals, or coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 4601 ---
In numerous open ocean areas drift algal mats provide food and cover for juvenile fish, turtles, and other organisms.

--- SENTENCE 4602 ---
The integrity of these communities depends largely on the condition of species that provide structure for them.

--- SENTENCE 4603 ---
This question is intended to address acute or chronic changes in both the extent of habitat available to organisms and the quality of that habitat, whether non-living or biogenic.

--- SENTENCE 4604 ---
It asks about the quality of habitats compared to those that would be expected in near-pristine conditions (see definition above).

--- SENTENCE 4605 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                                          |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Good      | Habitats are in near-pristine condition.

--- SENTENCE 4606 ---
|
| Good/Fair | Selected habitat loss or alteration is suspected and may degrade some attributes<br>of ecological integrity, but has not yet caused measurable degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4607 ---
|
| Fair      | Selected habitat loss or alteration has caused measurable but not severe<br>degradation in some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4608 ---
|
| Fair/Poor | Selected habitat loss or alteration has caused severe degradation in some but not<br>all attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4609 ---
|
| Poor      | Selected habitat loss or alteration has caused severe degradation in most if not<br>all attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4610 ---
What are contaminant concentrations in sanctuary habitats and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4611 ---
**

Habitat contaminants result from the introduction of unnatural levels of chemicals or other harmful material into the environment.

--- SENTENCE 4612 ---
Contaminants may be introduced through discrete entry locations, called point sources (e.g., rivers, pipes, or ships) and those with diffuse origins, called nonpoint sources (e.g., groundwater and urban runoff).

--- SENTENCE 4613 ---
Chemical contaminants themselves can be very specific, as in a spill from a containment facility or vessel grounding, or a complex mix, as with urban runoff.

--- SENTENCE 4614 ---
Familiar chemical contaminants include pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and nutrients.

--- SENTENCE 4615 ---
Contaminants may also arrive in the form of materials that alter turbidity or smother plants or animals, therefore affecting metabolism and production.

--- SENTENCE 4616 ---
This question is focused on risks posed primarily by contaminants within benthic formations, such as soft sediments, hard bottoms, or structure-forming organisms (see notes below).

--- SENTENCE 4617 ---
Not only are contaminants within benthic formations consumed or absorbed by benthic fauna, but resuspension due to benthic disturbance makes the contaminants available to water column

organisms.

--- SENTENCE 4618 ---
In both cases contaminants can be passed upwards through the food chain.

--- SENTENCE 4619 ---
While the contaminants of most common concern to sanctuaries are generally pesticides, hydrocarbons, and nutrients, the specific concerns of individual sanctuaries may differ substantially.

--- SENTENCE 4620 ---
Notes: 1) Contaminants in the water column addressed in the water quality section of this report should be cited, but details need not be repeated here; 2) many consider noise a pollutant, but in the interest of focusing here on more traditional forms of habitat degradation caused by contaminants, ONMS recommends addressing the impacts of acoustic pollution within the living resource section, most likely as it impacts key species.

--- SENTENCE 4621 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                              |  |  |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|
| Good      | Contaminants have not been documented, or do not appear to have the potential<br>to negatively affect ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4622 ---
| Good/Fair | Selected contaminants are suspected and may degrade some attributes of<br>ecological integrity, but have not yet caused measurable degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4623 ---
|  |  |
| Fair      | Selected contaminants have caused measurable but not severe degradation in<br>some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4624 ---
|  |  |
| Fair/Poor | Selected contaminants have caused severe degradation in some but not all<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4625 ---
| Poor      | Selected contaminants have caused severe degradation in most if not all<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

### **8.

--- SENTENCE 4627 ---
What are the levels of human activities that may adversely influence habitats and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4628 ---
**

Human activities that degrade habitat quality do so by affecting structural (physical), biological, oceanographic, acoustic, or chemical characteristics of the habitat.

--- SENTENCE 4629 ---
Structural impacts, such as removal or mechanical alteration of habitat, can result from various fishing methods (e.g., trawls, traps, dredges, longlines, and even hook-and-line in some habitats), dredging of channels and harbors, dumping dredge spoil, grounding of vessels, anchoring, laying pipelines and cables, installing offshore structures, discharging drill cuttings, dragging tow cables, and placing artificial reefs.

--- SENTENCE 4630 ---
Removal or alteration of critical biological components of habitats can occur due to several of the above activities, most notably trawling, groundings, and cable drags.

--- SENTENCE 4631 ---
Marine debris, particularly in large quantities (e.g., lost gill nets and other types of fishing gear), can degrade both biological and structural habitat components.

--- SENTENCE 4632 ---
Changes in water circulation often occur when channels are dredged, fill is added, coastlines are armored or other construction takes place.

--- SENTENCE 4633 ---
Management actions such as beach wrack removal or sand replenishment on high public-use beaches, may impact the integrity of the natural ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 4634 ---
Alterations in circulations can lead to changes in food delivery, waste removal, water quality

(e.g., salinity, clarity and sedimentation), recruitment patterns, and a host of other ecological processes.

--- SENTENCE 4635 ---
Chemical alterations most commonly occur following spills and can have both acute and chronic impacts.

--- SENTENCE 4636 ---
Many of these activities can be controlled through management actions in order to limit their impact on protected resources.

--- SENTENCE 4637 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                          |  |  |  |
|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|--|
| Good      |

--- SENTENCE 4638 ---
Few or no activities occur that are likely to negatively affect habitat quality.

--- SENTENCE 4639 ---
|  |  |  |
| Good/Fair |

--- SENTENCE 4640 ---
Some potentially harmful activities exist, but they have not been shown to<br>degrade habitat quality.

--- SENTENCE 4641 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4642 ---
| Fair      | Selected activities have caused measurable resource impacts, but effects are<br>localized and not widespread or persistent.

--- SENTENCE 4643 ---
|  |  |  |
| Fair/Poor | Selected activities have caused severe impacts that are either widespread or<br>persistent.

--- SENTENCE 4644 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4645 ---
| Poor      | Selected activities have caused severe, persistent, and widespread impacts.

--- SENTENCE 4646 ---
|  |  |  |

## *Living Resources*

#### **9.

--- SENTENCE 4647 ---
What is the status of keystone and foundation species and how is it changing?

--- SENTENCE 4648 ---
**

Certain species are defined as "keystone" within ecosystems, meaning they are species on which the persistence of a large number of other species in the ecosystem depends (Paine, 1966).

--- SENTENCE 4649 ---
They are the pillars of community stability (among other things, they strongly affect both resistance and resilience) and their contribution to ecosystem function is disproportionate to their numerical abundance or biomass.

--- SENTENCE 4650 ---
Their impact is therefore important at the community or ecosystem level.

--- SENTENCE 4651 ---
Keystone species are often called "ecosystem engineers" and can include habitat creators (e.g., corals, kelp), predators that control food web structure (e.g., Humboldt squid, sea otters), herbivores that regulate benthic recruitment (e.g., certain sea urchins), and those involved in critical symbiotic relationships (e.g., cleaning or co-habitating species).

--- SENTENCE 4652 ---
"Foundation" species are single species that define much of the structure of a community by creating locally stable conditions for other species, and by modulating and stabilizing fundamental ecosystem processes (Dayton, 1972).

--- SENTENCE 4653 ---
These are typically dominant biomass producers in an ecosystem and strongly influence the abundance and biomass of many other species.

--- SENTENCE 4654 ---
Examples include krill and other zooplankton, kelp, forage fish, such as rockfish anchovy, sardine, and coral.

--- SENTENCE 4655 ---
Foundation species exhibit similar control over ecosystems as keystone species, but their high abundance distinguishes them.

--- SENTENCE 4656 ---
Changes in either keystone or foundation species may transform ecosystem structure through disappearances of or dramatic increases in the abundance of dependent species.

--- SENTENCE 4657 ---
Not only do the abundances of keystone and foundation species affect ecosystem integrity, but measures of condition can also be important to determining the likelihood that these species will persist and continue to provide vital ecosystem functions.

--- SENTENCE 4658 ---
Measures of condition may include growth rates, fecundity, recruitment, age-specific survival, contaminant loads, pathologies (e.g., disease incidence, tumors, deformities), the presence and abundance of critical symbionts, or parasite loads.

--- SENTENCE 4659 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                                                              |  |  |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|
| Good      |

--- SENTENCE 4660 ---
The status of keystone and foundation species appears to reflect near-pristine<br>conditions and may promote ecological integrity (full community development and<br>function).

--- SENTENCE 4661 ---
|  |  |
| Good/Fair |

--- SENTENCE 4662 ---
The status of keystone or foundation species may preclude full community<br>development and function, but has not yet led to measurable degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4663 ---
|  |  |
| Fair      |

--- SENTENCE 4664 ---
The status of keystone or foundation species suggests measurable but not<br>severe degradation in some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4665 ---
|  |  |
| Fair/Poor

--- SENTENCE 4666 ---
The status of keystone and foundation species suggests severe degradation in<br>some but not all attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4667 ---
| The status of keystone and foundation species suggests severe degradation in<br>most if not all attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4668 ---
|  |  |

#### **10.

--- SENTENCE 4669 ---
What is the status of other focal species and how is it changing?

--- SENTENCE 4670 ---
**

This question targets other species of particular interest from the perspective of sanctuary management.

--- SENTENCE 4671 ---
These "focal species" may not be abundant or provide high value to ecosystem function, but their presence and health is important for the provision of other services, whether conservation, economic, or strategic.

--- SENTENCE 4672 ---
Examples include species targeted for special protection (e.g., threatened or endangered species), species for which specific regulations exist to minimize perturbations from human disturbance (e.g., touching corals, riding manta rays or whale sharks, disturbing white sharks, disturbing nesting birds), or indicator species (e.g., common murres as indicators of oil pollution).

--- SENTENCE 4673 ---
This category could also include so-called "flagship" species, which include charismatic or iconic species associated with specific locations, ecosystems or are in need of specific management actions, are highly popular and attract visitors or business, have marketing appeal, or represent rallying points for conservation action (e.g., humpback and blue whales, Dungeness crab).

--- SENTENCE 4674 ---
Status of these other focal species can be assessed through measures of abundance, relative abundance, or condition, as described for keystone species.

--- SENTENCE 4675 ---
In contrast to keystone and foundation species, however, the impact of changes in the abundance or condition of focal species is more likely to be observed at the population or individual level, and less likely to result in ecosystem or community effects.

--- SENTENCE 4676 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                       |  |  |  |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|--|
| Good      | Selected focal species appear to reflect near-pristine conditions.

--- SENTENCE 4677 ---

|

--- SENTENCE 4678 ---
Good/Fair | Reduced abundances in selected focal species are suspected but have not yet<br>been measured.

--- SENTENCE 4679 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4680 ---
| Fair      | Selected focal species are at reduced levels, but recovery is possible.

--- SENTENCE 4681 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4682 ---
| Fair/Poor | Selected focal species are at substantially reduced levels, and prospects for<br>recovery are uncertain.

--- SENTENCE 4683 ---
|  |  |  |

| Poor      | Selected focal species are at severely reduced levels, and recovery is unlikely.

#### **11.

--- SENTENCE 4686 ---
What is the status of non-indigenous species and how is it changing?

--- SENTENCE 4687 ---
**

This question allows sanctuaries to report on the threat posed and impacts caused by nonindigenous species.

--- SENTENCE 4688 ---
Also called alien, exotic, non-native, or introduced species, these are animals or plants living outside their native distributional range, having arrived there by human activity, either deliberate or accidental.

--- SENTENCE 4689 ---
Activities that commonly facilitate invasions include vessel ballast water exchange, restaurant waste disposal, and trade in exotic species for aquaria.

--- SENTENCE 4690 ---
In some cases, climate change has resulted in water temperature fluctuations that have allowed range extensions for certain species.

--- SENTENCE 4691 ---
Non-indigenous species that have damaging effects on ecosystems are called "invasive" species.

--- SENTENCE 4692 ---
Some can be extremely destructive, and because of this potential, non-indigenous species are usually considered problematic and warrant rapid response after invasion.

--- SENTENCE 4693 ---
For those that become established, however, their impacts can sometimes be assessed by quantifying changes in affected native species.

--- SENTENCE 4694 ---
In some cases, the presence of a species alone constitutes a significant threat (e.g., certain invasive algae and invertebrates).

--- SENTENCE 4695 ---
In other cases, impacts have been measured, and may or may not significantly affect ecosystem integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4696 ---
Evaluating the potential impacts of non-indigenous species may require consideration of how climate change may enhance the recruitment, establishment, and/or severity of impacts of nonindigenous species.

--- SENTENCE 4697 ---
Altered temperature or salinity conditions, for example, may facilitate the range expansion, establishment and survival of non-indigenous species while stressing native species, thus reducing ecosystem resistance.

--- SENTENCE 4698 ---
This will also make management response decisions difficult, as changing conditions will make new areas even more hospitable for nonindigenous species targeted for removal.

--- SENTENCE 4699 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                                   |  |  |  |
|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|--|
| Good      | Non-indigenous species are not suspected to be present or do not appear to<br>affect ecological integrity (full community development and function).

--- SENTENCE 4700 ---
|  |  |  |
| Good/Fair | Non-indigenous species are present and may preclude full community<br>development and function, but have not yet caused measurable degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4701 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4702 ---
| Fair      | Non-indigenous species have caused measurable but not severe degradation in<br>some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4703 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4704 ---
| Fair/Poor | Non-indigenous species have caused severe degradation in some but not all<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4705 ---
|  |  |  |

--- SENTENCE 4706 ---
| Poor      | Non-indigenous species have caused severe degradation in most if not all<br>attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4707 ---

#### **12.

--- SENTENCE 4708 ---
What is the status of biodiversity and how is it changing?

--- SENTENCE 4709 ---
**

Broadly defined, biodiversity refers to the variety of life on Earth, and includes the diversity of ecosystems, species and genes, and the ecological processes that support them

--- SENTENCE 4710 ---
[Convention on Biological Diversity\)](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/exit.html?url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.cbd.int%2Fconvention%2Farticles%2F%3Fa%3Dcbd-02).

--- SENTENCE 4711 ---
This question is intended as an overall assessment of biodiversity compared to that expected in a near-pristine system (one as near to an unaltered ecosystem as people can reasonably expect, given that there are virtually no ecosystems completely free from human influence).

--- SENTENCE 4712 ---
It may include consideration of measures of biodiversity (usually aspects of species richness and evenness) and the status of functional interactions between species (e.g., trophic relationships and symbioses).

--- SENTENCE 4713 ---
Intact ecosystems require that all parts not only exist, but that they function together, resulting in natural symbioses, competition, predator-prey relationships, and redundancies (e.g., multiple species capable of performing the same ecological role).

--- SENTENCE 4714 ---
Intact structural elements, processes, and natural spatial and temporal variability are essential characteristics of community integrity and provide a natural adaptive capacity through resistance and resilience.

--- SENTENCE 4715 ---
The response to this question will depend largely on changes in biodiversity that have occurred as a result of human activities that cause depletion, extirpation or extinction, illness, contamination, disturbance, and changes in environmental quality.

--- SENTENCE 4716 ---
Examples include collection of organisms, excessive visitation (e.g., trampling), industrial activities, coastal development, pollution, activities creating noise in the marine environment, and those that promote the spread of non-indigenous species.

--- SENTENCE 4717 ---
Loss of species or changing relative abundances can be mediated through selective mortality or changing fecundity, either of which can influence ecosystem shifts.

--- SENTENCE 4718 ---
Human activities of particular interest in this regard are commercial and recreational harvesting.

--- SENTENCE 4719 ---
Both can be highly selective and disruptive activities, with a limited number of targeted species, and often result in the removal of high proportions of the populations, as well as large amounts of untargeted

species (bycatch).

--- SENTENCE 4720 ---
Extraction removes biomass from the ecosystem, reducing its availability to other consumers.

--- SENTENCE 4721 ---
When too much extraction occurs, ecosystem stability can be compromised through long-term disruptions to food web structure, as well as changes in species relationships and related functions and services (e.g. cleaning symbioses).

--- SENTENCE 4722 ---
This has been defined as "ecologically unsustainable" extraction (Zabel et al., 2003).

--- SENTENCE 4723 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                                               |  |  |
|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|
| Good      | Biodiversity appears to reflect near-pristine conditions and promotes ecological<br>integrity (full community development and function).

--- SENTENCE 4724 ---
| Good/Fair | Selected biodiversity loss or change is suspected and may preclude full<br>community development and function, but has not yet caused measurable<br>degradation.

--- SENTENCE 4725 ---
|  |  |
| Fair      | Selected biodiversity loss or change has caused measurable but not severe<br>degradation in some attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4726 ---
|  |  |
| Fair/Poor | Selected biodiversity loss or change has caused severe degradation in some but<br>not all attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4727 ---
| Poor      | Selected biodiversity loss or change has caused severe degradation in most if not<br>all attributes of ecological integrity.

--- SENTENCE 4728 ---
|  |  |

### **13.

--- SENTENCE 4729 ---
What are the levels of human activities that may adversely influence living resources and how are they changing?

--- SENTENCE 4730 ---
**

Human activities that degrade the condition of living resources do so by causing a loss or reduction of one or more species, by disrupting critical life stages, by impairing various physiological processes, or by promoting the introduction of non-indigenous species or pathogens.

--- SENTENCE 4731 ---
(Note: Activities that impact habitat and water quality may also affect living resources.

--- SENTENCE 4732 ---
These activities are dealt with in the following human activity questions, and some may be repeated here as they also directly affect living resources).

--- SENTENCE 4733 ---
For most sanctuaries, recreational or commercial fishing and collecting have direct effects on animal or plant populations, either through removal or injury of organisms.

--- SENTENCE 4734 ---
Related to this, lost fishing gear can cause extended periods of loss for some species through entanglement and "ghost fishing."

--- SENTENCE 4735 ---
In addition, some fishing techniques are size-selective, resulting in impacts to particular life stages.

--- SENTENCE 4736 ---
High levels of visitor use in some places also cause localized depletion, particularly in intertidal areas or on shallow coral reefs, where collecting and trampling can be chronic problems.

--- SENTENCE 4737 ---
Mortality and injury to living resources has also been documented from cable drags (e.g., towed barge operations), dumping spoil or drill cuttings, vessel groundings, or repeated anchoring.

--- SENTENCE 4738 ---
Contamination caused by acute or chronic spills or increased sedimentation to nearshore ecosystems from road developments in watersheds (including runoff from coastal construction

or highly built coastal areas), discharges by vessels, or municipal and industrial facilities can make habitats unsuitable for recruitment or other ecosystem services (e.g., as nurseries or spawning grounds).

--- SENTENCE 4739 ---
And while coastal armoring and construction can increase the availability of surfaces suitable for hard bottom species, the activity may disrupt recruitment patterns for other species (e.g., intertidal soft bottom animals), and natural habitat may be lost.

--- SENTENCE 4740 ---
Oil spills (and spill response actions), discharges, and contaminants released from sediments (e.g., by dredging and dumping) can all cause physiological impairment and tissue contamination.

--- SENTENCE 4741 ---
Such activities can affect all life stages by direct mortality, reducing fecundity, reducing disease resistance, loss as prey and disruption of predator-prey relationships, and increasing susceptibility to predation.

--- SENTENCE 4742 ---
Furthermore, bioaccumulation results in some contaminants moving upward through the food chain, disproportionately affecting certain species.

--- SENTENCE 4743 ---
Activities that promote the introduction of non-indigenous species include bilge discharges and ballast water exchange, commercial shipping and vessel transportation.

--- SENTENCE 4744 ---
Intentional or accidental releases of aquarium fish and plants can also lead to introductions of non-indigenous species.

--- SENTENCE 4745 ---
Many of these activities are controlled through management actions in order to limit their impact on protected resources.

--- SENTENCE 4746 ---
| Rating    | Status Description                                                                                                                 |  |  |  |
|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|--|
| Good      |

--- SENTENCE 4747 ---
Few or no activities occur that are likely to negatively affect living resource<br>quality.

--- SENTENCE 4748 ---
|  |  |  |
| Good/Fair |

--- SENTENCE 4749 ---
Some potentially harmful activities exist, but they have not been shown to<br>degrade living resource quality.

--- SENTENCE 4750 ---

--- SENTENCE 4751 ---
| Fair      | Selected activities have caused measurable living resource impacts, but effects<br>are localized and not widespread or persistent.

--- SENTENCE 4753 ---
|  |  |  |

| Poor      | Selected activities have caused severe, persistent, and widespread impacts.
